full_text: ATLANTA, GA - OCTOBER 25: Atlanta place kicker Nick Folk (6) attempts a field goal during the NFL game between the San Francisco 49ers and the Atlanta Falcons on October 25th, 2026 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images After Nick Folk missed for the first time since 2017 inside 40 yards, dropping his season field goal percentage to 72.2%, it seemed very likely the Falcons would move on. Now they’ve reportedly done so, signing away Baltimore Ravens practice squad kicker Jake Moody to replace him. The Falcons gave Folk a two-year deal in the offseason, banking on a player who led the NFL in field goal percentage in 2023, 2024, and 2025 reversing their kicking woes. Instead, Father Time finally wind sprinted to catch up with Folk, who went 13/18 on field goals and 17/18 on extra points through nine weeks in Atlanta, with some truly costly misses along the way highlighted by Week 1 struggles against Pittsburgh and the chip shot miss last Sunday against the Bengals. We’ll wish him well, but this may be the end of the road for a kicker with a long and storied career who is now 42 years old and declining. Sources: The #Falcons are releasing K Nick Folk, who was 13/18 on FGs this season. Jake Moody is the new kicker in Atlanta. https://t.co/Iqi0PKghTu pic.twitter.com/l4R6jsc0Si — Jordan Schultz (@Schultz_Report) November 10, 2026 Moody, meanwhile, will get a chance to audition for the Falcons’ kicking job going forward. He’s had a turbulent career as a former third round pick for the 49ers in 2023, hitting 84% of his field goal tries in year one but struggling badly in year two to the tune of a 72% hit rate. After he went just one-for-three in the first game of the 2025 season with the 49ers, he’s bounced around between the Bears (8/9), Commanders (10/11), and Ravens this year (1/1 from 53 yards). The early career struggles seem to have evened out for Moody, who has always had the leg to be a good kicker, and he was just hoping for an opportunity to prove he’s more than a fill-in option or practice squad elevation. He’ll get it for the Falcons, who would love to get an under-30 kicker who can can deliver consistent performance after the past few frustrating years at the position. Congratulations to Moody, and may he be the kicker the Falcons have been looking for.

title: The Falcons aren’t giving up on 2026 because they exist in the NFC South
summary: After the Falcons traded away Jessie Bates yesterday, Kevin Stefanski had to get in front of microphones and talk to reporters about two seemingly contrary thoughts: The team is not “punting” on the 2026 season, in his words, but they couldn’t pass up the chance to trade one of their most impactful defenders nine weeks […]
full_text: After the Falcons traded away Jessie Bates yesterday, Kevin Stefanski had to get in front of microphones and talk to reporters about two seemingly contrary thoughts: The team is not “punting” on the 2026 season, in his words, but they couldn’t pass up the chance to trade one of their most impactful defenders nine weeks into that season. Those two warring thoughts, captured well in Tori McElhaney’s piece for AtlantaFalcons.com , seem difficult to square when you first look at them. How could trading Jessie Bates not undercut Atlanta’s 2026 fortunes? A team looking to take full advantage of a weak NFC South should be trying to acquire talent, not sell, right? Right? But spending a little more time with the seeming divide between selling off and contending reveals a simple truth: Their division is a gallon jug of steamed butt. If we’re being real about what’s happening here, the Falcons aren’t quitting on 2026 because it’s impossible to quit on 2026 in the NFC South. They are one game behind the Carolina Panthers, thanks to a head-to-head tiebreaker, and just a half game behind the New Orleans Saints. It’s not completely outlandish to suggest seven wins could actually earn the divisional title this year, and the Falcons are certainly good enough in their best weeks to win four out of their next eight games with matchups against the Browns, Commanders, diminished Lions, and rest of the NFC South still on the docket. If they continue to sell, as Carl Dukes at 92.9 suggested they would , it does nothing to change the fact that they’re still a team with some promising pieces and the same number of wins as everyone else in the division, and they have young players they wouldn’t mind getting a look at dotting the roster. That’s certainly true at safety, where Sydney Brown, Billy Bowman Jr., and DeMarcco Hellams could all be in the mix for snaps. It could prove true at inside linebacker, where the Falcons have been getting plenty from Kendal Daniels and Harold Perkins Jr. and may be willing to move Divine Deablo. It might be true at tackle, where the Falcons could potentially move Jawaan Taylor or even Jake Matthews if they get a really interesting offer and turn to Mike Jerrell, Cameron Williams, or Ethan Onianwa, though the prospect of Michael Penix Jr. getting pressured even more frequently is not an appealing one. And so on. For a team that is sitting on the highest projected cap space of any team in 2027 and now has two second round picks and eight selections overall, the prospect of continuing to stock resources to truly remake this team is an appealing one. Ian Cunningham didn’t have the draft capital to remake this team in one offseason and spent free agency rummaging around for appealing veteran on short-term deals, both to give a new coaching staff fresh faces and talent to work with, but to avoid making long-term investments the team could not easily pivot away from in 2027. They locked up the players they definitely want around for next year and can otherwise take off in any direction they please next year to give Kevin Stefanski and company a foundation that’s truly theirs, and Cunningham a roster that truly bears his philosophy. We’ve bandied about the term transformative for many offseasons in recent years, but 2027 has the potential to be that sort of year the way 2023, 2024, and 2025 were not. Viewed through the team’s obvious affinity for the near future, the deal for Bates makes a lot of sense; you’re not going to get a second round pick and change for a nearly 30-year-old safety on an expiring deal very often. It has a very apparent short-term cost given that nobody in line to replace him is Jessie Bates , an aging but still terrific safety and team captain, but this team’s modest 2026 ceiling was obviously only so high with him. Losing Bates makes the job tougher for Jeff Ulbrich and the defense, but the sledding was already difficult and the Falcons can bring numbers to bear at their new safety vacancy. It was a price the Falcons were willing to pay for a brighter future, and we should not be surprised to see them pay a price like that again before the deadline comes and goes. And they can do so with Stefanski insisting they’re not punting the season and meaning it, because all it will take is a couple of unexpected wins in the next few weeks for the Falcons to stay afloat. They still have the nucleus of their offense, young talent up front and in the secondary, and a coaching staff still trying to figure out how to squeeze more out of this roster all working to win, and they’re unlikely to blow any huge holes in the side of a team that does not look considerably worse than the flailing Panthers (who fired their defensive coordinator), Saints (who barely beat the Browns and seem to be a two game skid away from firing their head coach), and Buccaneers (who just sank a ton of money into Baker Mayfield just in time to see him shrivel into a raisin). It’s having your cake and eating it too, as Terry Fontenot once said , and if the cake isn’t very delicious right now there’s at least a specter of a more delicious one on the horizon. The Falcons aren’t quitting on the NFC South any time soon, in other words, even if they keep selling off today. The state of the division ensures that even a diminished Falcons team is likely going to be relevant for weeks to come.

title: We asked, you answered: Ravens should sell at deadline
summary: The Baltimore Ravens have been buyers so far this season, acquiring center Cam Jurgens from the Philadelphia Eagles in October and quarterback Jacoby Brissett from the Arizona Cardinals last week. But the Ravens’ 2026 season seems unlikely to turn around. The 4-5 squad now has a 7.5-win over/under and +560 odds to make the playoffs […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - FEBRUARY 24: Eric DeCosta of the Baltimore Ravens speaks during a press conference at the 2026 NFL Scouting Combine on February 24, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens have been buyers so far this season, acquiring center Cam Jurgens from the Philadelphia Eagles in October and quarterback Jacoby Brissett from the Arizona Cardinals last week. But the Ravens’ 2026 season seems unlikely to turn around. The 4-5 squad now has a 7.5-win over/under and +560 odds to make the playoffs ( via FanDuel Sportsbook ). 87% of fans think general manager Eric DeCosta should sell before Tuesday’s trade deadline, according to last week’s SB Nation Reacts survey, including a 57% majority who think an aggressive sale is warranted. Reasonable minds can disagree on some of Baltimore’s borderline core players, but three are irrefutably foundational: Lamar Jackson, Zay Flowers, and Kyle Hamilton. Players like Roquan Smith, Derrick Henry and Ronnie Stanley are signed through next season, but they may not be part of the team’s long-term plans. Here’s one out of left field: Nate Wiggins. The 23-year-old is allowing 11.1 yards per completion and 6.1 yards per target, both career-bests but still middling among starting cornerbacks. There was optimism about his development under Jesse Minter and his staff, but Wiggins’ strengths as a press-man corner may not be an optimal fit in Minter’s zone-heavy scheme. Is he going to be worth a high-end contract in a cornerback market that has exploded in the last year? If not, he could be a sneaky trade candidate. His fifth-year option is currently projected to be an affordable $14.25 million (via OverTheCap), making him an attractive short- and long-term addition to another team’s secondary. Teams are always more desperate around the deadline, especially for one of the NFL’s most important and often-injured positions. Of course, the Ravens’ remaining hope for Lamar Jackson to return and propel a playoff run will dissuade them from moving starters like Wiggins unless a truly ludicrous offer comes in. Adding another player at this point would seem like a mistake , unless DeCosta can dig up the kind of deal he normally swings in the offseason. It should be a quiet Tuesday in Baltimore.
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: Ravens news: Eric DeCosta gets mixed grades for Jacoby Brissett trade
summary: Welcome back to Loose Feathers, a regular round-up of the latest news and analysis about the Baltimore Ravens. In today’s edition, we cover a weak trade market for some of the Ravens’ veterans, grades for Eric DeCosta’s acquisition of Jacoby Brissett, and an assessment of first-year offensive coordinator Declan Doyle, Let’s dive in: ‘No real […]
full_text: Nov 1, 2026; Arlington, Texas, USA; Arizona Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett (7) walks off the field after the game against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Jerome Miron-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Welcome back to Loose Feathers, a regular round-up of the latest news and analysis about the Baltimore Ravens. In today’s edition, we cover a weak trade market for some of the Ravens’ veterans, grades for Eric DeCosta’s acquisition of Jacoby Brissett, and an assessment of first-year offensive coordinator Declan Doyle, Let’s dive in: ‘No real market’ for Stanley, Andrews, Humphrey Apologies to the Ravens fans hoping to flip some of the team’s highly-paid, underperforming veterans for draft picks at the deadline. If Baltimore is holding out any hope of getting Lamar Jackson back, they will not trade away his left tackle, and neither Andrews nor Humphrey can be seen as upgrades right now. All three were listed under “no real market” in Jeff Zrebiec’s recent trade deadline round-up. One name remains: Roquan Smith. His contract seems untenable heading into the offseason, but another team could be interested in upgrading their linebacker corps this season. Getting rid of his future salary could help Baltimore’s tight future cap picture and maybe even free up the money to re-sign Trenton Simpson. Some would even argue that a Simpson-Teddye Buchanan duo might actually be an improvement over Smith’s up-and-down (mostly down) play this year. But the Ravens love Smith. They loved him coming out of Georgia in 2018, and they loved him enough in Chicago to send a second-round pick to the Bears. And again, Jackson is still in the picture, albeit on the margins. With no clarity to be had before Tuesday’s deadline, Smith seems likely to stay put. It’s worth noting that trading Smith might be less of an option in the offseason. Linebackers tend to have more value during the season when teams are desperate to make up for injuries and/or push all-in. But in the offseason, teams will have more (and cheaper) options at linebacker, allowing them to focus on premium positions instead. The same is true of running back. This might be the best time to trade Smith and Derrick Henry, but the Ravens will not pull the trigger. The Ravens should be sellers at the trade deadline. What do they actually have to offer? – Jeff Zrebiec (The Athletic) It’s hard to say whether there will be any interest in Smith. He’s still an effective player, but he’s 29 now, he’s not making the same number of impact plays and he still has another year left on a big-money contract. A purge of some veteran defensive players seems overdue, and moving on from Smith would save them $8 million in cap space, which would come in handy this offseason. However, shipping off the team’s vocal leader and defensive signal-caller could make it seem like the Ravens are waiving the white flag on the season. They probably wouldn’t get much in return, either. Ravens get mixed grades for Jacoby Brissett trades Jacoby Brissett trade grade: Ravens try to salvage season; Cardinals improve draft capital – Daniel Popper (The Athletic) Ravens grade: C I’m mostly unmoved by this deal. Brissett does give first-year coach Jesse Minter and offensive coordinator Declan Doyle a higher floor on offense. Still, it’s hard to see the Ravens contending in any meaningful capacity, especially with the disappointing way Minter’s defense is playing. General manager Eric DeCosta gave up marginal draft capital, so it’s a fine bet to try and salvage something from a season slipping away. NFL trade deadline grades: Deals for Jordan Davis, Jessie Bates III, Andre Cisco – Ben Solak and Seth Walder (ESPN) Ravens grade: B+ The Ravens lost 33-10 to the Jaguars on Thursday night with Fagnano (and also some Derrick Henry in the Wildcat) at quarterback. In all likelihood, Baltimore’s season is over with Jackson currently on injured reserve and the team at 4-5. Ravens coach Jesse Minter has said Jackson’s injury is “potentially” season-ending. But Brissett gives the team at least a sliver of hope of staying afloat long enough to hand the reins back to Jackson with a shot at the playoffs. But make no mistake, those chances are extremely slim. Even knowing Brissett is about to take over at QB (and assuming Jackson has, say, a 30% chance of coming back in games starting in Week 14, ESPN’s Football Power Index gives Baltimore only a 3% chance of reaching the playoffs. If Jackson is indeed able to come back, that number goes up, but it’s still a long shot. The cost here is low. By ESPN’s draft pick valuations, the swap works out to the equivalent of an early sixth-round pick. Considering the team’s upside if it does get Jackson back, I think that is easily worth it for Baltimore. Jesse Minter optimistic regarding Kyle Hamilton, Nate Wiggins injuries News & Notes: Jesse Minter Gives Injury Update on Kyle Hamilton – Clifton Brown (BaltimoreRavens.c0m) Head Coach Jesse Minter gave a positive update Monday on All-Pro safety Kyle Hamilton, who left Thursday night’s game against the Jacksonville Jaguars with a hip injury. “I think everything looks fairly good,” Minter said. “We’ll find out as the guys come back in tomorrow (Tuesday). But I wouldn’t expect that to be something where … hopefully he doesn’t miss time.” Minter was also optimistic about cornerback Nate Wiggins (illness) and safety Jaylinn Hawkins (knee) returning to action this week. Wiggins did not play against the Jaguars, while Hawkins has missed the last three games. “There’s definitely optimism there,” Minter said regarding Hawkins rejoining practice. “I think (Nate) will be okay. It was an unfortunate timing of an illness.”

title: The quantitative proof of Buffalo Bills defense making strides
summary: The Buffalo Bills have allowed 16 total points the past two games, but the unit has certainly faced lesser competition at quarterback. How much should we take from Buffalo’s recent defensive efforts? Is it all a mirage because they faced one snap of Lamar Jackson, only a few attempts from Tyler Huntley, then Joey Fagnano, […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills have allowed 16 total points the past two games, but the unit has certainly faced lesser competition at quarterback. How much should we take from Buffalo’s recent defensive efforts? Is it all a mirage because they faced one snap of Lamar Jackson, only a few attempts from Tyler Huntley, then Joey Fagnano, Carson Wentz, and Max Brosmer? Or is Buffalo really onto something defensively? These type of questions are precisely why I created Defensive Impact on Passing (DIP) . I introduced the new metric a few weeks ago, and if you missed that article, here’s how I can summarize DIP — it measures how well a defense performs against opposing quarterbacks relative to how those same quarterbacks perform against other defenses on their schedule. Pretty straightforward right? Baked into DIP is the exclusion of garbage time, and, like all EPA-based defensive stats, a negative figure is better. Also, quarterbacks need at least 30 attempts against other opponents to be counted toward a defense’s DIP. Here are the full DIP rankings after Week 9: You can see the Bills defense has moved all the way up to 15th in DIP. Buffalo’s unit made a steady climb after the first month or so of the season. It was 20th after Week 8 and 23rd through Week 6. And considering Buffalo’s current DIP placement, here’s where I land on what we can take from the club’s defensive efforts in Weeks 8 and 9 — for as much as the Bills defense was likely “helped” by low-level quarterback play these past two weeks it was close to equally as “hurt” by top-level quarterbacks it played in the first month-ish of the season. The analysis has to go both ways. And from that chart, you’ll notice that the DIP of the Bills defense is actually now into the negatives. That means, opposing pass games are actually performing slightly worse against the Bills than in their other games right now. That in an of itself is an encouraging development for a defense that was universally panned in the first six contests before the bye week. This quantitative truth feels incredible too — Buffalo’s defense is fifth in the AFC in DIP right now. Now, this metric only measures opposing pass games on a per dropback basis. Scrambles are counted. But there’s nothing regarding the opposition’s run game built into this stat whatsoever. In today’s NFL, efficiently passing and stopping the pass remain most vital. And through DIP we know, with quarterback — and overall pass game — competition being considered, the Bills defense is now playing respectably.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Buffalo Bills make history in 23-6 win over Minnesota Vikings
summary: For a while Monday night, the Buffalo Bills and Minnesota Vikings seemed to be competing to see which offense could frustrate its fans the most.  Neither team could get much going, and Josh Allen wasn’t doing much to hide his irritation. Playing without both his starting left tackle and left guard as Dion Dawkins and […]
full_text: For a while Monday night, the Buffalo Bills and Minnesota Vikings seemed to be competing to see which offense could frustrate its fans the most. Neither team could get much going, and Josh Allen wasn’t doing much to hide his irritation. Playing without both his starting left tackle and left guard as Dion Dawkins and Alec Anderson watched from the sidelines, Allen spent far too much time trying to escape a Minnesota defense that was coming through Buffalo’s offensive line like it had been invited. Fortunately, the Bills’ defense was giving the Vikings just as much trouble, and the scoreboard wasn’t moving much in either direction. But there’s only so long you can keep Josh Allen and the Bills’ offense quiet. Once Buffalo had a chance to figure out what Minnesota was throwing at them, the adjustments started paying off. It wasn’t the high-octane, 30-plus-point offense Bills fans have grown accustomed to watching, but it didn’t need to be. James Cook got rolling, Allen found a way to move the ball, and Tyler Bass quietly put together an 11-point night that deserves a little more attention. And let’s not forget fellow special-teams specialist Tommy Doman getting in on the tackling action. Because who doesn’t love seeing a punter-moonlighting-as-a-kicker make a tackle ? By the time it was over, Buffalo had turned an aggravating start into a 23-6 win, improved to 7-1, and climbed to the top of the NFL standings. Not just the AFC East. Not just the AFC. All 32 teams. And while the offense was busy figuring things out, the defense was putting together another performance worth talking about. Three takeaways, fewer than 200 yards allowed, and a Minnesota offense that couldn’t convert a single third down. Of course, the win also came with a few entries in the record books. Josh Allen passed 5,000 career rushing yards and tied Peyton Manning’s mark of 322 total touchdowns through a player’s first 10 seasons. James Cook joined the 5,000-yard rushing club himself , giving the Bills two major career milestones in the same game. And that was just the beginning. Here’s who else earned a Shout! out in Monday night’s win. _____________________________________________________________________________ The best start in more than three decades The Bills are off to their best start in 33 years, matching the 1993 team’s record through eight games. It’s still early in the season, but Buffalo has put itself in a pretty good position heading into the second half. The Bills have improved to 7-1, marking the team's best start since 1993 (7-1). pic.twitter.com/l1QvxdcF51 — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 10, 2026 _____________________________________________________________________________ Bass is perfect Tyler Bass has been one of Buffalo’s most reliable weapons this season, and Monday night was no exception. The Bills needed his leg against Minnesota, and he delivered every time. Tyler Bass improves to 18-of-18 in 2026, marking the best start to a season by a Bills kicker in team history. pic.twitter.com/83LTH0yKD6 — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 10, 2026 _____________________________________________________________________________ Defense doing its job The Buffalo defense has been particularly impressive over the past two weeks, keeping opposing offenses from getting much of anything going. And the numbers show just how dominant the unit has been. Each of the last two games, the Bills defense has: – 3+ takeaways – Multiple sacks – Allowed under 200 total yards – Allowed under 50% completions – Allowed no passing TDs The last NFL team to do that in back-to-back games was the 1985 Bears (3 straight games from Nov. 10-24). pic.twitter.com/Au8kD3ubzF — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 10, 2026 _____________________________________________________________________________ Brady’s road success continues Joe Brady has yet to lose a road game since taking over as Buffalo’s head coach. Monday’s win put him in some pretty good company among NFL coaches over the past 25 years. Joe Brady became the fifth coach this century to win each of his first four career road games, joining Sean McVay (2017), Jim Harbaugh (2011), Jim Caldwell (2009) and Herm Edwards (2001). pic.twitter.com/LQu8mjaT3C — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 10, 2026 _____________________________________________________________________________ Cook keeps finding the end zone James Cook has been one of Buffalo’s most consistent offensive weapons this season. Whether the Bills are putting up 30-plus points or grinding through a defensive battle, Cook keeps finding ways to produce. James Cook III has recorded at least one rushing TD and 75+ rushing yards in seven consecutive games, the longest streak in team history. Cook's streak also marks the longest by any NFL player since LaDanian Tomlinson (8 games) in 2006. pic.twitter.com/4swQqzizjs — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 10, 2026 _____________________________________________________________________________ Williams leads the way Dorian Williams added another interception to Buffalo’s growing collection of takeaways Monday night. He’s now leading the team in that category. Dorian Williams records his second interception of the season, which marks a team-high. pic.twitter.com/csfYaGd0d4 — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 10, 2026 _____________________________________________________________________________ A first for Latu Keleki Latu picked up a career milestone Monday night, hauling in his first NFL touchdown on a pass from Josh Allen. The 25-yard score helped Buffalo finally get its offense moving against Minnesota. Keleki Latu catches his first career TD on a 25-yard pass from Josh Allen. pic.twitter.com/XDRk967BFC — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 10, 2026 _____________________________________________________________________________ Rousseau isn’t slowing down Greg Rousseau is having another strong season along Buffalo’s defensive front. And with nine games still remaining on the schedule, he’s already reached a mark that twice took him an entire season to achieve. And that mark, it ties him for second in the NFL. Greg Rousseau tallies his 8th sack of the season, tying his career-high for sacks in a season (set in 2022 & 2024). pic.twitter.com/HNftTvn908 — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 10, 2026 Through Week 9, Greg Rousseau is tied for second in the NFL with 8.0 sacks. pic.twitter.com/R2yXpn1zK4 — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 10, 2026 _____________________________________________________________________________ It may not have been the prettiest win of the season, and there were certainly a few moments that tested the patience of Buffalo fans and players alike. But a win is a win, and the Bills are sitting at 7-1 with the best record in the NFL. Not a bad place to be as the season reaches its halfway point. And despite all the Monday night struggles, there was still plenty to Shout! about when it was over.

title: Takeaways from Bills win over Vikings
summary: The Buffalo Bills beat the Vikings 23-6 in Week 9 on Monday Night Football, a dominant defensive effort that paired wonderfully with fine performances from Josh Allen and James Cook. The win moved Joe Brady’s team to 7-1 on the season. These are my takeaways from Buffalo’s victory. The defense was sensational… even if Carson […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills beat the Vikings 23-6 in Week 9 on Monday Night Football , a dominant defensive effort that paired wonderfully with fine performances from Josh Allen and James Cook. The win moved Joe Brady’s team to 7-1 on the season. These are my takeaways from Buffalo’s victory. The defense was sensational… even if Carson Wentz was not The Bills defense had an epic performance in this game, I don’t care who the quarterback was. Carson Wentz was 8-of-25 for 81 yards with two picks. And the goalposts can’t be moved here. While rumors have swirled of Minnesota trading for a quarterback this past week, there were many who believed the Vikings weren’t really downgrading at the position going from Kyler Murray to Wentz for this primetime battle. Let’s not forget, in Week 1, in a relief appearance after Kyler Murray was injured, Wentz was 12-of-19 for 133 yards with three touchdowns and no interceptions. On paper, as a veteran pocket passer, he should be better suited for Kevin O’Connell’s offense. And it’s not as if Wentz had a pedestrian outing. He had a quarterback rating of 8.9 against the Bills defense. That’s the lowest rating a quarterback with at least 25 attempts in a game has managed since… 2019. Now, of course, Wentz missed on a handful of throws in this contest, but the Bills defense forced him to hold onto the football often — his 2.82-second average time to throw was higher than Josh Allen in this game — with outstanding coverage downfield for the vast majority of this matchup. The pass rush and coverage were married throughout, and Buffalo only had to blitz on 25.9% of Wentz’s dropbacks to affect the pocket consistently. And I’ll finish with this storyline that probably won’t be talked about enough given how abysmal the Vikings pass game was — Minnesota ran it 12 times for 51 yards, which equates to a 4.3 yards-per-tote average. Aaron Jones averaged 3.2 yards per carry. Only 27.3% of the Vikings runs were successful — determined by yards gained relative to down and distance — the fifth-lowest rate for a run game in Week 9. Buffalo’s run defense is steadily improving each week, and it’s already much more consistent than it was a season ago. Josh Allen was excellent The stats will miss the sheer brilliance of Allen in this game. His rating was only 87.3. But beyond his slightly floated interception — that did come on a 3rd and 23, mind you — the Bills quarterback excelled against the most unique and aggressive defense in football, a truly elite unit, on its home turf. To start 3-of-5 for 24 yards with a pick and finish the evening 21-of-31 for 234 with a touchdown through the air was immaculate from Allen. He commanded the offense, both pre and post snap exactly how it should be done. He made smart decisions and threw with proper velocity/touch starting with that touchdown drive near the end of the first half. His ball placement was superb as well. And, heck, no quarterback is going to be perfect for 60 minutes against that Vikings defense. Allen did all this without Dion Dawkins and Alec Anderson. MVP-caliber performance from him in this game. Hats off to Tylan Grable + Austin Corbett Grable and Corbett allowed four pressures each. Not exactly what clubs want from starting blockers. But after a few miscommunications early that led to quick pressures, I thought both depth players settled in nicely, and really got after it in the run game in the second half. The Brian Flores defensive scheme is designed to create offensive line miscommunication, and Grable and Corbett have never played alongside each other in an NFL game before. But instead of their presence on the field becoming a story throughout this game, an issue that severely hampered the Bills offense all night, Grable and Corbett were steady in the second half, as run and pass blockers. The Bills linebackers played tremendously The responsibilities in Jim Leonhard’s defense are starting to become second nature to Terrel Bernard, Dorian Williams, and Kaleb Elarms-Orr. Williams and Bernard snagged a pick each in this one, and Bernard dropped probably the most gift-wrapped interception opportunity of his NFL career. They are flowing freely in coverage, rapidly reacting to route concepts, and getting to proper depth at the intermediate level. Against the run, they’re triggering quickly and regularly not allowing blocks to stick to them. In this game, Bernard led the team with six tackles. Dorian Williams had three without a miss. And Elarms-Orr added three tackles of his own on just 13 snaps. This trio has become an underrated three-down group. Joe Brady called one heck of a game Sure, it wasn’t idyllic to start. But once Brady understood the outside pitch plays weren’t working on the ground, he went away from them. Then, later, when he realized the interior run game was doing just enough to keep the Vikings defense on its heels and burn clock, he stuck with it. But it wasn’t a one-dimensional attack for Buffalo in this game. There was a fine collection of play-action, throws to tight ends in the flat, running backs involved through the air. Lots of 13 personnel. Over-the-middle looks for Khalil Shakir, some classic first-read looks outside for DJ Moore, and well-timed quick screens to receivers. Again, it’s never going to be flawless against a Flores defense that has the horses on the Vikings roster. But Brady was in his bag as a play-caller in this convincing win. The special teams unit was damn good, again Whether it was Tyler Bass making his 18th consecutive field goal (a team record) to begin the season, Tommy Doman Jr. handling punt and kickoff duties and laying the lumber to force a fumble, or Greg Dortch’s big return to begin the game, special teams coordinator Jeff Rodgers has built a fantastic unit that was showcased in this Monday Night Football win. In a low-scoring, defensive clash like we got in the first half, I can’t stress enough how important Bass making those kicks was to avoid field-position and momentum shifts. Doman even proved capable of kicking a “dirty ball” that hits within the landing zone but isn’t immediately fielded by the returner. Buffalo’s special teams were once again stellar in victory.

title: James Cook passes Josh Allen for fourth in Bills rushing history
summary: James Cook has moved ahead of Josh Allen on the Buffalo Bills’ all-time rushing list, taking over fourth place in franchise history during Monday’s game against the Minnesota Vikings Cook entered the game with 4,966 career rushing yards, just 25 behind Allen’s 4,991. Cook needed to outgain his quarterback by at least 26 yards to move into […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - DECEMBER 10: James Cook #4 of the Buffalo Bills reacts after scoring a touchdown during the first half of the game against the Kansas City Chiefs at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium on December 10, 2023 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images James Cook has moved ahead of Josh Allen on the Buffalo Bills’ all-time rushing list, taking over fourth place in franchise history during Monday’s game against the Minnesota Vikings Cook entered the game with 4,966 career rushing yards, just 25 behind Allen’s 4,991. Cook needed to outgain his quarterback by at least 26 yards to move into fourth place, but it wasn’t quite that simple. Allen had 60 minutes to add to his total as well. Cook added 107 yards Monday night to bring his career total to 5073. Allen added just 15 and now has 5006. Interestingly, the pair are the first teammates in NFL history to join the 5k-Club on the same night. This is crazy. 🤯 #GoBills | #BillsMafia pic.twitter.com/kFgiAXPzFV — Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) November 10, 2026 Cook now trails only Thurman Thomas (11,938), O.J. Simpson (10,183), and Fred Jackson (5,646) on Buffalo’s all-time rushing list. With nine games remaining in the regular season, Cook also has a shot at catching Jackson for third place in 2026. With 573 separating the two, Cook would need to average just over 63 yards per game over the remaining nine games to move up another spot before the season ends. Of course, Allen isn’t going to stop running the ball either, so Cook may have to defend his new spot on the list a few times. The move up the franchise leaderboard comes just a few weeks after Cook passed Joe Cribbs for fifth place during Buffalo’s game against the Detroit Lions. Cook moved ahead of Cribbs’ 4,445 career rushing yards with a 22-yard run in the fourth quarter, continuing his climb through a list that includes some of the biggest names in Bills history. Cook has been making up ground on Allen throughout the season, but the gap narrowed considerably in Buffalo’s Week 6 game. Cook rushed for 95 yards against the Las Vegas Raiders, while Allen finished with just 1. That performance cut Allen’s lead from 169 yards to 75. The two players have taken very different paths to their places on the list. Cook, now in his fifth NFL season, has become the centerpiece of Buffalo’s running game, while Allen has built his rushing total as one of the league’s most dangerous dual-threat quarterbacks. Allen also holds the NFL record for rushing touchdowns by a quarterback.

title: Bills at Vikings Week 9 instant analysis: Buffalo batters Minnesota
summary: The Buffalo Bills walked out of U.S. Bank Stadium with a 23-6 win on Monday Night Football. Here’s everything I wrote down along the way. 1st Half 2nd Half Final Thoughts The Bills’ offense isn’t always the most exciting one in the league, but they’re a nightmare to stop, and even if it takes more […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - NOVEMBER 09: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates as he walks off the field after defeating the Minnesota Vikings in the game at U.S. Bank Stadium on November 09, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills walked out of U.S. Bank Stadium with a 23-6 win on Monday Night Football . Here’s everything I wrote down along the way. 1st Half Joe Brady chose to start with the ball on offense again. You have to be very secure you’ll make them pay with it. A 3-and-out going backwards shows they weren’t good enough for this choice. James Cook has to catch those checkdowns. 2nd game in a row he starts with a drop. Pre-snap penalties by the OL with 2 backups in a loud venue are expected, unfortunately. The Bills WRs have to be able to beat their matchups quickly, or Brian Flores will send everybody after Josh Allen all night. Josh must have an easy button against it, and DJ Moore is my hope here. Great 1st defensive drive by the Bills. Quick 3-and-out. The Vikings’ offense isn’t anything special, but with the way Buffalo’s D played before the bye, we couldn’t be sure about them being able to do that to start the game. 2nd offensive drive, and the run game has struggled so far, but they must be patient with it. Josh has 2 quick completions on 3rd downs against the blitz, to Moore and Khalil Shakir. Easy buttons start to appear as the Bills use motion pre-snap to confuse the Vikings D. A Josh Allen intentional grounding penalty put the O in a bad spot in a promising drive until that point. Man coverage on a PA bootleg play, and Josh couldn’t get the ball to the line of scrimmage as he was tackled by Andrew Van Ginkel. 3rd and long, and Josh airs it out as he gets hit. Moore was open deep, but the ball seemed to go too inside, giving time to the opposite-side CB to make the play on the ball. It was kind of an arm punt, but the return was great. Tylan Grable made a great play to stop it at midfield. Defense’s back on the field and making plays. I think it was a backward pass, and the Bills will have the ball. Brady with a good challenge here. After the replay, Bills ball. Also after the replay, the INT was an awesome play by Byron Murphy. No way Josh could have expected it from him. First Bills points on a Tyler Bass FG. Every point should be valuable today, game of patience. 3-0 Bills. Whoa, Tommy Doman forcing a fumble , and it flies right to the arms of another Vikings player. The Bills almost create another TO. Bills D continues to succeed as Justin Jefferson gets hurt. Everything’s under control on that side of the ball so far. Offense has to take care of the ball and play safe, be patient. The O strategy hasn’t worked. They have to insist on the run game, but they can’t have Josh under center on obvious passing downs. The OL is struggling to deal with those pressure packages. Jefferson is back, and Christian Benford is following him everywhere. Carson Wentz has struggled to deliver the ball to him so far. Bills D is also aggressive. Why in the world is Kyle Allen warming up? Grable with a false start. Rough game for him, Corbett, and the rest of the OL so far. I guess I’ll write 3 and out a lot today. Another one. Damar Hamlin literally hugs T.J. Hockenson running his route. Easy for the refs. Greg Rousseau starts to change the game for Buffalo. How fun it has been watching Groot this season. Bills will get the ball again. What a punt. Down at 1. Josh Allen is crushed at the 1-yard line and fumbles the ball. Thankfully he was down already, and it got reversed. Bills punt, and Vikings get great field position, almost in FG range already. What an ugly game. Bills D continues to do its job and holds the Vikings to an FG here. 3-3. Yeah, it’s a great defense and all, we’re missing the left side of the OL , I know. But it’s frustrating to see a top offense in the league show no different alternatives when their go-to style doesn’t work. No spreading WRs out and trying to explore mismatches vs the secondary one-on-one; no change in the tempo. A top offense should have more repertoire. 2 min warning, 3-3. Bills going shotgun on 1st down for a change and running out of it, not usual. Show more unusual stuff Brady, so far it hasn’t been pretty. Now RPO and uptempo, let’s go. We have Josh Allen, and the offense is always run like he’s an ordinary QB. Spread those WRs and make them pay for one-on-ones. See? TD Bills. Empty formation, Allen buys time, finds Latu at the back of the endzone. 44 seconds left, 10-3 Bills. Run more 2 min offense during the game. The defense can hold their own, score a couple of TDs, and put the Vikings in a tough situation. The Bills’ “regular” O can be very good 80% of the time doing their usual stuff with heavy formations, run game, and PA, but you gotta be able to do something different in those 20% of the time, especially having Josh fricking Allen. Jefferson with his 1st catch in the game , for 24 yards. Jordan Addison catches another one and the Vikings are in FG range. Not anymore, false start penalty. Another completion to Jefferson and a spike. Hoecht dives and almost makes the play of the year, intercepting the spike. It goes through his hands, though. Vikings kick the FG and make it a 10-6 game. Half time. 2nd Half Vikings start with the ball and start the drive well, but Dorian Williams makes a huge play in man coverage versus Hockenson. Interception, Bills ball. Bills offense back to heavy formations and run game. It has worked for now. The impact of showing their defense you can do different stuff as well. Keep them off balance. There’s nothing as obvious as the Bills PA from under center after a bad 1st down run. Defenders go straight to the QB every time. Pass incomplete. Awesome 3rd-and-8 completion to Ty Johnson downfield , running a fly route from outside, as a WR. Another PA puts Josh in a bad spot with Van Ginkel all over him. He somehow makes him miss and delivers a strike to Dawson Knox for a 1st down. Some zone read and inverted veer on back-to-back plays. Runs from shotgun are welcome to avoid the predictability. It’s funny how obvious it is that Keon Coleman incorporated some of Stevie Johnson’s tempo and change of pace into his route running. It’s been great for him. 3rd and goal, Josh puts it on the money for Knox (who’s having a good game), but it goes through his hands. Blake Cashman was all over him, but that’s a ball you’d like to see your TE come down with. Why wasn’t it Dalton Kincaid there running this route? Bass FG is good, 13-6 Bills. Buffalo has controlled the ball possession in this game , but Minnesota starts the drive with three very good runs in a row. Terrel Bernard with the INT. He has looked healthy today, and this INT was reminiscent of his best days. Grable gets schooled by Pace , and Josh is sacked, seemed hurt. Then a pre-snap penalty, 2nd and 24. Hook and ladder gets just 6 yards. 3rd and 18. Tipped pass falls onto Kincaid’s arms , which gets enough yardage for a FG attempt. Bass hits it from 54 yards , but a false start penalty denies it. Brady decides to punt it, and then another false start, are you kidding me? Oh my God, TB, there isn’t an easier INT than that. Joshua Palmer level drop. Bills D forces another punt. Max Hairston almost tackles Dortch in the return. Start of the 4th, Allen changes the play at the LOS , moves from under center to shotgun and quickly finds Coleman for a 1st down. Love to see it. That’s (4th quarter) normally when the insistence with the run game pans out. No big play by Cook yet, but 4 to 6 yards a pop in the last few runs. How do the refs rule it short? In every sport and in every league, the stars get some “special treatment”, but when it’s the Bills and Josh Allen, they’re always ready to call it against Buffalo. Thankfully, the booth reversed this awful call. Great hands by Kincaid on a 3rd-and-3 conversion. Josh had to adjust to Van Ginkel’s pressure, and it…

title: James Cook powers through against Vikings for important Bills win
summary: ESPN named James Cook the player of the game in their postgame show and it’s easy to see why. The Buffalo Bills leaned on their running back against the Minnesota Vikings, and despite a slow start, Cook delivered over the course of the game and scored what felt like the game-ending touchdown with 6:17 left […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images ESPN named James Cook the player of the game in their postgame show and it’s easy to see why. The Buffalo Bills leaned on their running back against the Minnesota Vikings, and despite a slow start, Cook delivered over the course of the game and scored what felt like the game-ending touchdown with 6:17 left in the fourth quarter. That’s seven straight games with a rushing touchdown for Cook. He also has 75+ rushing yards in those games, the longest streak in team history with 75 yards and a touchdown run. That combo is the longest streak by a player since 2006 when LaDanian Tomlinson had eight straight. Cook’s previous career high in carries came in 2025 when he ran the ball 32 times with two offensive lineman injured against a really talented Pittsburgh Steelers defense. The same thing happened in Minnesota, when two Bills offensive linemen were on the shelf and Buffalo needed the help. Cook toted the rock 31 times for 107 yards at a tough 3.5 yards per carry. Cook’s long was only 11 yards on Monday. In the passing game, Cook was targeted once but let the Allen pass go through his hands but he probably wouldn’t have picked up many yards anyway. The rest of the rushing game was shaky at best. Josh Allen ran the ball five times for 16 yards (outside the first half kneel down), mostly on designed runs. Ray Davis had two runs for two yards. Ty Johnson had one rush for one yard. There was some consternation about signing Cook to his current contract a while ago, but that seems to have passed. Cook deserves a ton of credit for continuing to grind against the Vikings. It’s a short week for the Blls heading into a Sunday game after a road trip on Monday night, so hopefully he can get iced up with a veteran rest day this week. After the game, Cook was nonchalant on how his body feels. “[I feel] excellent. Feel like I didn’t play a game.” Hopefully he feels that way in the morning.

title: Buffalo Bills stock report: Horns Up, Horns down in gritty win vs. Minnesota Vikings
summary: The Buffalo Bills and Minnesota Vikings played the kind of knock-down, drag-out football most of us anticipated tonight. The No. 1 defense in the NFL resides in Minnesota, and it was as-advertised throughout the evening. Defensive coordinator Brian Flores and his charges made life miserable for the league’s No. 1 scoring offense for most of […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - NOVEMBER 09: Terrel Bernard #8 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates with teammates after intercepting a pass intended for Justin Jefferson #18 of the Minnesota Vikings during the third quarter of the game at U.S. Bank Stadium on November 09, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills and Minnesota Vikings played the kind of knock-down, drag-out football most of us anticipated tonight. The No. 1 defense in the NFL resides in Minnesota, and it was as-advertised throughout the evening. Defensive coordinator Brian Flores and his charges made life miserable for the league’s No. 1 scoring offense for most of the evening, but especially in the first half. Flores’ defense flustered, frustrated, beat, and battered Buffalo’s offense for most of the first 28 minutes of the contest, but Buffalo eventually broke through. Like the eponymous Rosie in my favorite AC/DC song, it wasn’t exactly pretty, but coming out of this game with a win wasn’t exactly small, either. For the Bills, emerging with a 23-6 victory tonight is a big statement. Buffalo’s defense looked great, and their offense did enough by moving the ball on an elite defensive unit to score enough points to win the game. Minnesota’s inept offense—combined with a strong effort from Buffalo’s much-maligned defense—gave Buffalo’s elite offense the time to find its footing. hat time was all Buffalo needed to come out with a win. There was plenty of good tonight, and there was enough bad to keep us talking throughout the week, as well. Here are our horns up and horns down for the Bills in this Monday night slug-fest. _____________________________________________________________________________ Horns Down: Austin Corbett Based on his play tonight, I don’t have to ask which Billy Joel album is Corbett’s favorite. While I also love Turnstiles , it’s not exactly how I want to see an offensive lineman perform. Yes, there is a reason why Corbett lost the preseason positional battle to Alec Anderson, but as a nine-year vet making his 79th career start, I didn’t expect him to be the guy consistently whiffing on blocks while quarterback Josh Allen ran for his life. Anderson was able to log a limited practice at the end of this past week, so he’s hopefully going to be able to play next week. I do wonder, though, if the Bills would consider using Tylan Grable at guard over Corbett in the future when both Dion Dawkins, who sat tonight with a rib injury, and Spencer Brown are both healthy. Horns Up: Greg Rousseau Groot was all over the offensive backfield at times, as he hit quarterback Carson Wentz three times, sacked him once, and whacked his throwing arm to cause an incomplete pass in the first half alone. Rousseau was a big problem in the passing game and the run game, as he consistently used his length to create issues for Minnesota’s offensive line. He even recovered a fumble on what was originally ruled an incomplete pass by Carson Wentz. He finished the game with just those first-half stats, but his presence was felt throughout the game. Horns Down: Early-Game Offensive Play Calls It took the Bills some time to settle into the game, as head coach and play-caller Joe Brady was far too predictable early. At one point, Buffalo had run the football on seven of nine first-downs. James Cook III is a great back, but when every first down is a handoff through the A-gap against a fantastic Minnesota defense, it becomes a little predictable. To his credit, Brady started to mix things up as the game progressed, and his calls diversified to include some spread looks—which really helped the Bills—as well as some better looks for Cook on second down runs. The adjustments helped Buffalo to move the ball against an elite defensive unit, putting up enough points for the game they were playing tonight. Horns Up: Jim Leonhard Kudos to the defensive boss, who was leading an awful unit through Buffalo’s first six games. Between tonight’s game and last week’s win over the Baltimore Ravens, Buffalo’s defense has looked like an entirely different unit. Granted, that success has come against two teams who were without their starting quarterbacks, but let’s not pretend that Carson Wentz is Joe Fagnano. Wentz might have looked like Fagnano for most of the evening, but part of that was thanks to the looks Buffalo’s defense gave him. Leonhard has done a nice job turning the tide for Buffalo’s stop unit over the last two weeks. If they can build on this, and maybe find some help on the trade market to supplement the group, things could be looking up. Horns Up: The Linebackers Dorian Williams and Terrel Bernard each made huge plays in the second half. Williams went up and made a big interception when he was one-on-one with tight end T.J. Hockenson, bringing an end to Minnesota’s first drive after the half. Then, after the Vikings had gashed Buffalo on the ground for four straight plays, Bernard undercut Justin Jefferson and intercepted Wentz off a play-action pass. Bernard had three pass breakups and Williams had one. Ultimately, both players looked good, as did rookie Kaleb Elarms-Orr, who was flying around the ball on his snaps, as well. Bernard led the Bills in tackles, totaling six on the evening to go with the aforementioned pass breakups. Williams had three tackles, and Elarms-Orr had two on his ledger. Horns Up: Keleki Latu Any time you catch your first career touchdown, it’s a horns up from me. Latu did a great job staying alive on the scramble drill, and Josh Allen did Josh Allen things by finding him in the back of the end zone when basically any other normal human would have thrown the football away. It was a 25-yard score where Latu found himself wide open, and it was a huge score in what was mostly a field goal-fest. Latu even mixed it up as a blocker, looking more than capable of holding his own all night long. Horns Down: Staying On the Snap Count Five false start penalties. Sure, they’re on the road, and yes, Vikings fans were loud tonight. But, five? This is a continuing theme this season where little things that hint towards a team’s discipline—of lack thereof—show up. Buffalo has the talent to overcome it most of the time, but the Bills committed too many penalties again tonight. Pre-snap penalties are absolute killers. Horns Down: Tylan Grable Alright, maybe this is harsh, because stepping in to play left tackle against this Minnesota defense is no easy task. However, for any of us who thought that Grable could easily come in and replace Dion Dawkins, tonight was a bit of a reality check. Grable held his own for much of the game, but he did whiff entirely on linebacker Ivan Pace in the second half, leading to a sack on Josh Allen. As the game progressed, Grable and the rest of Buffalo’s offensive line was able to open holes for James Cook in the run game, but tonight’s performance didn’t show me that either Dawkins or Anderson should be anywhere but the starting lineup for the foreseeable future. Horns Up: James Cook III What a tough performance out of Cook tonight. He was an old-school workhorse in a game where the running game was an absolute necessity. This was just the fifth time in Cook’s career that he’s had more than 25 carries in a game, and just the second time in his career that he totaled 30 carries in a game. He handled the workload—and the punishment that came with it—beautifully. Cook totaled 107 yards and a game-sealing touchdown on his 31 carries. He dropped his only target, which came on Buffalo’s first possession of the game. Horns Up: Khalil Shakir Allen’s safety blanket was explosive in this one, coming up with big plays every time he touched the football. Whether it was on screen passes or crossing routes, Shakir made the most of his four targets, catching them all for 58 yards. It’s not the kind of stat line that impresses you in fantasy football, but against the NFL’s best defense, it’s the kind of performance that…

title: Panthers restructure Taylor Moton’s contract to free up cap room
summary: The NFL trade deadline is 4:00pm Eastern time today (Tuesday). There’s been more activity around the trade deadline in recent years as teams have started to find the utility in becoming buyers or sellers based on the way their seasons are going. The Carolina Panthers are just 3-5, but they do technically lead the NFC […]
full_text: The NFL trade deadline is 4:00pm Eastern time today (Tuesday). There’s been more activity around the trade deadline in recent years as teams have started to find the utility in becoming buyers or sellers based on the way their seasons are going. The Carolina Panthers are just 3-5, but they do technically lead the NFC South. That would suggest they’re more likely to be buyers at the deadline if anything, and they did a bit of bookkeeping to confirm that. The Carolina #Panthers converted $5.3M of Taylor Moton's salary into signing bonus, creating $3.5M of 2026 cap space. Updated Cap Hits 2026: $17.4M 2027: $30.2M 2028: $8.7M (void) — Spotrac (@spotrac) November 10, 2026 According to Spotrac, the Panthers restructured offensive tackle Taylor Moton’s deal to save themselves $3.5 million against this season’s salary cap. It’s the typical restructure move. They converted some of his base salary (which counts entirely against this season’s cap) to a signing bonus (which is spread across the length of the deal). The team was right at the salary cap before this move, and now they have some wiggle room to add a piece at the deadline if there’s one that suits them. The $3.5 million number isn’t going to fit any blockbuster acquisition, even if it is only a player’s base salary. If anything, the Panthers will peruse the league’s worst teams for some inexpensive veterans that can fill the void in the secondary while Jaycee Horn, Mike Jackson, and Will Lee recover from their injuries. Same could be said for the offensive line, where injuries have caused problems and subpar play has caused even more. However, it’s more likely that his move is to give the team some wiggle room to sign or claim free agents. The team hosted cornerback Jack Jones for a visit the other day but haven’t yet offered him a contract. Moves like that would require the kind of space the Moton restructure opens up, so that seems like the route in which the Panthers will spend the extra money they’ve freed up.

This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the […]
full_text: IOWA CITY, IOWA- OCTOBER 26: Offensive lineman Trevor Lauck #59 of the Iowa Hawkeyes blocks during the second half against defensive lineman Michael Kilbane #47 of the Northwestern Wildcats at Kinnick Stadium on October 26, 2024 in Iowa City, Iowa. (Photo by Matthew Holst/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In this series, we’ll only be looking at prospects the Panthers could seriously consider. Today our profile will focus on Iowa Hawkeyes offensive tackle Trevor Lauck. Bio Lauck (6’5”, 315 lbs.) was a three time all-state player in Indianapolis on both sides of the ball in high school. Earning a four star ranking while also playing basketball and throwing shotput, he committed to Iowa over powerhouse schools like Michigan and Ohio State. Lauck didn’t earn much playing time until 2025 when he won the starting left tackle job after a couple years of backup duty. He started all 13 games for Iowa that year, allowing zero sacks and just six pressures. He was rewarded with a Third Team All-Big Ten selection. So far this season, he has started all nine games so far for the Hawkeyes. He’s been rock solid, only allowing five pressures and one sack while earning a PFF grade of 80.7 overall. Strengths/Weaknesses Lauck’s technique is surprisingly good for his level of starting experience. He has advanced hand placement, strong punches, balanced mirroring, and excellent footwork. By the time the Draft rolls around, he’ll have two full seasons of left tackle starting experience, more than most other highly ranked tackles. His stunt and twist recognition is up to Iowa’s usual impressive standards, showing a level of coachability. In order to be as effective as he is, Lauck has to have that good technique because his physical abilities aren’t wowing anyone. He has average foot speed, so wide rushers are able to really test him on outside rushes. He also lacks the elite left tackle length the NFL looks for, so some teams might want to push him inside to guard. Projection Lauck is your typical Iowa offensive lineman. He’s big, strong, skilled in run and pass blocking, and very smart. He has plenty of starting experience on the blindside, rarely making mistakes (flagged just three times this season). While he already has a lot of veteran savvy at such a young age, his physical limitations will make it unlikely he ends up as an elite blindside protector. At this point, though, I doubt Bryce Young and the Panthers would turn their noses up at “good but not elite” protection. Rasheed Walker has been not good, and we still don’t know if/when Icky Ekwonu will return to the lineup. If the Panthers are concerned about Lauck’s length on the outside, they need help at guard as well. Lauck has shown the coachability to be able to pick up the nuances of the interior relatively quickly. What do you think, Panthers fans? If Trevor Lauck is available when the Panthers select in the 2027 NFL Draft, should they take him? Sound off in the comments!
author: Daniel Belton

title: Discussion: Was the Panthers loss to the Broncos a moral victory?
summary: There’s no such thing as a moral victory, right? That’s what people like to say, but I think that mindset misses a lot of nuance that can be useful when assessing the state of the team and what could be expected going forward. The Carolina Panthers lost at home to the Denver Broncos on Sunday. […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - NOVEMBER 08: Tommy Tremble #82 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates after scoring a touchdown with Chuba Hubbard #30 during the second quarter against the Denver Broncos at Bank of America Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Grant Halverson/Getty Images) | Getty Images There’s no such thing as a moral victory, right? That’s what people like to say, but I think that mindset misses a lot of nuance that can be useful when assessing the state of the team and what could be expected going forward. The Carolina Panthers lost at home to the Denver Broncos on Sunday. They didn’t put up as many points, but they outgained the Broncos and averaged more yards per play. The run defense that had been embarrassingly bad at times this season limited Denver to 3.0 yards per carry and got in the backfield on a number of plays. Bryce Young through for 276 and Chuba Hubbard averaged nearly five yards per carry. On a play to play basis, the team played well enough to win. However, untimely penalties and the flukiest of interceptions massively swung the momentum of the game in the Broncos favor, and the Panthers ultimately couldn’t overcome that. That brings us to our question… Was Sunday’s loss to the Broncos a moral victory? MY TAKE: I think so. The Panthers needed to show some life after disastrous outings in their last two games. The beginning of the game looked like another disaster was incoming, but the team righted the ship in the second quarter and more than held their own. The Broncos have had a weird season, but they are 6-2 and in contention for the top seed in the AFC. They’ve also got some rabbit’s foot black magic voodoo going on where they keep snatching victory from the jaws of defeat. The Panthers seemed to be victimized by that in a way yesterday. The interception was one of the flukiest I’ve ever seen, to the point where the player that intercepted the pass didn’t even realize he had an interception. There also should have been a pass interference on the play, but the officiating crew that was spamming pass interference calls all day somehow missed that one. Otherwise, the Panthers’ undoing was a result of penalties largely from the practice squad players that are currently occupying the starting cornerback spots. And even then, I thought at least a couple of them were questionable flags. The parts of the defense that you’d want to look improved under a new defensive coordinator did look better. The offense had a good day against a very good Broncos defense. Bryce Young looked like the version of himself we saw earlier in the season and posted a season high 86.5 QBR. The schedule lightens up significantly in the next month or so. If the Panthers play like they did today minus the penalties, they can post a good record in that stretch of games. So while the result of yesterday’s game was bitterly disappointing, I think there were enough positives to take away that we can feel good about what this team is capable of going forward.
author: Jonathan DeLong

title: 3 Reasons Why the Chicago Bears Won vs. the Buccaneers
summary: Well that was ugly. Unlike our beloved Denmaster, I do believe in such things as ugly wins. But one thing we all agree on is a win is a win and going into our BYE week at 7-2 is as good as it gets since the letdown in Lambeau back in week 5 that feels […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 8: Devin Bush #12 of the Chicago Bears hypes up his teammates before before the game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Soldier Field on November 8, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Well that was ugly. Unlike our beloved Denmaster, I do believe in such things as ugly wins. But one thing we all agree on is a win is a win and going into our BYE week at 7-2 is as good as it gets since the letdown in Lambeau back in week 5 that feels like ages ago. Considering the Chicago Bears are on the verge of a certain level of success the franchise hasn’t experienced in decades thanks to Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams, I am going to leave them out of this piece from now on – as it is a given that both were instrumental to Chicago’s success. Go ahead and throw in All-World DT Jeffery Simmons into that category too. Instead, I will be highlighting 3 other factors that contributed to Chicago’s win or loss. So let’s get to it. 1. Devin Bush Though it’s been a while – we Chicago Bears fans have seen our share of exceptional linebacker play over the years. That’s not to say we haven’t seen flashes of brilliance from guys like T.J. Edwards, Tremaine Edmunds and even Jack Sanborn. But what we saw out of Devin Bush on Sunday night reminded me of prime Roquan Smith when the All-Pro roamed the middle for the Monsters of the Midway before he was shipped out to Baltimore. Similarly built at right around 6ft and 230lbs, both players provide unusual explosion from the position with an uncanny ability to zoom past reaching guards and/or tackles to blow up runs behind the LOS while also covering the middle of the field from sideline to sideline in the passing game. Ever since the arrival of Jeffery Simmons, Bush’s talents have been on full display and that continued against the Buccaneers. Whether it was blowing up a ball carrier on 3rd or 4th down for a loss or absolutely de-cleating Emeka Egbuka on a jet sweep, Bush was a force to be reckoned with, and I don’t think we win that game without him. Bush posted season highs in stuffs (tackles at or behind the line of scrimmage) and passes defensed Sunday night, and I would imagine those marks will be surpassed before we reach the playoffs. It is clear to see why Bears GM Ryan Poles brought in the former Michigan Wolverine, and Chicago will need more games like that if they want to make a deep run at the Lombardi Trophy. 2. 3rd Down Defense I could have said Dennis Allen here, but that isn’t specific enough for my liking. Additionally, Allen calls the plays but the players have to execute so it’s a team-effort with coaches included. Prior to Sunday nights game, Tampa was 38% on 3rd downs on the season. Against Chicago, Tampa went 2 for 12, which is 16.7%. That is a remarkable stat that shows how Chicago’s defense truly impacted the game. Additionally, only 1 of Chicago’s 4 sacks and neither interception came on 3rd down – meaning the team is playing technically sound and effective football when it matters most without relying on the big play or turnover like they seemed to do a year ago. Again, that can absolutely be credited to the coaching staff but the way these players were flying around on the most important down of a drive is encouraging. Especially after giving up 2 TDs and almost 5 yards per carry and 100 yards to Bucky Irving. They say 3rd down is the money down and if Chicago wasn’t as successful against Tampa on 3rd downs Sunday night – there is no way they win that ball game. 3. Jaylon Johnson This one was harder than I expected as Cam Lewis, Rome Odunze and Luther Burden III were all deserving. But at the end of the day, the pick-6 that Jaylon had absolutely was the difference in this game. Though Chicago turned the ball over 5 times, not one of them was returned for a score like Jaylon’s 67 yard interception return was and it couldn’t have come at a better time. Up by 4 points with Tampa primed for another drive, Jaylon put Chicago ahead with an 11-point lead, and they would never look back. After the disappointing season that Jaylon has had, it was great to see him read and react so quickly and snag the INT before racing more than half the field for a score. If Jaylon Johnson can use this game as a springboard for the rest of the season, it would be a huge boost to this defense and team down the stretch. It was easily his best game of the season and a great thing to see for Chicago’s CB1. Jaylon Johnson earned the lone game ball after the Bears' 27-24 win over the Bucs with his strongest performance of the season. Johnson allowed just one reception for six yards on five targets in coverage in Week 9 and returned a third-quarter interception for a 67-yard… — Courtney Cronin (@CourtneyRCronin) November 9, 2026 What about you? Who, outside of Caleb, Ben, and Big Jeff, felt most important to the Bears’ win on Sunday night?
author: Bryan Orenchuk

title: 10 Thoughts on the NFL Week 9: The Good, The Bad, and The (Winning) Ugly
summary: 1. Is it just me, or was there a lot of bad football happening this past week? The Monday night game between the Bills and Vikings, who were absolutely offensive offensively, was just the cherry on top. Maybe it’s just the number of backup/backup-level quarterbacks playing across the league due to injuries and ineptitude. It […]
full_text: Nov 8, 2026; Chicago, Illinois, USA; Chicago Bears defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons (99) reacts after the game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Soldier Field. Mandatory Credit: Talia Sprague-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect 1. Is it just me, or was there a lot of bad football happening this past week? The Monday night game between the Bills and Vikings, who were absolutely offensive offensively, was just the cherry on top. Maybe it’s just the number of backup/backup-level quarterbacks playing across the league due to injuries and ineptitude. It made teams and quarterbacks who are actually good, like Joe Burrow and Jordan Love, look like they’re playing an entirely different sport. Maybe we should just give everyone a bye week next week. 2. The Vikings are cooked. Brian Flores’ defense is awesome. But even they can’t carry quarterback play this bad for a whole season and postseason. It’s just unrealistic. Eventually, as happened against a persistent Bills offense in the second half, being on the field three-quarters of the game breaks you. Minnesota, to be fair, did try to address their QB situation by signing Kyler Murray. Unfortunately, he’s been hurt a lot and not that effective when on the field. Can’t get worse than what Carson Wentz just did against Buffalo, though. Their defense will win them a few games, but they can’t win their division like this. 3. Speaking of which…the Chicago Bears now lead the NFC North through nine weeks. Exactly how they drew it up! Slogging through a 2-1 record without Caleb Williams and then winning the ugliest offensive game since the Miracle in the Desert back in 2026? The Bears are back, baby. For real, though: being 7-2, with wins over both of last year’s Super Bowl participants, is a major accomplishment so far for a team many expected to take a step back. The road doesn’t get easier from here, including plenty of games against their divisional opponents (all of whom have six wins or more). But they’re built for it. 4. I don’t know whom the Chargers think they are, exactly. But there need to be a bunch of veteran players not on that team by the time the trade deadline passes this afternoon at 4 p.m. ET. That is a thoroughly uncompetitive, unserious football team, and they should have no delusions about making the playoffs. Follow the Eagles’ example. They just traded defensive tackle Jordan Davis to the Jaguars after trading starting center Cam Jurgens away to the Ravens last month. Khalil Mack, Rashawn Slater, Derwin James. Hell, trade Dicker the Kicker if anyone will send anything for him. Start selling. Now. Otherwise, everyone’s got to get fired immediately. 5. The Jags are getting cooked already for sending a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-rounder to Philly for Davis. That’s a pretty steep price, and that’s coming from a guy whose team just traded two firsts for Jeffery Simmons. Draft capital—the idea of the unknown—is extremely valuable, which Eagles general manager Howie Roseman knows well. When you’re as good as he is at drafting defensive linemen, sending away a good one is no big deal. Here’s what I’ll say in Jacksonville’s defense, though: we as a football community might not be fully appreciating how “premium” a good/great defensive tackle is. But the league seems to be angling in that direction. Great interior defenders make everyone behind them better, meaning you don’t have to allocate as much capital to the positions behind them. Plus, interior pressure on quarterbacks is probably even more devastating than edge pressure. Bottom line: yeah, it’s an overpay. But that doesn’t mean the price isn’t worth it if Davis is even partly what Simmons has been for the Bears so far. 6. Not going to lie, I’m loving the trend of calling horrible, interception-worthy throws “deli meat” or “meatball subs.” I’m not sure if it originated with defensive players, reactor culture, or transitioning from baseball, where throwing one right down the middle to a hitter is a “meatball.” I don’t care. Give whoever came up with this idea a raise, and give Tom Brady a few million more for leaning into it. It’s hilarious. 7. I hope the Eagles start Joe Milton for the rest of the year for the entertainment value alone. Because yeah, this guy is going to struggle to complete the most basic throws (and might accidentally kill one of his receivers with a screen pass). But when it comes to rolling out or chilling way back in the pocket on play-action, the anticipation of wondering how far/how hard he’s about to chuck the ball is intoxicating. Just once, we need him to try to air one out from like his own 25-yard line to the end zone. I bet he could do it. And the Eagles are going absolutely nowhere. So you might as well live with it. 8. For a guy leading a 3-5 football team, C.J. Stroud has been playing some insane ball. He’s on track for easily the best statistical year of his career with 16 touchdowns (his previous season-high is 23) and just two interceptions, and he just dropped 384 yards and five scores on the Chargers with a patchwork-quilt offense around him. The Texans might not do anything this year, unfortunately, especially with the Jaguars running away with the AFC South. But if there’s any argument for still extending Stroud after this season is over, even if they miss the playoffs, this is as good as any. It won’t be what, say, Caleb Williams or Drake Maye is likely to sign in the next few years. But someone’s going to pay Stroud handsomely as long as he keeps this up. 9. My verdict on the Shedeur Sanders performance, since you’re so interested in it? If I’m grading on a curve, let’s call it “B+,” especially because of the plays he made down the stretch to get the Browns in position to send the game to overtime and eventually challenge for a shot to win it in the end. He definitely outperformed most backups pressed into service this week. But in terms of “representative NFL starting quarterback,” that game is a C at best. Not discounting what he did down the stretch, but even some of the big plays he produced down the field were on underthrown balls his receivers had to adjust to or make incredible catches on. It’s hard to come away thinking anything but, “Thanks for your service, kid. Now sit right back down on that bench.” Again, not bad after that rough first half. But let’s not get ahead of ourselves saying he needs more burn. He really doesn’t. 10. Question for the group: who’s the next head coach to get the axe this season? My hot take: Jim Harbaugh. Because ain’t no way that Chargers team should be this awful. Others, like Aaron Glenn with the Jets or Shane Steichen with the Colts, are playing for teams actively tanking/blowing things up. They know the score. The Harbaugh experiment has run its course, and one more loss might send him. Let us know what you think.
