title: For the Detroit Lions, ugly wins are a thing of beauty
summary: Winning the ugly ones is just as important as the pretty ones—they count the same in the standings, after all—and that’s where the Detroit Lions need to keep pace with an NFC North that refuses to ease up. For yet another week, everyone in the Black and Blue division with a quarterback capable of performing […]
full_text: Nov 8, 2026; Miami Gardens, Florida, USA; Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell celebrates with defensive back Brian Branch (32) after an interception during the second half against the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Nathan Ray Seebeck-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Winning the ugly ones is just as important as the pretty ones—they count the same in the standings, after all—and that’s where the Detroit Lions need to keep pace with an NFC North that refuses to ease up. For yet another week, everyone in the Black and Blue division with a quarterback capable of performing the forward pass picked up wins. It’s maddening, it’s odds-defying, it feels like it has to let up at some point, but until it does, winning is all that matters for this Lions team. Most of the noise on game day centered on the new guy at left guard, Miles Frazier, stepping in for starter Christian Mahogany . In real time, people scrambled to find an explanation. Was Mahogany hurt in pregame warmups? What were his PFF grades over the last three games? Did he catch the South Beach Flu? People hardly had enough time to investigate before Detroit took the field and mustered up a measly 110 yards and six points on offense in the first half. Prior to halftime, fans had lost their patience with Frazier’s performance. Jared Goff was sacked three times, Jahmyr Gibbs had four carries of zero or negative yards, and the Lions were up just three points at halftime against a 1-6 Miami Dolphins team. Enough was enough: Mahogany needed to be put in at left guard to help the Lions offense get back on track. Except that didn’t happen. Mahogany played just five snaps on Sunday in Miami, all of those opportunities coming on field goal kicks. The Lions offense turned things around just enough in the second half. Goff stayed upright, Gibbs broke into the end zone for the game’s only touchdown, and the Lions defense (!) made sure this one ended in a victory. Not for them, but for their leader, Jack Campbell, who had to watch his defense from a hospital room, still regaining his physical faculties—but determined to return to the field. Social media was filled with videos and photos of the Honolulu Blue takeover at Hard Rock Stadium, fans chanting and holding signs in support of Campbell and the Lions. Your feed was filled with as much love and support as it was with people wondering how Mahogany’s crime could justify the time he spent on the sideline. Dan Campbell offered no further insight into the infraction immediately after the game, but has since alluded to the fact that Mahogany had broken team rules “multiple times.” Dan Campbell made the right decision when it came to holding Mahogany accountable. There’s no room in their building for anyone to be above the standard, whether you’re a starter or a healthy inactive on game day. That isn’t a new sentiment—it’s been the foundation since the afternoon Campbell walked through the door. “But I’ll guarantee you this: these guys are gonna fight, and they’re gonna scratch and claw, and they’re gonna be something this city is proud of because they’re going to take on the identity of this city,” Campbell said in his introductory press conference. “It ain’t always going to be roses up here. ‘Everything’s gonna be the way that we all want it to be and look perfect,’ but I know this, man, we’re gonna fight, we’re gonna scratch, and we’re gonna claw, and I know the good teams find a way to get it done.” Campbell told us it wasn’t always going to be pretty, and we’ve been reminded over these past couple of weeks just how ugly football can get, but there’s something beautiful in it all. “If somebody goes down, the next one steps up, and he’s expected to produce enough to help those guys next to him when these guys are going to learn to play together, play for one another.” From the disciplinary action against Mahogany to Jack Campbell’s absence in the middle of Detroit’s defense, from the offense’s struggles to Kelvin Sheppard’s unit getting the job done, Sunday was a testament to how they’ve become that good team Campbell referenced over five years ago. Their 6-2 record is a reflection of the image this football team was built on by Dan Campbell. “It’s not about the best 53, it’s about the right 53.”
author: Ryan Mathews

title: NFL Week 10 power rankings: Despite 4 straight wins, Detroit Lions sit behind NFC North rivals
summary: The Detroit Lions (6-2) have now won four in a row, are 2-0 in the division with wins over the Packers and Vikings, and sit in second place in the NFC North, just a half-game back of the Chicago Bears. For the first time this season, the Lions rank in the top 10 of every […]
full_text: Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell watches a play Miami Dolphins during the second half at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions (6-2) have now won four in a row, are 2-0 in the division with wins over the Packers and Vikings, and sit in second place in the NFC North , just a half-game back of the Chicago Bears. For the first time this season, the Lions rank in the top 10 of every national power ranking that we track. But it’s not all sunshine and roses in the Lions’ relationship with the national media. Of the eight rankings we track, the Lions dropped this week in over half of them. Even more surprising, they dropped behind the Packers in two (Yahoo Sports and Sports Illustrated) and remain behind the Vikings in two others (Sporting News and ESPN)—despite having the same (Vikings) or better (Packers) record—and winning both head-to-head matchups. Let’s take a closer look at this week’s national power rankings. Sports Illustrated: 6 ( Previous rank: 4) From Connor Orr : Having spent time in Buffalo after Damar Hamlin’s near-death experience in a Bills-Bengals game, I can still only begin to fathom the heaviness this Lions team is dealing with on a daily basis in the aftermath of the Jack Campbell injury . It makes the Dolphins victory feel very different… and somehow more amazing. USA Today: 6 (Previous rank: 7) From Nate Davis : WR Amon-Ra St. Brown hasn’t scored since September and only has two 100-yard receiving games this season. Think the German-American star might break out Sunday in Munich − especially given how the Pats secondary just got shredded? NFL.com: 7 (Previous rank: 5) From Nick Shook : Sunday’s victory wasn’t pretty by any means, but sometimes a team needs to find a way to win an ugly one. The Lions did that in Miami, getting just enough from Jahmyr Gibbs to leave with a W. That’s what I’d expect from a team in the top 10, but I’m hoping this was an informative experience to grow from, not a harbinger of things to come. The Athletic: 8 (Previous rank: 7) From Chad Graff and Josh Kendall : It hasn’t always looked pretty (including in Miami on Sunday), and the underlying defensive stats (they rank 30th in EPA per play) remain concerning. But the offense has been among the game’s best as they now head abroad to face the reeling New England defense. CBS Sports: 8 (Previous rank: 9) From Pete Prisco : It wasn’t pretty against the Dolphins, but they found a way. They can’t play that way this week against a wounded Patriots team or else. Yahoo Sports: 9 (Previous rank: 8) From Frank Schwab : Is the Lions’ defense good? It has been better recently. For the third straight game the Lions’ opponent failed to top 17 points. Two of those games happened against the offensively challenged Vikings and Dolphins; the third game in that streak was against the Packers. Advanced metrics are kind to the Lions’ defense over the past three weeks too, as Detroit is eighth in EPA per play allowed and fifth in success rate allowed. Star safety Brian Branch returned from an Achilles injury three games ago, and it’s not a coincidence the Lions’ defense is much better with him back. The Lions have held opponents to 21 or fewer points in four straight games, the first time that has happened since 2016, according to the team’s site. The Lions allowed just 228 yards and 12 first downs Sunday, and while that was against Miami, it’s still a lot better than Detroit looked on defense early in the season. “We’ve cleaned a lot up,” Lions head coach Dan Campbell said, via the team’s site. “Guys are trusting what they’re being taught, they’re executing it and with that execution comes confidence.” ESPN: 10 (Previous rank: 9) From ESPN Staff, excerpt from Eric Woodyard : International games are rare for the Lions, who haven’t played outside the U.S. since 2015. And this matchup in Munich is a homecoming of sorts for WR Amon-Ra St. Brown, whose mother is German and who has spent considerable time in the country. This contest also marks Detroit’s first game in Germany and the first time it is the designated home team for an international game, so this is certainly a huge deal. “You kind of need that extra story to tell,” NFL Germany GM Alexander Steinforth told ESPN. “You need that extra link into the market to have a really meaningful impact, and that’s Amon-Ra St. Brown.” Sporting News: 10 (Previous rank: 11) From Vinnie Iyer : The Lions’ once-maligned defense has allowed only a total of 62 points during their four-game winning streak. They will get a good test against the Patriots in Munich, Germany, in Week 10, where Jared Goff needs to shake off back-to-back sub 200-yard, one-INT games.

title: Detroit Lions Kerby Joseph won’t play in Germany
summary: On Tuesday morning, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell held his weekly interview with local sports radio station 97.1 The Ticket. When discussing the recovery progress of All-Pro safety Kerby Joseph, Campbell said that he doesn’t expect Joseph to be able to play in Week 10 against the New England Patriots in Germany. “I’ll cut it […]
full_text: Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph (31) looks on during warm up ahead of the New Orleans Saints game at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co On Tuesday morning, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell held his weekly interview with local sports radio station 97.1 The Ticket. When discussing the recovery progress of All-Pro safety Kerby Joseph, Campbell said that he doesn’t expect Joseph to be able to play in Week 10 against the New England Patriots in Germany. “I’ll cut it out (the speculation). I don’t see him playing. I don’t see him playing in Germany,” Campbell told 97.1, per Will Burchfield . Joseph injured his knee in 2025 during training camp, and limped through the first month of the season before succumbing to his injury. For just over a year, Joseph underwent rehabilitation, working to build strength in his knee. In late October, Joseph finally gained enough stability in his knee to start practicing once again and started his 21-day injury evaluation clock. Over the last two weeks of practices, Joseph has slowly ramped up his participation levels, as he acclimates back to football activities. On Monday, Campbell said Joseph continues to make progress; they like where he is at and hope to get him even more involved this week. “He did a good job last week, so we want to get him some more work.” While Joseph is steadily improving, the early decision to keep him out of Sunday’s game overseas may seem premature, but for a player who hasn’t played in well over a year, it’s not unusual and shouldn’t necessarily be viewed as a negative regarding his progress. Campbell also noted on Monday, when discussing the trade for Andre Cisco, that he expected Joseph to return this season and would give the Lions’ secondary some flexibility. “We get Kerby back eventually here. Kerby gives you flexibility, keep him where you need him or move him back and forth.“ The Lions don’t want to rush Joseph back into game action, but they are working against the injury evaluation clock, which expires on Tuesday, November 17. At that time, the Lions will need to activate Joseph to the active roster, or they can elect to keep him on the PUP list, which would end his season. If activated, Joseph could potentially return to the field in Week 11 when the Lions host the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

title: Discussion: What is your dream trade deadline move for the Detroit Lions?
summary: Welcome to NFL trade deadline day. After 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday, no more trades can be executed until the start of the league year in 2027. For the Detroit Lions, that likely means this is their last opportunity to make a roster upgrade for the 2026 season. And while the Lions don’t have any […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - OCTOBER 18: Philadelphia Eagles linebacker Zack Baun (53) looks on after the game between the Carolina Panthers and Philadelphia Eagles on October 18, 2026 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Kyle Ross/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome to NFL trade deadline day. After 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday, no more trades can be executed until the start of the league year in 2027. For the Detroit Lions, that likely means this is their last opportunity to make a roster upgrade for the 2026 season. And while the Lions don’t have any massively pressing needs, they are in a bit of an arms race in the NFC. The Chicago Bears added DT Jeffery Simmons a couple of weeks ago. The Seattle Seahawks added guard Quenton Nelson. The 49ers brought back DeForest Buckner. Detroit is in a good spot in the NFC—currently holding onto the fifth seed in the NFL playoff standings—but just about everyone in contention for a postseason spot is playing decent football right now. The Lions have already made one minor move before the deadline, trading for reserve safety Andre Cisco . But I’m guessing most Lions fans want more. So today’s Question of the Day is: What is your dream trade scenario for the Lions? My answer: Trading for Eagles linebacker Zack Baun. Philadelphia has already shown a willingness to trade amid their 2-7 start to the season. On Monday, they sent defensive tackle Jordan Davis to the Jacksonville Jaguars for a first-round pick and a future second-round pick. That’s a pretty penny to pay, and it may be indicative that Baun will be costly if the Eagles are going to let him go. But in Baun, the Lions would be getting a dynamic playmaker. Baun does everything in that Eagles defense. He’s above average in coverage—grading 71.4 or better in each of the last three seasons, per PFF. He’s a pass-rushing threat, with nine sacks since 2024. And he’s an absolute force in the run game, as well. He’d also come with an insanely team-friendly contract, seeing as most of his money is currently tied up in signing and option bonuses that stay with the Eagles upon a trade. Detroit would only be due a prorated version of his $1.215 million salary this year, then they would have an option for 2027 to pay Baun a $14.4 million option bonus to keep him around in 2027. Now, that low salary would likely mean shelling out significant draft capital to lure him away from Philly. We’re likely talking about a second-round pick, minimum. But if that’s the price, I’d pull the trigger. The Lions don’t just have questions at linebacker this year—with Jack Campbell’s future in football unknown, Jimmy Rolder on season-ending IR, and Devin White also on IR. But Detroit also has questions beyond this year. Only Campbell, Derrick Barnes, and Rolder are signed for 2027, and there’s an out in Barnes’ contract if Detroit wishes to move on. Baun would give the Lions a head start on fortifying their linebacker room for the future. What is your dream trade for the Lions before the 4 p.m. ET deadline on Tuesday? title: Teams interested in Sam LaPorta believe Lions want to ‘work out a long-term deal’
summary: With the trade deadline looming, the Detroit Lions are reportedly getting calls about the potential availability of former All-Pro tight end Sam LaPorta. According to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler, teams are under the impression that the Lions are not interested in making a deal, preferring to keep him and reach a long-term contract extension. LaPorta is […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Nathan Ray Seebeck-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect With the trade deadline looming, the Detroit Lions are reportedly getting calls about the potential availability of former All-Pro tight end Sam LaPorta. According to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler, teams are under the impression that the Lions are not interested in making a deal, preferring to keep him and reach a long-term contract extension. The Lions have received calls on TE Sam LaPorta, but teams have gotten the impression that Detroit would like to keep him and try to work out a long-terms deal eventually. pic.twitter.com/1OYQbcqq1U — Jeremy Fowler (@JFowlerESPN) November 9, 2026 LaPorta is in the final year of his rookie contract, and both he and the team have been open about wanting to sign an extension. Unfortunately, reports have surfaced that the team and LaPorta’s agent have reached a stalemate, leading to some very public venting of frustration from LaPorta . “I think the combination of getting your heartstrings twisted as well as the violent sport we play—it sucks,” LaPorta said on the Pardon My Take Podcast. “It’s disappointing that you go out there every week and you bear the risk of getting hurt. Like last year, whatever it was, Week 9, Week 10, I break my (expletive) back for this team. And then I’m going out there this year, and I’m ballin’, and maybe they’re just not showing the love.” LaPorta spoke with the media just days after the podcast aired, wanting to add further context to his appearance. “I guess I wouldn’t expect anybody else to really even care, but, emotionally, for me and my family, it’s an important thing for us. We want to have stability,” LaPorta explained. “We’re excited; in the upcoming months, we’re going to have our first kid, me and my wife. We’re going to welcome our baby girl into the world in Metro Detroit. We want to be here with the Lions. “And I guess I’m getting emotional about it, but in the grand scheme of things, it’s really a business. And you have to respect what the front office is doing, because they’re the ones calling the shots. They’re the ones that brought me in. It’s my first team. They’ve been nothing but supportive of me and my career.” Lions coach Dan Campbell insists LaPorta’s contract situation—and his comments—hasn’t distracted the team because they know who he is as a person and teammate, but Campbell didn’t directly address the situation or the team’s desires beyond the playing field. General manager Brad Holmes has previously expressed a desire to reach a long-term deal with LaPorta, but has yet to address the media since reports of stalled negotiations. While not definitive, this report from Fowler suggests the Lions haven’t given up on getting a deal done. For more information, you can follow along with all the Lions trade rumors and transactions in our tracker .
author: Erik Schlitt

title: Detroit Lions confirm Andre Cisco trade; still looking to see if ‘something else makes sense for us’
summary: The NFL trade deadline is set to expire on Tuesday, November 10, at 4 p.m. ET, and while the Detroit Lions have finalized a trade to acquire safety Andre Cisco from the New York Jets (and released tight end Jackson Meeks in a corresponding move), coach Dan Campbell said that general manager Brad Holmes “hasn’t […]
full_text: Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell, left, and general manager Brad Holmes walk off the field after practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The NFL trade deadline is set to expire on Tuesday, November 10, at 4 p.m. ET, and while the Detroit Lions have finalized a trade to acquire safety Andre Cisco from the New York Jets (and released tight end Jackson Meeks in a corresponding move), coach Dan Campbell said that general manager Brad Holmes “hasn’t stopped” exploring options to upgrade their roster. While the Lions are getting healthier at safety—with the anticipated return of Kerby Joseph and potentially Thomas Harper—Cisco is a system fit, understands the team’s verbiage from his time with former Lions defensive coordinator turned Jets head coach Aaron Glenn, and helps upgrade the Lions’ secondary as a whole. “We’ve liked Cisco from afar, having played against him and then even in free agency when he was at Jacksonville coming out,” Campbell said. “So, he’s athletic, he’s versatile. He knows our system. He knows the verbiage. So, we feel like this is a guy that can help us here a little bit. So yeah, we’re excited.” Beyond the talent Cisco brings to the field, he also offers the Lions the flexibility to shift some of their existing players’ roles around, meaning a player like rookie Keith Abney, who switched to safety mid-season, could see his role expand back into some work in a more natural nickel role. “Well, it gives us flexibility,” Campbell continued. “Cisco’s obviously played safety, played nickel. He can play other things on third down in your dime package. So can (Brian) Branch. We get Kerby (Joseph) back eventually here. Kerby gives you flexibility; keep him where you need him or move him back and forth. And then you mentioned Abney. Abney’s got flexibility now: nickel and safety. So, it does. It gives us flexibility, is what it does, and gives us depth too in some regard, wherever that happens at.” As far as any other potential areas the Lions may want to upgrade, Campbell reiterated that Holmes is exploring options, but it needed to be the right fit at the right price: “It’s about: is there a piece that could help upgrade us? Is there really, and what is it going to cost you? […] Doesn’t mean that we’re not still looking; see if there’s something else that makes sense for us. But our unit is playing pretty good football right now. title: Detroit Lions trade for veteran safety from Jets
summary: The Detroit Lions are on the board for the 2026 NFL trade deadline. According to ESPN’s Adam Schefter, the Lions are trading for New York Jets safety Andre Cisco. In return, the Lions are sending the Jets a 2028 sixth-round pick. Cisco was drafted in the third round of the 2021 NFL Draft and spent […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 4: Andre Cisco #8 of the New York Jets talks to teammates in a huddle prior to the game against the Chicago Bears at Soldier Field on October 4, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions are on the board for the 2026 NFL trade deadline. According to ESPN’s Adam Schefter, the Lions are trading for New York Jets safety Andre Cisco. In return, the Lions are sending the Jets a 2028 sixth-round pick. Cisco was drafted in the third round of the 2021 NFL Draft and spent the first four years of his career with the Jacksonville Jaguars. He played in 63 games for the Jaguars, starting 47 games for them over that time. After his rookie deal was up, he signed a one-year, $8.5 million deal with the Jets in 2025 and re-signed with the team on a one-year, $2.5 million deal this offseason. This season, Cisco has seen his role diminished in New York after starting eight games for them last year. After starting the first three games for the Jets in 2026, Cisco has played a total of just 23 snaps with New York over the past five games. In Detroit, Cisco should give the Lions some much-needed depth at the safety position. Brian Branch recent returned from his Achilles injury and Kerby Joseph could be on the path to returning now that his practice window has been opened up. However, the Lions have been struggling with their depth at the position. Veteran Chuck Clark has been the primary reserve and has played okay, tallying his second interception of the season on Sunday. But Christian Izien has been benched, Thomas Harper remains on injured reserve, and the Lions have scaled back the work of rookie Keith Abney, who moved to safety midseason. This move could open up the opportunity to move Abney back to nickel cornerback. As for Cisco, he’s a versatile safety capable of playing both in the box and as a deep, coverage safety. He’ll be appealing to the Lions, because he’s an aggressive run defender. But he also has pretty good ball skills. In college, he tallied 13 interceptions for Syracuse, including seven in his freshman season. At the NFL level, Cisco has eight interceptions, 26 passes defended, four forced fumbles, and 2.5 sacks.

summary: Welcome to NFL Trade Deadline day! full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - OCTOBER 18: Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur and Green Bay Packers General Manager Brian Gutekunst talk prior to a game between the Green Bay Packers and the Dallas Cowboys on October 18, 2026 at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, WI. (Photo by Larry Radloff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome to NFL Trade Deadline day! All trades need to be finalized by 4 p.m. Eastern time today as teams try to make the last-minute moves they think they need to become contenders or stockpile future assets. We’ve already seen quite a few moves leading up to the deadline with a few big-name players arriving at new teams, but the eternal question in these parts is whether or not the Packers will do anything. Certainly the Packers have needs. They could use some help on the offensive line, even as the guard situation seems to stabilize, and a running back with any amount of actual juice would be a blessing. And, if you believe the rumors going around, they’ve been sniffing around just about any trade-worth defensive lineman with a pulse. But the question is whether or not any of those moves would actually fix anything for them. Would throwing a new running back behind the offensive line as it’s presently constituted actually improve the running game? That seems doubtful, and I’m skeptical of the idea that they could add any linemen who would make a real difference, either. And there’s also the question of price. Take Jonathan Taylor, for instance. He’d definitely be a better running back option than anything the Packers currently have, but it sounds like it’s going to take a king’s ransom to pry him out of Indianapolis. The best intersection of price and value might be on the defensive line, but even then price is a huge consideration, since the Packers are already without a first round pick next year. Brian Gutekunst has gone on record about his high opinion of the 2027 draft class, and that seems to be the consensus view. Would he really surrender another valuable pick for a short-term player? The Packers, again, undeniably have needs. But what it’d take to fix them might take them out of the trade market this year. full_text: (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Monday, the Green Bay Packers worked out six players, all either quarterbacks or tight ends. Currently, the team does not have an open roster spot on the active roster, but they do on the practice squad. In theory, they have space to add, at least until running back Chris Brooks and edge defender Micah Parsons return to the 53-man roster, which could displace someone to the practice squad. Let’s break down these players. QB Carter Bradley Bradley turned down college scholarships to power programs like Indiana, Mississippi, Pittsburgh, Rutgers, West Virginia and Wisconsin to start his college football career at Toledo, where he posted a 5-5 record before transferring to South Alabama for his final two seasons of eligibility. In the Sun Belt, he was named an all-conference player, earning him an opportunity with the Las Vegas Raiders as an undrafted free agent in 2024. He’s also had previous experience with the San Francisco 49ers and Jacksonville Jaguars, whose head coaches come from the same coaching tree as head coach Matt LaFleur. So far, Bradley — the son of long-time defensive coordinator Gus Bradley — has yet to throw a regular-season pass. This is Bradley’s second workout since he was waived with an injury settlement at the cutdown deadline. His other workout came with the Arizona Cardinals, coached by LaFleur’s brother. QB Jalen Morton Morton was previously a Green Bay Packer, as he signed with the team as an undrafted free agent back in 2020. He was cut during the preseason, but he eventually signed a reserve-futures deal with the Indianapolis Colts for the 2021 season, and he was waived again during the preseason. Since his stints in the NFL, he’s gone to play with the Hamilton Tiger-Cats (CFL), Birmingham Stallions (USFL/UFL), Southwest Kansas Storm (CIF), Houston Roughnecks (UFL) and Columbus Aviators (UFL). Notably, he’s a running threat, which could be one reason why the Packers want to add him before facing the likes of Kyler Murray and/or Carson Wentz. This is Morton’s first workout with an NFL team since the Aviators’ season concluded in the spring. Last season, Morton was 31 of 72 for 433 yards, four touchdowns and three interceptions for the Aviators. He also ran the ball 25 times for 140 yards and two touchdowns. TE Zach Davidson Zach Davidson is a TE prospect in the 2021 draft class. He scored a 8.79 RAS out of a possible 10.00. summary: Many moves are expected over the next two days, whether or not they happen. Follow along and voice your opinion on these moves in the comments section, if […]
full_text: (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Many moves are expected over the next two days, whether or not they happen. To try to cut through the fat and keep everything contained, we’re going to launch a tracker to give you all the news from the trade deadline. Follow along and voice your opinion on these moves in the comments section, if you have the chance. Jets EDGE Will McDonald IV demands a trade McDonald wants out of New York after being displaced by Kingsley Enagbare and first-round rookie Joseph Ossai. McDonald was picked right after Lukas Van Ness in the 2023 draft, when the Packers and Jets flipped first-round picks as part of the Aaron Rodgers trade. Colts QB Daniel Jones isn’t being traded Multiple reports are claiming that Jones won’t be moved, even though the Indianapolis Colts’ season is functionally over. Minnesota is a team that would have made sense if Jones were made available. Falcons trade S Jessie Bates to Jaguars Jacksonville sent a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick to Atlanta for the 29-year-old All-Pro safety. In the deal, the Falcons agreed to eat most of Bates’ salary for 2026. He’ll be a free agent in 2027, so the Jaguars will be able to collect a 2028 compensatory pick to backfill for their losses if they don’t spend on outside additions next offseason. Saints trade DT Davon Godchaux to Jaguars This one is interesting, from a Packers perspective, because Godchaux was a pre-draft visitor for Green Bay — players that the Packers usually attempt to target when available. Jacksonville needed more depth at the position after some injuries, which is why Green Bay is in the same market. For what it’s worth, I’ve heard buzz about the Packers being interested in the running back and defensive line market. Other teams looking around at defensive tackles are the New York Giants and the Minnesota Vikings (Jacksonville seemingly called everyone for a lineman). Moro Ojomo is probably the biggest name that’s out there right now, but I’m not sure there’s an offer out there that Howie Roseman likes. Jets trade S Andre Cisco to Lions The Lions’ secondary needs help, and they’re getting it in the form of safety Andre Cisco. He’s being moved for a 2028 sixth-round pick, according to ESPN’s Adam Schefter . Eagles trade Jordon Davis to Jaguars Well, I told you guys that the Jaguars called everyone about defensive tackles, didn’t I? Can’t say I expected them to be able to pull this one off, though. Davis, who once set the market for nose tackle this offseason before being passed by Vita Vea and Dexter Lawrence, is being sent to Jacksonville for the cost of a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick. ESPN’s Adam Schefter is now reporting that the Eagles will not be trading Moro Ojomo, who is on an expiring contract. No team has gone more “all in” on the deadline than the Jaguars, who have now made three trades and have lost a first-round pick, two second-round picks, a fifth-round pick and a sixth-round pick today.

title: LaFleur talks Ty’Ron Hopper, Aaron Banks injuries
summary: We got some injury updates from Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur on Monday, as he discussed the injuries to linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper and left guard Aaron Banks for the first time. According to LaFleur, Hopper’s injury actually happened pre-game, leading to Hopper bringing up that he felt something in his chest going into […]
full_text: (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images We got some injury updates from Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur on Monday, as he discussed the injuries to linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper and left guard Aaron Banks for the first time. According to LaFleur, Hopper’s injury actually happened pre-game, leading to Hopper bringing up that he felt something in his chest going into the game. After two defensive snaps, Hopper was pulled from action, replaced by special teams linebacker Nick Niemann. LaFleur doesn’t think that it’s a major factor moving forward, so there’s a good chance we see Hopper back on the field on Sunday. On the subject of Isaiah McDuffie, LaFleur said he wasn’t worried. Hopefully, the Packers have more than just two linebackers available versus the Minnesota Vikings, which was the scenario the team was in late in the game on Sunday. On the Banks front, LaFleur stated that Banks was dealing with a groin injury during the game. While getting his groin worked on, Kevin Zeitler entered the game (at right guard, with Laken Tomlinson flopping to left guard). After that one drive, Banks came back onto the field but was eventually displaced by Zeitler again. LaFleur stated that was a coaching decision. When asked about the guard situation, he replied, “We’ll evaluate that moving forward.” So far, six players have played the position for the Packers this season. LaFleur also said he’s “hopeful it’s not” a lingering injury for Banks. Lastly, when the subject of running back Josh Jacobs’ surgery came up, the head coach was hesitant to commit to a timeline. Going into the press conference, there were mixed reports on whether the injured reserve was on the table for Jacobs .

full_text: (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs dropped out early against the New England Patriots due to a broken ring finger on his right hand, which got caught on a facemask. Now, CBS Sports’ Matt Zenitz is reporting that Jacobs will have surgery and can miss up to three weeks — which thankfully includes the Packers’ bye week. If the Packers do want to work a three-week timeline with Jacobs, it means that he won’t be going on the injured reserve. That’s an important piece of the puzzle, as Green Bay is running out of injured reserve spots that will eventually be designated to return . Without Jacobs, the Packers have MarShawn Lloyd, Pierre Strong Jr. and Kaleb Johnson on the 53-man active roster at the moment. Lloyd did miss last week’s action with a knee injury, though. With that being said, the team has another back, Chris Brooks, with an open practice window — so there’s a good chance that he’ll be returning to the active roster eventually. — Update : Netflix’s Tom Pelissero is now reporting that Jacobs could go on IR, which would cost him four games (five weeks with the Packers’ bye). title: The NFL’s Other Credibility Problem: Replays
summary: It’s been a rough year for NFL officiating, as penalties are way up in frequency and, as a result, calls are still having a major impact on games. This has been discussed to death; however, I wanted to raise the additional issue of the NFL’s broadcast partners’ complicity. Yesterday, late in the Packers-Patriots game, when […]
full_text: (Photo by Billie Weiss/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s been a rough year for NFL officiating, as penalties are way up in frequency and, as a result, calls are still having a major impact on games. This has been discussed to death ; however, I wanted to raise the additional issue of the NFL’s broadcast partners’ complicity. Yesterday, late in the Packers-Patriots game, when the Packers had victory well in hand, and backup quarterback Tommy DeVito had replaced Drake Maye, the officials made a call that, in the grand scheme of things, didn’t matter. Patriots right tackle Caleb Lomu completely blew a block on Packers edge rusher Dani Dennis-Sutton, who capitalized by forcing a rushed throw from DeVito. Dennis-Sutton made some light contact with DeVito just after the throw, best described as “maybe a light push” or perhaps “brushing by.” Here, take a look. Dennis-Sutton was flagged for a 15-yard unnecessary roughness penalty on this play for the love tap, which is ridiculous, but if you were watching the game, you probably didn’t know how ridiculous it actually was. You see, Fox never showed a replay, which would have almost certainly led to yet another discussion of how the league is protecting quarterbacks to an absurd extent, or worse. Let’s talk about the “or worse” because while this play did not have an impact on the outcome of the game, it absolutely did have an enormous impact on the outcome of the drive . The result of this play would have been a third and goal from the Green Bay eight-yard line, and a good chance that they Packer defense holds the Patriots to either three or zero points, depending on how aggressive they wanted to be. Instead, the call gifted the Pats a first down at the Packer four-yard line, and on second down, backup running back Corey Kiner punched it in from the four, cutting the Packer lead to 45-27. The Pats would fail on the two-point try after a false start penalty. Major League Baseball has suffered several pitch-rigging scandals in the last year , where bettors conspired with pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz to throw specific pitches for balls in order to win hundreds of thousands of dollars. With live-action betting now ubiquitous, it is now possible to bet on individual events that don’t matter (much) to the overall outcome of a game, and with it comes extra temptation. One of the best ways to defend against such things (other than reversing course on the ubiquity of gambling) is to cover your games as transparently as possible, so that at the very least, anything suspicious is out in the open. The NFL, along with its broadcast partners, too often opts for the alternative, where they elect not to show replays of controversial or poor calls if they can avoid it. Sometimes this is impossible, but every football fan has experienced a play where they are screaming at their TV about not getting a replay. That strategy may have worked in 1996, but here in 2026 all it did was send me and several of my colleagues looking for the clip the following day because we were all wondering what we missed. It turned out what we missed was an extremely bad call that gifted the Patriots an extra three-ish (or six-ish) points. I have no issues assuming that a random poor call is just a mistake; however, once people start trying to hide things from me, they lose the benefit of the doubt. The league has an officiating problem this year. If they’re not going to show it and talk about it, I’m going to assume they are in on it. I am quite sure I am not alone.
author: Paul Noonan

title: Kevin Zeitler looked like Kevin Zeitler on Sunday
summary: I’ve watched so much bad interior offensive line film this season, and this was such a nice breath of fresh air. The signing folks spent all summer clamoring for finally got his first material snaps this Sunday, and boy did the royal we look correct. The Green Bay Packers’ Kevin Zeitler only had four pass-pro […]
full_text: (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images I’ve watched so much bad interior offensive line film this season, and this was such a nice breath of fresh air. The signing folks spent all summer clamoring for finally got his first material snaps this Sunday, and boy did the royal we look correct. The Green Bay Packers’ Kevin Zeitler only had four pass-pro snaps, but didn’t allow a pressure and even handled a stunt better than just about any interior lineman has in what feels like literal years at this point. Given that most of his snaps came in near-or-actual garbage time, most of those snaps involved running the ball, which the Packers actually did pretty well in his snaps. The important caveat is a lot of this came in garbage-ish time, when the Patriots were not going full bore. The counterpoint is that everyone in the building knew Green Bay was running. The Packers had a yards-per-carry of 4.93 in Zeitler’s 15 run snaps, and a success rate of 53%. If you don’t include the final drive, which was just to burn out the final bit of clock, the yards-per-carry number jumps up to 6.25 and the success rate all the way to 67%. In the non-Zeitler snaps, the run game was atrocious, with a yards-per-carry of 3.18 and a success rate of a truly abysmal 17.2%. Now, is Zeitler responsible for all of that difference? No. No offensive lineman is that important. But it’s not nothing. And how does the film look? Zeitler does fine here (more vertical displacement than anyone else). Morgan just gets beat across his face really badly and it blows the play up. pic.twitter.com/8eIT36DbmG — rcon14 (@rcon14) November 9, 2026 The Pacekrs don’t convert here because Morgan can’t successfully pull off a pretty difficult reach block, but Zeitler does his job. wins the initial rep and then Belton whiffs so badly he runs into Zeitler's guy and throws Zeitler off balance. pic.twitter.com/imhjbfgP9y — rcon14 (@rcon14) November 9, 2026 Belton, who had his worst game in over a month, ends up running into Zeitler’s man here, but there’s nothing wrong at all with this rep. don't get beat inside. Didn't get beat inside. pic.twitter.com/W43RShacfh — rcon14 (@rcon14) November 9, 2026 Designed quarterback draw where the entire objective is to not let the man beat you across your face, and Zeitler makes sure he has to take the long way around. split zone look here, kinda think Johnson shouldn't have hard cut this and just followed the hole right behind Zeitler. Solid gain either way. Good job by the OL. pic.twitter.com/3YFqtEiUKc — rcon14 (@rcon14) November 9, 2026 This is well-blocked across the board. Williams and Zeitler displace the nose, and Zeitler gets his butt into the hole and seals out the nose. I don’t think Johnson should have cut this back against the grain, but rather have taken this right off of Zeitler’s butt, but it ends up being a solid gain either way. this ends up turning into kind of a mess and Williams gets beat back across his face to plug up what had become a decent hole pic.twitter.com/vXBYBUa3gk — rcon14 (@rcon14) November 9, 2026 If Williams doesn’t get beat back inside, this play might have picked up a few more yards. Zeitler and Williams get plenty of vertical displacement here. Everyone else? Not so much. pic.twitter.com/386ylQ9pVb — rcon14 (@rcon14) November 9, 2026 Exhibit A of why Jager Burton was seen as a center prospect. He gets isolated with the three-tech here and gets stonewalled, which wastes the displacement Zeitler and Williams get on the nose. Belton has to make a pretty tough reach here given the front alignment, and can’t pull it off. Zeitler doesn't let the man across his face. John Williams just doesn't take the backer for some reason. Redman completely whiffs the edge man. pic.twitter.com/93kAvTMH02 — rcon14 (@rcon14) November 9, 2026 Zeitler does his job on outside zone, as he successfully reaches the 1-tech. Redman whiffs hard, and it blows the whole thing up, only worsened by no one (John Williams) accounting for the play-side linebacker. nothing life changing. Just not losing. pic.twitter.com/tUm0kHDYct — rcon14 (@rcon14) November 9, 2026 just doing the job pic.twitter.com/CBWKIi9fKh — rcon14 (@rcon14) November 9, 2026 A couple snaps of just doing your job. Not moving bodies, just winning the body shape battle. Zeitler does his job. Tough beat for John Williams. NE runs a run blitz into his gap and the nose is clearly holding him. Should have been a penalty, but the refs understandably just want this game to end. pic.twitter.com/6IXGqRp4Pd — rcon14 (@rcon14) November 9, 2026 Watching live, I thought John Williams just whiffed this, but it’s a tough beat for him here. New England calls a run blitz into his gap (always rough on combo blocks), and he gets held by the nose tackle, so he can’t even reach the linebacker. OZ here. Jonnu and Belton lose the end man here and blows up the angle. OL got enough shift to create a crease and it's still a four yard gain. pic.twitter.com/sw1RTYdtWi — rcon14 (@rcon14) November 9, 2026 Another successful reach by Zeitler, but the front side of the play blows it up here. Jonnu Smith and Anthony Belton combine to not block the end man, forcing a sharp cutback that still ends up being a workable run. How much of the improvement in the run game is the game being mostly over? How much of it is not having Aaron Banks, who has been abysmal in both the run and pass game in his two games, and Travis Glover, who has not played well even if he’s been modestly better than the apocalyptic play of Jacob Monk, Donovan Jennings, and Jager Burton? Hopefully we find out. Based on his snaps this week, and the play of Aaron Banks, there’s no reason the Packers shouldn’t start Laken Tomlinson at left guard against Minnesota and Kevin Zeitler at right guard. Especially with the exotic pressure looks Brian Flores brings, the veteran’s experience and the more successful run game are going to be very important in a game that will more or less determine if Green Bay can make a run at the division this season.

title: Packers By The Numbers: Stats from the Week 9 win over the Patriots
summary: As we do every week in this space, we’re looking at some stats from the Green Bay Packers’ most recent game, courtesy of SumerSports. Today we’re looking at the 45-27 win over the New England Patriots in Week 9. Offense Let’s start with personnel usage. For the game, the Packers leaned primarily into 11 personnel […]
full_text: (Photo by Jaiden Tripi/Getty Images) | Getty Images As we do every week in this space, we’re looking at some stats from the Green Bay Packers’ most recent game, courtesy of SumerSports . Today we’re looking at the 45-27 win over the New England Patriots in Week 9. Offense Let’s start with personnel usage. For the game, the Packers leaned primarily into 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR), but not overly so. If you look at the full game numbers, they weren’t a huge 11 team: A lot of that is driven by the full-game nature. This game was well in hand by the 4th quarter, so it’s pretty safe to throw those numbers out. Through 3 quarters, here is what that breakdown looks like: 11 personnel: 65.4% (+0.387 EPA/play) 12 personnel: 30.8% (+0.454 EPA/Play) 13 personnel: 3.8% (-0.604 EPA/Play) As we’ve seen over the last few weeks, this seems to be their preferred way to operate. The 13 personnel EPA/play is lower than we’ve been seeing, but Whyle’s injury likely factors into that. Either way, an 11 personnel that features Tucker Kraft and a 12 personnel that features Tucker Kraft & Mark Redman seems like the best way to operate. Let’s talk about the passing game, because that’s what we really need to be talking about. Before the game, I went on Patriots on CLNS and said that Love was “ chucking chucking”, and he proved me correct. The protection was fine, but not elite, with Love being pressured on 42.4 of his dropbacks. That’s been par for the course, so got rid of the ball pretty quickly. For the game, Love’s average time to throw was 2.5 seconds, but his ADOT (Average Depth Of Target) was 13.0 yards. For reference, the highest ADOT for a QB who has taken more than 60 snaps this year is JJ McCarthy at 11.5 yards (for the season, Love is at 9.7 ADOT). Will those pressure numbers look better if we see a guard tandem of Tomlinson (LG) and Zeitler (RG) going forward? That’s certainly something I’ll be keeping an eye on. Love was tremendous no matter how you looked at it. When pressured? When blitzed? By coverage? One of the big things was Love in play action. The Patriots’ defense came into the game as a subpar play-action defense, and the Packers dialed up their usage a bit this week. They came into this week with a play action rate of 18.9%. This week they used play action on 31% of their passes, with an EPA per play of +1.16 on those dropbacks. Love’s success is certainly tied to the receivers, and they did their part. Matthew Golden was a monster. He caught all 10 of his targets (no drops!) for 164 yards and a TD. He had an EPA per target of +1.28 and an ADOT of 12 yards. MATTHEW GOLDEN IS TAKING OVER GBvsNE on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/GRgg5MOShA — NFL (@NFL) November 8, 2026 Golden’s best route was a Go route (2/2, 92 yards, +2.98 EPA per Reception). He was targeted most on Out routes (4/4, 39 yards, +0.82 EPA per Reception). Matthew Golden caught 10 passes for 164 yards and 1 TD and was still eclipsed in terms of yardage by Christian Watson. Watson 7 of his 8 targets for 171 yards and a TD (+2.07 EPA per Reception). Golden’s ADOT of 12 yards was high enough, but Watson’s ADOT of 23.75 is insane. He averaged 6.1 yards per route run and 2.4 yards after catch. He also had a remarkably casual one-handed catch that I’ll be thinking about for a while. Christian Watson just casually snagged it with one hand 😳 GBvsNE on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/rrMHQlpP7t — NFL (@NFL) November 8, 2026 In The New Thinking Man’s Guide to Pro Football , the late, great Paul Zimmerman (aka, Dr. Z), relayed an anecdote about about a catch from Don Hutson. As Dr. Z tells it: Edmond F. Rovner, a lawyer from Bethesda, MD, says that he will take a lie detector test that he once saw Hutson catch a low pass, one-handed, in full stride, with the palm of his hand facing downward. Dr. Z goes on to say that he does not believe this story. Until this week, it always seemed like an insane catch. After seeing this catch from Watson, I’m starting to believe. (That’s one of the all-time great football books, by the way. If you haven’t read it, you should fix that.) Defense The Patriots were primarily in 11 personnel (65.6%), but, even then, the Packers leaned more heavily into Nickel than the Patriots leaned into 11 (Packers played Nickel on 77% of snaps). That’s essentially been the trend since Edgerrin Cooper went down, but I like that it’s continuing. Less Nickel means less Javon Bullard, and I’m not really a fan of a defensive group that doesn’t have Bullard in the mix. It’s a fairly common sense thing, but it’s something not every DC would do: find a way to keep your best players on the field. The Packers dialed up their blitz this week, blitzing on 41.3% of their plays and getting pressure on 47.8% of Drake Maye’s dropbacks. The blitz worked, too. We’re 9 weeks into the Jonathan Gannon experience and I’ve been extremely impressed. He does a great job of changing his approach every week, depending on the opponent. More than anything, he does such a great job at putting his players in their best position to succeed. It’s been a remarkably fun unit to watch every week…and Micah Parson should be added to the mix in the next couple weeks. Albums listened to: Lydia Loveless – Accolades EP ; Spanish Love Songs – Future Nausea
author: Dusty Evely

title: Packers Film Room: The snaps behind Trey Smack’s perfect day
summary: In this space, we look at the snap-to-hold operation on field goals and extra points. We’ve got a heavy week (7 kicks), so let’s get to it. Last week was rough. There was a missed kick, but more than that, Matt Orzech had his least accurate game of the season. How did he do this […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images In this space, we look at the snap-to-hold operation on field goals and extra points. We’ve got a heavy week (7 kicks), so let’s get to it. Last week was rough. There was a missed kick, but more than that, Matt Orzech had his least accurate game of the season. How did he do this week? One week after his worst performance, Orzech turned in his best. Even the snaps to the body were splitting the difference between body and hold point. Kick 1: Extra Point (Make) Nice snap, if a bit slow. Slightly to the body of Whelan, with the spin of the ball allowing him to catch it by the laces and get it down for a nice, easy hold. Ball is leaning slightly forward and away from Smack. Karl Brooks [94] is on the right side of the screen. He gets his arm wide, but it doesn’t do much to divert the path of the rusher. This was closer than it should have been. This was also the slowest snap-to-kick time of the day (1.32 seconds), which led to this being closer than it should have been. That’s on Orzech: his snap-to-holder time was 0.36 seconds, his slowest time of the day. Kick 2: Extra Point (Make) Nice snap. More or less the same as the last one. Slightly to the body, with the spin allowing Whelan to catch it by the laces. Good hold. Good kick. Brooks is slightly slow out of his stance on the right side and only barely gets a hand on the nameplate as the rusher flies past him. Snap-to-holder: 0.32 seconds Snap-to-kick: 1.27 seconds Kick 3: 41-yard Field Goal (Make) Same as the last two. Great snap, great hold, kick is a no-doubter. Once again, Brooks barely gets a hand on the rusher. With this kick set up on the right hash (as opposed to the dead-center positioning of the first two), the ball has to travel slightly back to the left, towards the rusher. This one was close. Snap-to-holder: 0.28 seconds Snap-to-kick: 1.24 seconds Kick 4: Extra Point (Make) Great snap, great hold, great kick. Brooks does a good job on the outside this time, but a rusher is able to split Aaron Banks [65] and Anthony Belton [71] and gets real close to blocking this one. This was Orzech’s second-slowest snap-to-holder time, which contributed to this close call. Snap-to-holder: 0.34 seconds Snap-to-kick: 1.31 seconds Kick 5: Extra Point (Make) Good snap, slightly to the body. Good hold. Good kick. Brooks gets a hand on the nameplate of the rusher as he dips past. It’s worth saying that, if the choice is a wide rusher or an interior rusher on these block attempts, you’ll take the man off the edge every time. Unless it’s a slow snap-to-kick time, it’s really hard to get a block off the edge. Still, it’d be nice to give up at least a little resistance. Snap-to-kick time here was 1.26 seconds, which won’t really give the edge a chance to block this. Snap-to-holder: 0.30 seconds Snap-to-kick: 1.26 seconds Kick 6: 51-yard Field Goal (Make) Good snap, to the body of Whelan. Orzech does a great job with his spin consistency: I can’t remember a kick this year where Whelan caught the ball by anything other than the laces in the same spot. Brooks gets a little bit more of the rusher this time as he tries to dip pass, so this is not particularly close to being blocked. Snap-to-holder: 0.28 seconds Snap-to-kick: 1.23 seconds Kick 7: 38 yard Field Goal (Make) Perfect snap, right over the hold point. Good hold. Good kick. There is no rush. The Patriots have given up at this point. Snap-to-holder: 0.32 seconds Snap-to-kick: 1.28 seconds For the first time this season, I tracked the snap-to-holder time and snap-to-kick time for every kick this week. I messaged briefly with Chris Kluwe over the past week and the range he gave me for snap-to-kick is between 1.2-1.28. Average time this week: 1.27 seconds. Albums listened to: The Gaslight Anthem – The ‘59 Sound ; Michael Nau – Popfly

title: The Day After the Day After: The Houston Texans bolt past the LA Chargers 44-22
summary: The Day After the Day After…when the raw, immediate emotions from the aftermath of a game diminish into the realm of clarity and the proverbial (or literal) hangover no longer haunts the mind. With that, a review of Week 9 Get right game (part deux): It might be harder to find a better opponent to […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 08: Calen Bullock #2 of the Houston Texans reacts with teammates after recovering a fumble during the second half against the Los Angeles Chargersat SoFi Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Ryan Sirius Sun/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Day After the Day After…when the raw, immediate emotions from the aftermath of a game diminish into the realm of clarity and the proverbial (or literal) hangover no longer haunts the mind. With that, a review of Week 9 Get right game (part deux): It might be harder to find a better opponent to face after a bye than the shockingly (pun somewhat intended) bad Chargers. While the Texans have underperformed based on preseason expectations, they are not like the Chargers. A fellow pre-season playoff contender, the Chargers opened the season 0-7. Catching a mercurial Texans team might have afforded them a chance to steal a win and salvage some pride in the season. Instead, this game went about as well as the Texans could hope for and then some. Houston put up a franchise-tying 44 points on the road, Stroud threw for 5 TDs and the defense got 8 sacks and 2 turnovers. Even the running game logged over 100 combined yards. All was not perfect, and Houston isn’t immediately back on the road to the Super Bowl, but this game checked a lot of boxes for Houston’s rebound hopes. Houston’s first get-well game came at the Titans to get off the winless streak. A second road-beatdown was a well-needed salve to start the second half of the schedule. Using the pass to set up the run: At times, it felt like the biggest problem for Stroud was not having enough footballs to throw around to all his receivers. 6 receivers had at least 2 receptions and over 20 yards receiving. Dell had his best game since he injured his leg at Kansas City in 2024, Boutte had a career day stretching the field and Collins merely added a catch-of-the-year option. Houston is never going to abandon the ground game but given that the offense moves more effectively through the air, the Texans might do well to favor the pass. Does it put pressure on the defense, especially if the team has multiple quick possessions? Yes. However, with the talent in the passing game and the noted shortfalls of the running game, Houston needs to play to their strengths. If nothing else, you borrow the Bill Walsh philosophy to use the pass to set up the run. Houston was more effective rushing the ball in the second half (69 yards vs. 35 1st half yards). With the Chargers needing to focus on limiting heavy aerial production, a decent ground game with Marks and company found a way to move the ball for effective gains. Trades all done?: At the time of publication, the Texans hadn’t added any new players via trade. If rumors are correct, the Texans are looking at help at the RB and safety position. Most might dream of Taylor, Barkley or Henry in the backfield, but would Houston want to pay up with their limited 2027/28 Draft capital for a back that is going to already stress a team that is going to be well over the cap at the start of the offseason. Pitre’s return aided the defensive backfield, but Blankenship’s absence and struggles are still issues. Plus, safety depth could help a squad that needs special teams reinforcements. While Caserio fears no trade, it does not seem likely that Houston will make another big move trade-wise (unlike division rival Jacksonville, which made some major trades in the past 36 hours to aid the defense). THE CRITICAL PLAY: 6:43, 2nd Quarter, HOU Ball @ HOU 37, 2nd and 5; QB CJ Stroud with a deep pass to WR Tank Dell for a 63-yard TD. Aside from the whole first-TD-in-almost-two-calendar-years-plotline, this play was actually critical to the game’s momentum. The Chargers just cashed in on Stroud’s INT to cut the deficit to 10-9. Houston, after scoring 10 points on their first two drives, had a punt and an INT on the next two. They needed to get something going. After a short 5-yard pass to Harrison, Houston set up in a shotgun passing formation. Dell, lined up in the slot on the right side, ran and out-and-up pattern, just getting behind the Chargers DB. Stroud hit Dell in stride with a deep strike, allowing Dell to sprint straight to end zone. While Houston would be forced to punt on its next possession, this TD seemed to uplift the overall play of the team, as it was the start of a 28-0 run in the game. FUN WITH NUMBERS: 12: Total number of TFLs for the Texans: This is what most expected from the Houston defense this year. This tied the Houston franchise for 3rd-most in a single game (@ TEN in 2023). The franchise record is 15, set against Seattle in 2009. The most in the Ryans’ regime: 14, against TEN in 2024. 2-1: Record in 2026 when Houston rushes for over 100 yards in a game. When we talk about Houston leaning into its effective passing game, this might be a counter to that. You can’t not run the ball (this isn’t the run-and-shoot), but finding that balance is critical. Play to your strengths, and if the passing game is doing its job, the running game will follow. GAME BALLS: WR Tank Dell: 4 receptions/105 yards/1 TD. Welcome back Mr. Dell. We’ve missed you. Now, about cleanly catching those punts… QB CJ Stroud : An INT…really? Well, he did make up for it with a 21-of-35/384 yard/5 TD day. I suppose that is adequate enough for a game ball. Texans DL: Logged 7 of the team’s 8 sacks and 9 of the teams 12 TFLs. Anderson, Clowney and Rankins are the first trio of Texans to ever record at least 2.0 sacks each in a single game. CB Kamri Lassiter: 2 tackles (1 solo)/1 TFL/4 PDs: If anyone needed a bounce-back game, it was Lassiter. Was he perfect? No (arguably the miscommunication on the Chargers’ 4th and 1 was more about miscommunication vs. individual corner play) but on this day, he looked more like the top CB2 of 2025 than whatever that was to start the 2026 season. Would be nice if he kept up that level of play. SHOULD BE FORCED TO PRESS ALL OF JIM HARBAUGH’S KHAKIS WHILE LISTENING TO HIS INANE PRESS CONFERENCES ON REPEAT: Texans punting game: If there was a part of the game that didn’t look all that great, it was the punting game. Only needed for 3 attempts, but Kroeger’s two first half punts are best not dwelt upon. Tank Dell, for all his receiving goodness, muffed a punt in the 1st half that could have seriously altered the momentum of the game. At least the squad didn’t allow the Chargers to even attempt a return. However, that part of the game is going to have to pick it up in the weeks ahead. Chargers OC Mike McDaniel: The Chargers did finally snap a 37 non-TD possession streak against the Texans, but that came in the 4th quarter of a game the Texans lead 38-9. The Chargers did add another TD, but aside from impacting the betting lines, the offense did not look good at all. Yes, LA was missing Ladd McConkey, but the team had struggled even with him on the field. Herbert still looks out of sorts and the McDaniel scheme with this offensive roster is the NFL version of square peg meets round hole. This first, and possibly only season in LA has been sheer [KITTEN] for McDaniel. The Texans, 3-5, continue their road trip with a jaunt to Cleveland to face the 5-4 Browns (and a few familiar faces). Kickoff is slated for this coming Sunday at noon CST on Fox

title: Horsepower or Horseplay? Individual performances to highlight from Colts’ Week 9 loss to Cowboys
summary: The Indianapolis Colts lost to the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday, 23-27, which wasn’t unexpected by any means given that the season has quickly snowballed into another lost year—with a fire sale now fully underway. To their credit, the reeling Colts, who have now lost 5 straight games and 14 of their last 16 games dating […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - NOVEMBER 8: Seth McGowan #20 of the Indianapolis Colts celebrates during the fourth quarter of a game against the Dallas Cowboys at Lucas Oil Stadium on November 8, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts lost to the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday, 23-27, which wasn’t unexpected by any means given that the season has quickly snowballed into another lost year—with a fire sale now fully underway. To their credit, the reeling Colts, who have now lost 5 straight games and 14 of their last 16 games dating back to last season’s brutal final stretch, showed more fight than in last weekend’s blowout ‘laugher’ loss in Jacksonville. Let’s get to the positives, the negatives, and maybe even a little in between: Horsepower Young Defensive Line: Despite veteran DeForest Buckner having departed back to the Bay, it was impressive to watch some of the ‘young pup’ Colts defensive linemen battle out there, including defensive tackle Ade Adebawore (5 QB pressures) , rookie Caden Curry (a sack and a fumble recovery), Laiatu Latu (a sack), and yes, even 2nd-year pro Jaylahn Tuimoloau (a sack), who’s begun to finally round into form, with longtime nose tackle Grover Stewart remaining the ‘veteran voice.’ RB Seth McGowan: In the midst of Jonathan Taylor trade rumors, McGowan has seen an increased workload as of late and taken advantage, averaging 7.5 yards per carry on 6 carries in this one, including a short 2-yard touchdown run near midway through the first quarter . I still think I’d ideally like McGowan more as a change-of-pace or the 2nd head of a two headed running back attack, than a featured every down rusher, but the rookie 7th round pick has been a pleasant find for Indianapolis so far this season and could be poised for a bigger role if Taylor is indeed moved before Tuesday’s trade deadline. WR Ashton Dulin: The 29-year-old continues to be one of the longer tenured ‘fan favorites’ still remaining on the Colts roster, as he’s gone from undrafted free agent to core special teamer to even starting wideout at times. Dulin showcased his elite speed in this one, turning a short Colts quarterback Daniel Jones wide receiver screen pass into a 55-yard touchdown catch-and-run down the sideline . Rookie Defenders: Safety Hunter Wohler, who missed all of his debut season with a season-ending Lisfranc injury, had a team-high 16 tackles (6 solo) filling in for injured starting rookie safety AJ Haulcy and was a force in run defense. Meanwhile, the pair of Colts rookie linebackers were also active, as CJ Allen had 10 tackles (4 solo) and Bryce Boettcher added 12 tackles (4 solo) respectively. That’ll certainly play. Spencer Shrader: Having his worst game of the season 2 weeks ago in Minnesota, Shrader looked more like himself, converting all 3 of his field goal attempts of 47-yards, 59-yards, and 50-yards . Perhaps most telling, the Cowboys coaching staff changed their minds on accepting a penalty, which the officiating crew said was legal(?), when they saw Shrader trotting on the field for a potential 61-yard field goal attempt. Horseplay QB Daniel Jones: At one point, the Colts had just 8 total passing yards midway through the 2nd quarter. Look, some of the wideouts playing meaningful snaps are preseason guys, and the offensive line hasn’t been great, especially in light of trading All-Pro left guard Quenton Nelson. However, it’s hard to win when your starting quarterback is dinking and dunking or checking down and rarely challenges the opposing defense downfield. At a certain point, you have to trust your receivers to win their one-on-one matchups downfield. This wasn’t a great Dallas defense coming in either, surrendering the 27th most points (26.6 avg. ppg). Jones’ game-sealing interception facing pass pressure off his back foot was about as predictable as it gets. RB: Jonathan Taylor: The main topic of ongoing national Colts trade rumors hasn’t looked like himself the past two weeks, perhaps making ‘business decisions’ or maybe because with limited carries in back-to-back games, he’s had trouble getting into the flow of the game. I’ve always thought Taylor is someone who gets better during the course of a game with the more carries he gets, sort of like a heavyweight fighter wearing the opponent down round-after-round, before eventually breaking a big ‘TKO’ run late. I’m not going to make excuses for him, because his fumble early in the 4th quarter with the Colts threatening to score a touchdown in the red zone simply can’t happen—and he has to keep his pad level down for that matter. That being said, if Taylor stays past the deadline, I think he’ll look more like his old self. I wouldn’t expect him to get 30 carries in a game anymore this season, but closer to the 20 carry mark we’ve seen. WR Josh Downs: Normally “Mr. Reliable” as a 3rd down slot target, Downs has been “Mr. Drops” over the past two weeks since reportedly requesting a trade from the Colts. He had a 3rd and 8 drop early in the 2nd quarte r , and then followed suit again with 1:45 left in the 4th quarter . If Downs wants to depart, fine, but he hasn’t backed up his surprising request with his play on the field, when such trade requests are typically reserved for more proven players with a longstanding history of production. The Colts are holding out hope for a 3rd round pick to move him, but after his recent performances, they may be realistically still looking at a 4th round pick. In the battle of ‘Downs brothers,’ his younger brother, starting Dallas safety, Caleb Downs, clearly got the upper hand of big brother with the game-clinching interception off Jones, a sack, and even better for him, leaving Indy with the road win. CB Sauce Gardner: Look, Sauce didn’t make the trade for the Colts to acquire him for two first round picks and AD Mitchell, but Indianapolis clearly hasn’t gotten the return for an elite shutdown cornerback that they were envisioning to-date. I actually thought Sauce had played well in this one, until he gave up a back-breaking 46-yard reception to Cowboys wideout Ryan Flournoy with 1:24 left that set up Dallas for the would-be game-winning touchdown. This wasn’t even All-Pro CeeDee Lamb who beat him deep, as an elite wideout that I could actually live with. Gardner’s just given up too many big plays downfield this year.
author: Luke Schultheis

title: What did you see from the Colts this week?
summary: I was able to watch the game in real time this week, as the Cowboys coverage reached all the way to the Southeast coast. When you get two teams that are not very good, sometimes a competitive game can take on the look of the teams playing well. I think this game took on that […]
full_text: I was able to watch the game in real time this week, as the Cowboys coverage reached all the way to the Southeast coast. When you get two teams that are not very good, sometimes a competitive game can take on the look of the teams playing well. I think this game took on that effect, at least at times. The Colts showing might not have been bad against a playoff caliber team, but the Boys came to town riding a 3 win mule. Neither team is going anywhere. We might say that we kept it close and had some good plays, but I think Dallas would point to multiple penalties hiding the fact that they outgained us by a couple hundred yards. Cee Dee did what many WRs do against the Colts, in the form of just going off. It didn’t matter that Pickins was out for the game and we have two good cover corners, as we seem to periodically let one person beat us. For the Colts part, it wasn’t brutal, and if coached by a slew of other offensive or defensive minds, they could have won. Expectations can’t be too high when you have traded your best offensive and defensive players (team captains to boot), while actively discussing other pieces of varying values. Your QB hasn’t demonstrated that he is healthy enough to be trusted with an offense and you have one interior defensive lineman that you can count on against the run. When we write Shane’s Colts coaching eulogy, and we will soon enough, traces of this game could be included. I will always believe that Jones was the better option than Richardson, until he wasn’t, which may have been game 1 this year. Jones is not willing to look past the outlet, which is far too often short of the sticks, even on 3rd down. He’s also not nearly as accurate from the pocket or on the run as his career numbers suggest. Even further, defenses do not have to honor his ability to beat you with his legs. Today, he got out there in space with one man to beat, or to find a receiver, and he couldn’t exploit it. SS’s end of game and half decisions just make you want to kick him. The defense gave up another 500+ yards. The lack of interior D is becoming clear with Buck gone. Tillery, Smith, and some guy named Givens (I swear, I didn’t know he was on the team), were rotating around Grove, but not effectively. I don’t know how long Haulcey will be out, but upon his return, I would have Wohler opposite Allen at LB, at least on passing downs. He is listed at 6’2” 213. Leonard once reported that he felt best, playing at 212, so Wohler is big enough to handle it and possibly the most willing tackler on the team. I saw enough to move on from JT. I know that everyone has a line drawn in the sand that they expect as a return, but I think we might blink at the deadline. He is the only player that will be under contract for next year, that I would expect a reasonable return for. I don’t know where the “price” we expect in return came from? The Colts have always been tight lipped, so why do we think that someone from the organization shared a price? I think that we as fans are buying into the speculation of those near the Colts, but not representing the Colts. I’d trade him simply because I think we can get as much out of the position for far less money, so I’d take a haul that most would not be happy with. I doubt that Dodds will have to answer the questions about the return he gets for traded players, as I haven’t heard him comment on the two he made, or toward any of the rumored deals. As for that, I think there is a lot of misinformation floating around about what has been offered. We have watched DJ play all season and based on that play, who believes that he is better than what they have in his current state? Too many dots are trying to be connected. Jones is currently not the QB that Minnesota saw in practices for a half of a season, two years ago. If they don’t move Downs or AR, it could be as simple as sending a message. If you want traded from the Colts, talk to the brass, not the press. We have facilitated deals for players who want to move on, or even cut them to do so, but it has always been perceived as us doing the player a solid, rather than caving. My main prediction is that most wont be happy with either our lack of movement, the return on a deal, or both. We are sort of in pitchfork mode, so I don’t know exactly what we could do that would make the majority of us happy. As far as positives from the game, I’d say Tenuta earned a start. From my perspective he looked to be an upgrade, but the Cowboys are not exactly known for their D. I like McGowan and as I have said, I wouldn’t be overly upset if I watched 20 instead of 28 carrying the load. I can’t always tell the difference anyway, as those numbers are hard to distinguish. On D, Allen will be fine with the green dot, unless he was the one telling the safety not to help. Wohlers was cleaning up a lot runs, just too far past the line of scrimmage. JTT is not a bust. I think Curry could be effective as a run stopping MLB in short yardage as well as offering some Edge help. I saw that Tankathon mocked us a DL at pick 38 and I can’t argue with that logic. What stood out to you?
