title: Jordan Davis modeled his game after John Henderson. Now he’s a Jaguar.
summary: After acquiring three different players the day before the 2026 NFL trade deadline, the Jacksonville Jaguars now have the third-lowest odds to win Super Bowl LXI (+750 on FanDuel Sportsbook). Jessie Bates, Davon Godchaux, and Jordan Davis are Jaguars. The future is looking bright. But let’s take a look in the rearview mirror for a […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - MAR 04: Jordan Davis #DL05 of the Georgia speaks to reporters during the NFL Draft Combine at the Indiana Convention Center on March 4, 2022 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Hickey/Getty Images) | Getty Images After acquiring three different players the day before the 2026 NFL trade deadline, the Jacksonville Jaguars now have the third-lowest odds to win Super Bowl LXI (+750 on FanDuel Sportsbook). Jessie Bates , Davon Godchaux , and Jordan Davis are Jaguars. The future is looking bright. But let’s take a look in the rearview mirror for a moment and go back to the 2022 NFL Combine. A 22-year-old Davis was coming off a unanimous All-American, national championship season at Georgia (while playing next to Travon Walker). He was a month away from becoming the 13th overall pick of the 2022 NFL Draft. When a reporter asked him which NFL players he modeled his game after, Davis chose a name familiar to every football fan in Duval County. YES! Jordan Davis brings up John Henderson as a guy he models his game on. @PFF_Steve , ADJUST THE RANKINGS! pic.twitter.com/IansQnmUHF — Sam Monson (@SamMonsonNFL) March 4, 2022 “One person that I really honed in [on] was John Henderson, from the Jacksonville Jaguars,” Davis said. “Very old name, and not a lot of kids say that nowadays, but he’s just one of those guys when I first started watching football that I was drawn to. He’s one of those guys that I studied. We’re compatible in stature and size. “In my eyes, he’s one of the greats.” Davis is uniquely built, even for an NFL defensive lineman. He measured in at 6’ 6” (98th percentile among DTs according to MockDraftable) and 341 pounds (96th percentile) at the combine. Other humans have that frame; very few have the explosiveness to match it. Davis also clocked a 4.78-second 40-yard dash (97th percentile) and a 123” broad jump (99th percentile). For comparison, Henderson stood at 6’ 7” (98th percentile) and recorded a 4.87-second 40-yard dash (90th percentile). Using PCA to find play comps for some of the combine standouts. Jordan Davis is definitely an outlier, and the top two comps are Ra'Shede Hageman and John Henderson pic.twitter.com/ulwopL1WCB — Pavel Vab (@Pavel_Vab) March 6, 2022 Through the first four and a half seasons of his pro career, Davis hasn’t panned out to be a Henderson clone. He’s collected 9.5 sacks and 86 solo tackles in 73 career games. Meanwhile, Henderson had 22 sacks and 245 solo tackles in his first 80 career games. Unfortunately, Henderson played long enough ago that I can’t use any advanced statistics to tell you why Big Jordan could still be the modern version of Big John. (For the record, Davis ranked fourth in run-stop win rate and run defense EPA among DTs last season.) Still, the comparison won’t end any time soon. Davis will be expected to help deliver the ring that long evaded Henderson, Marcus Stroud, DaVon Hamilton, and other DT franchise legends. Jacksonville has always been known for its standout running backs. Now that Davis is here, the defensive tackle position could be the bigger reason that the Jaguars are celebrated.

title: 3 things you didn’t know about new Jaguars safety Jessie Bates III
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars have made a major statement of intent by acquiring three-time second-team All-Pro safety Jessie Bates III from the Atlanta Falcons. The 29-year-old arrives in Duval County with an impressive NFL résumé, having established himself as one of the league’s premier defensive backs during his time with the Cincinnati Bengals and Atlanta Falcons. […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 25: Jessie Bates III #3 of the Atlanta Falcons appeals to referees after an interception during the third quarter against the San Francisco 49ers at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jacksonville Jaguars have made a major statement of intent by acquiring three-time second-team All-Pro safety Jessie Bates III from the Atlanta Falcons. The 29-year-old arrives in Duval County with an impressive NFL résumé, having established himself as one of the league’s premier defensive backs during his time with the Cincinnati Bengals and Atlanta Falcons. But there’s considerably more to Bates than his ability to take the ball away from opposing quarterbacks. Here are three things you might not know about Jacksonville’s newest defensive star. He pledged $1 million to help single mothers @jlbiii3 giving Falcons fans free pizza & Falcons swag through his JB3 Foundation . This lucky fan won a signed jersey from Jessie. #nfl #dirtybirds pic.twitter.com/1aPipsp9xs — Alison Mastrangelo (@AlisonWSB) August 16, 2026 Bates’ mother, Theresa, played an enormous role in shaping the person he is today. Growing up in Fort Wayne, Indiana, Bates and his siblings were raised by their mother, who regularly worked two jobs to provide for her family. His father wasn’t particularly involved in their upbringing, leaving Theresa to shoulder much of the responsibility. Bates has never forgotten those sacrifices. After entering the NFL in 2018, he and his mother established the JB3 Single Mother’s Initiative, a charitable project dedicated to supporting single mothers and their children. The initiative has organised special experiences for families, including shopping trips, Christmas presents, sporting events and weekends away. Bates was even named the NFLPA’s Week 15 Community MVP in 2022 after organising a memorable three-day experience for six single mothers and their children. His commitment to the cause became even more significant when he signed with Atlanta in 2023. Bates pledged to donate $1 million over the four years of his contract to organisations supporting single mothers in Atlanta and his hometown of Fort Wayne. It’s a cause that clearly means a great deal to Bates, who has spoken openly about the sacrifices his own mother made to help him achieve his NFL dream. His tattoos tell the story of his life Jessie Bates III has a legacy in Atlanta. A very special one. JBIII is one of the best to do it, imo. I am proud to have gotten to know him, to have learned a few things from him along the way. Jessie has traits and abilities you can't teach, and as a lover of the game, you… — Tori McElhaney (@tori_mcelhaney) November 9, 2026 Bates has plenty of ink, but there’s a lot more meaning behind his tattoos than simply filling up available skin. His mother, Theresa, is honoured with her name and birthday tattooed across his wrist, while his older sister and younger brother have their birthdays represented in Roman numerals on his shoulders. His chest features the words “Jesus gave me the strength to spread my wings”, while his tattoos also include references to his faith, his family and his hometown. Perhaps the most interesting is an Indiana state outline incorporating personal and popular landmarks from Fort Wayne, sitting beneath the words “Small city, big dreams”. Bates has also had his JB3 logo and the words “Just Believe” tattooed across his right ribcage, following an eight-hour sitting. In an interview with the Falcons, Bates explained that his tattoos serve as reminders of everything he’s been through and the people who helped him get there. They aren’t simply decorative. They’re a permanent reminder of where he came from and what matters most. He was a touchdown machine at Wake Forest Before he was an NFL All-Pro, new Jacksonville Jaguars safety Jessie Bates was an All-ACC playmaker for Wake Forest. pic.twitter.com/7aGDbOCM0f — Underdog CFB (@UnderdogCFB) November 9, 2026 Bates spent three seasons at Wake Forest between 2015 and 2017, establishing himself as one of the most exciting defensive playmakers in college football. After redshirting his first season, Bates announced himself nationally in 2016. As a redshirt freshman, he recorded five interceptions, returning two of them for touchdowns. Remarkably, he was the only freshman in the country to achieve that feat. His breakout performance came against Indiana, in his home state, with dozens of friends and family members watching. Bates intercepted two passes in a 33-28 victory, returning one 55 yards for a touchdown. He also recovered Indiana’s final onside kick to help secure the win. He wasn’t finished there. In the 2017 Belk Bowl against Texas A&M, Bates showcased his versatility by returning a punt 59 yards for a touchdown. It was the first punt-return touchdown in Wake Forest bowl history. He finished his college career with 179 tackles, six interceptions and 195 interception-return yards, the third-highest total in program history. The Bengals subsequently selected him with the 54th overall pick in the 2018 NFL Draft, and the rest is history. Jacksonville are hoping he can bring that same playmaking ability to Duval County. But wait – there’s more! If tattoos, philanthropy and college exploits isn’t enough knowledge about the Jaguars’ big trade acquisition, we’ve got you covered… He’s a massive car enthusiast: Bates inherited a fire-engine red 2008 Dodge Charger from his mother, eventually modifying it with new wheels, a radio and an upgraded exhaust. He was so attached to the car that he drove it all the way from Indiana to Cincinnati for his first Bengals training camp. His dream car? A Mercedes-Benz G-Wagon, although he admitted he would have to wait for his next big NFL contract before making that purchase! Perhaps that now comes in Duval County… His first NFL game featured his future team: Bates was taken to his first NFL game by his mother when he was in fifth grade. The matchup? Cincinnati Bengals against Baltimore Ravens. He was actually a Ray Lewis fan growing up, making his eventual selection by Cincinnati a rather remarkable full-circle moment. He’s a basketball and baseball guy, too: Football wasn’t the only sport Bates excelled at growing up. He played point guard for Snider High School’s basketball team and center field in baseball. He’s also remained a keen sports fan, regularly attending Fort Wayne TinCaps baseball games and local basketball events. He’s borderline obsessive about film study: Bates has previously revealed that his preparation begins long before the weekly practice schedule. During his time in Atlanta, he would spend Tuesdays organising defensive backs and linebackers for additional players-only film sessions. He carries two iPads – one for watching game film and another for taking detailed notes – and even creates individual folders for opposing offensive coordinators. That’s some serious homework! He became a father in Atlanta: Jessie Bates IV was born in 2023, during his father’s first season with the Falcons. He has spoken about how fatherhood changed his outlook and priorities, drawing parallels between his own parenting and the sacrifices his mother made raising three children. He’s got some interesting entertainment tastes: In a 2018 interview with Cincy Jungle, Bates revealed that his favourite television show was *Power*, his favourite film was *Southpaw*, and his favourite musical artist was Drake. His favourite food? Steak from Jeff Ruby’s Steakhouse. He also admitted that he was yet to try Cincinnati chili, although I imagine after five seasons in the Queen City I imagined he subsequently scratched that itch. His biggest fear is losing his mother: Asked about his biggest fear during that same interview, Bates gave a simple answer: God and losing his mom. Given everything Theresa sacrificed to help him reach the NFL, it’s perhaps no surprise that family remains…

title: Another trade! Jaguars land their defensive game-changer in Jordan Davis
summary: If there was any lingering doubt about the Jacksonville Jaguars’ ambitions this season, James Gladstone has just put it to bed. The Jaguars have agreed a blockbuster trade with the Philadelphia Eagles for defensive tackle Jordan Davis, sending a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick to Philadelphia in exchange for the former first-round […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 26: Jordan Davis #90 of the Philadelphia Eagles walks off the field for halftime during the second quarter against the Dallas Cowboys at Lincoln Financial Field on October 26, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images If there was any lingering doubt about the Jacksonville Jaguars’ ambitions this season, James Gladstone has just put it to bed. The Jaguars have agreed a blockbuster trade with the Philadelphia Eagles for defensive tackle Jordan Davis, sending a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick to Philadelphia in exchange for the former first-round selection. It’s the third defensive addition Jacksonville has made in a remarkable day of activity, following the acquisitions of Davon Godchaux from New Orleans and Jessie Bates III from Atlanta. But this is a different level of investment. Jacksonville hasn’t simply dipped into its draft capital to patch up a few holes. It has surrendered two premium selections to acquire a 26-year-old defensive lineman who could become a cornerstone of its defense for years to come. The Jaguars aren’t just buying to secure a place in the playoffs. They’re buying for a Super Bowl. Why Jordan Davis? EAGLES BLOCK THE KICK AND JORDAN DAVIS SCORES A TOUCHDOWN BECAUSE WHY NOT pic.twitter.com/XNcYthVUMm — NFL (@NFL) September 21, 2025 There aren’t many players in the NFL who can physically dominate the interior of an offensive line quite like Jordan Davis. Standing at 6-foot-6 and weighing 336 pounds, Davis is an imposing presence who brings an entirely different dimension to Jacksonville’s defensive front. Selected 13th overall in the 2022 NFL Draft, Davis arrived in Philadelphia with enormous expectations. His development has seen him become an important component of one of the league’s most formidable defensive fronts, earning a Super Bowl ring along the way. His 2025 campaign was arguably his best yet. Davis recorded career highs of 72 tackles, 4.5 sacks and nine tackles for loss, demonstrating that he could offer more than simply occupying blockers and clogging running lanes. He’s registered 31 tackles, 1.5 sacks and two tackles for loss through nine starts this season. Those numbers don’t necessarily jump off the page, but Davis’ value extends beyond the traditional box score. His ability to occupy multiple blockers, control the line of scrimmage and create opportunities for the players around him makes him an incredibly valuable defensive asset. For defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile, adding a player of Davis’ physical profile could be transformational. The Jaguars have already lost Davon Hamilton for the season, creating an obvious need in the middle of their defensive line. Godchaux provides an experienced replacement, but Davis offers something considerably more exciting: a potential long-term answer at the position. And there’s a further attraction. Davis has spent his entire professional career playing in Philadelphia’s defensive system under Vic Fangio, giving Jacksonville another player with experience in a defensive environment that shares some philosophical similarities with Campanile’s approach. The price of doing business The Jaguars are trading a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick to the Eagles for DT Jordan Davis, per @AdamSchefter . The Jaguars are making MOVES with this being their third trade for a defensive player today 👀 pic.twitter.com/B9i9STSy5p — Yahoo Sports (@YahooSports) November 9, 2026 Let’s not pretend this is a cheap acquisition. A first-round pick in 2027 and a second-round selection in 2029 is an enormous amount of draft capital to surrender for one defensive player. Especially when you consider that Chicago recently paid two first-round picks to acquire Tennessee Titans defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. But context matters. Jacksonville is 6-2, sitting atop the AFC South and playing some outstanding football. Its offense is among the league’s best, while Campanile has developed a defense capable of competing with anybody. The opportunity is there. The Jaguars have recognised it, and they’re acting accordingly. There’s also a longer-term consideration. Davis is only 26 and was signed to a three-year, $78 million contract extension by Philadelphia in March. This isn’t a rental player brought in for a desperate postseason push. Jacksonville is acquiring a player who can help them now and remain an important part of the defensive front beyond this season. The first-round pick could ultimately be a relatively late selection if the Jaguars continue on their current trajectory. That doesn’t make it insignificant, but it does change the calculation. At some point, teams have to stop treating draft picks as lottery tickets and start using them to improve a roster capable of winning a championship. Jacksonville has reached that point. Why would Philadelphia let him go? This is a question that needs answering. Whenever a blue-chip player gets moved from one roster to another, there has to be a reason, right? The Eagles have invested heavily in Davis, handing him a three-year, $78 million extension earlier this year. He’s also been an important leader in their locker room, making his departure all the more surprising. However, Philadelphia’s season has taken a significant turn for the worse. The Eagles have been struggling, and moving a player of Davis’ value for two premium draft selections gives Howie Roseman an opportunity to reshape the roster. The return is substantial. Philadelphia now has an additional first-round pick in 2027 and another second-round selection in 2029, giving Roseman even more ammunition to replenish a roster that has some significant questions to answer. There is also the situation surrounding Moro Ojomo. Philadelphia had reportedly been reluctant to move him, and Davis’ departure potentially creates a clearer path towards retaining the younger defensive tackle. It’s a significant financial and football decision, particularly after extending Davis just eight months ago. But Roseman has built his reputation on knowing when to sell, and he’s extracted a substantial return here. The Eagles may ultimately be comfortable with the decision. Jacksonville certainly will be hoping they regret it. Jaguars trade grade: A Jacksonville Jaguars’ trades today: 🏈Traded a 2nd and 5th to the Falcons for S Jessie Bates. 🏈Traded a 1st and 2nd to the Eagles for DT Jordan Davis. 🏈Traded a 6th to the Saints for DT Davon Godchaux. https://t.co/dbsP3sN9kp — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) November 9, 2026 There’s always a danger in handing out top grades for blockbuster trades. Draft capital matters, and surrendering a first and second-round pick is a considerable commitment. But the Jaguars have a genuine opportunity to do something special this season. They’ve lost important defensive starters to injury, identified the positions that need strengthening and gone out to acquire established NFL talent. Godchaux brings experience. Bates brings leadership and playmaking ability. Davis brings size, power, youth and the potential to anchor the defensive interior for the foreseeable future. Most importantly, these additions complement a roster that was already performing at an exceptionally high level. James Gladstone and Liam Coen clearly believe this team is ready to compete for the biggest prize in football. Rather than sitting back and hoping their existing roster is good enough, they’ve invested heavily in making sure it is. This is what going ALL IN looks like. The Jaguars have made their intentions abundantly clear, and the rest of the league have just been put on notice.
author: Simon Carroll

title: Jaguars double down on defense, trade for Davon Godchaux
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars aren’t messing around. Just hours after agreeing a blockbuster trade for Atlanta Falcons safety Jessie Bates III, the Jaguars have returned to the negotiating table, acquiring New Orleans Saints defensive tackle Davon Godchaux in a second significant defensive addition ahead of Tuesday’s NFL trade deadline. According to reports, Jacksonville will send a […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - SEPTEMBER 27: Davon Godchaux #92 of the New Orleans Saints looks on from the sideline during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Cesars Superdome on September 27, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jacksonville Jaguars aren’t messing around. Just hours after agreeing a blockbuster trade for Atlanta Falcons safety Jessie Bates III, the Jaguars have returned to the negotiating table, acquiring New Orleans Saints defensive tackle Davon Godchaux in a second significant defensive addition ahead of Tuesday’s NFL trade deadline. According to reports, Jacksonville will send a 2028 sixth-round pick to New Orleans in exchange for the veteran defensive tackle. The selection could be upgraded to a 2027 sixth-round pick if the Jaguars acquire one through the compensatory selection process, or via another trade. It’s another relatively modest price for an experienced NFL starter, but the bigger picture is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore: Jacksonville are going all-in. What does Davon Godchaux bring to Jacksonville? TRADE: Saints trading DT Davon Godchaux to the Jaguars. (via @CameronWolfe ) pic.twitter.com/RstMWuJrZy — NFL (@NFL) November 9, 2026 At 6-foot-3 and 330 pounds, Godchaux brings some considerable bulk to the Jaguars’ defensive interior. The 31-year-old was originally selected by the Miami Dolphins in the fifth round of the 2017 NFL Draft, spending four seasons in South Florida before moving to New England in 2021. He subsequently spent four seasons with the Patriots before returning to his home state of Louisiana with the Saints in 2025. Godchaux has built a reputation as a run-stuffing defensive tackle, providing a sizeable presence in the middle of the defensive line. He isn’t somebody Jacksonville should expect to transform their pass rush, however. Across 144 career appearances, including 128 starts, he has recorded 486 tackles and 5.5 sacks. His value comes primarily from his ability to occupy blockers, hold his ground against the run and make life more difficult for opposing offenses between the tackles. There is an obvious need for that in Jacksonville. The Jaguars have lost defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton to a season-ending quadriceps injury, leaving a gaping hole in the middle of their defensive front. Godchaux provides an experienced replacement who can contribute immediately, rather than asking the coaching staff to rely exclusively on younger, less experienced options. His 2026 production hasn’t been particularly impressive, with 14 tackles in seven appearances for New Orleans and no sacks. There are legitimate questions about how much he has left to offer at this stage of his career. Nevertheless, Jacksonville isn’t acquiring Godchaux to be a superstar. They’re acquiring him to provide some much-needed depth and physicality at a position where they have been hit by injury. A familiar face for Anthony Campanile Godchaux's not much of a pass rusher, but you'll be hard pressed to find many better gap controllers in run defense. Very good combination of instincts, play strength, awareness, and competitive toughness. Should be instant impact run defender up the middle. https://t.co/sT8UNeAeu9 — AJ Schulte (@AJSchulteFB) November 9, 2026 There is another interesting aspect to this acquisition: Godchaux has previous experience working within a coaching staff led by Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile. Campanile spent four seasons as the Miami Dolphins’ linebackers coach between 2020 and 2023. Godchaux was also in Miami from 2017 through 2020, meaning the pair overlapped during the 2020 season. That familiarity could prove useful as Godchaux makes the transition to Jacksonville. Campanile knows the type of player he is getting, while Godchaux should have some understanding of the defensive philosophy and coaching expectations that Jacksonville are trying to establish. It’s worth remembering that Campanile was coaching the linebackers rather than the defensive line in Miami, and their shared time was relatively brief. Godchaux was placed on injured reserve in October 2020 after appearing in five games. Still, there is a connection there, and the familiarity certainly won’t hurt when it comes to integrating a midseason acquisition. Campanile has already demonstrated his ability to build a formidable defensive unit in Jacksonville. Godchaux gives him another experienced body to work with as the Jaguars attempt to maintain that standard through the second half of the season. Jaguars trade grade: B This is a sensible piece of business from Jacksonville. A sixth-round selection for a veteran defensive tackle with 128 career starts is a relatively small investment, particularly when the team has an immediate need at the position. Godchaux isn’t going to solve every problem on the defensive line, and his declining production this season means there is some risk attached to the acquisition. There’s also the faint sting of reality after star names like Jalen Carter and Christian Barmore were bandied around as potential options. However, Jacksonville isn’t paying a premium for a player who needs to develop. They’re bringing in somebody who has spent almost a decade in the NFL and understands the demands of playing defensive tackle at the highest level. The injury to Hamilton makes this move particularly understandable. It’s not a spectacular acquisition, but it addresses a genuine weakness without costing the Jaguars significant draft capital. The Jaguars are ALL IN Jags 2027 draft picks after acquiring Jessie Bates and Davon Godchaux today: Round 1 Round 3 Round 4 Round 5 Round 5 (projected comp pick) Round 6 (projected comp pick) Round 6 (projected comp pick) Round 7 — Gus Logue (@gus_logue) November 9, 2026 Perhaps the most significant part of this trade isn’t actually the player Jacksonville has acquired. It’s what the move represents. The Jaguars had already made a substantial statement with the Jessie Bates trade; a genuine difference-maker at safety who brings elite experience, ball skills and leadership to the back end of Campanile’s defense. Now, they’ve followed that up by addressing another defensive weakness with the acquisition of Godchaux. That’s two defensive reinforcements in a single day, with the Jaguars surrendering considerable future draft capital to improve their chances of competing right now. Jacksonville entered the deadline at 6-2, leading the AFC South and looking increasingly like a legitimate contender in the AFC. There is little point pretending these moves come without risk. Bates is in the final year of his contract, and Godchaux is a veteran whose best football may already be behind him. The Jaguars are also reducing their collection of future draft picks, limiting some of the flexibility they would otherwise have had. But this is what competing for a Super Bowl looks like. The Jaguars have a talented roster, an explosive offense under Liam Coen and a defense that has already demonstrated its ability to compete with the best in the league. They have identified weaknesses, recognised an opportunity and acted decisively to address them. The Bates acquisition was the headline move. Godchaux is the reinforcement that helps make the first deal even more meaningful. Jacksonville isn’t sitting back and hoping their current roster is good enough – they’re making sure of it. And with time still left on the trade deadline clock, don’t be surprised if the Jaguars aren’t finished just yet.

title: Arrowhead Pride Midseason Awards: The Chiefs’ Most Improved Player
summary: There are eight games in the books — with nine more to go. The Kansas City Chiefs’ 2026 season reaches its midpoint in Week 10. Because the team’s bye came so early in Week 5, we have decided to move our annual awards to midseason. Nine members of the Arrowhead Pride writing staff each had one […]
full_text: (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images There are eight games in the books — with nine more to go. The Kansas City Chiefs ’ 2026 season reaches its midpoint in Week 10. Because the team’s bye came so early in Week 5, we have decided to move our annual awards to midseason. Nine members of the Arrowhead Pride writing staff each had one vote for our seven midseason awards, so nine votes will be tallied for each award. In this post, we’ll reveal our most improved player to this point in the season. DB Chris Roland-Wallace VOTING: DB Chris Roland-Wallace (4), DE Felix Anudike-Uzomah (3), DE Ashton Gillotte (1), CB Nohl Williams (1) Defensive back Chris Roland-Wallace joined the Chiefs as a rookie free agent out of USC following the 2024 NFL draft. An impressive camp saw him succeed in his long-shot bid for the final roster, and he instantly became one of Kansas City’s best special teams players. He flashed on defense throughout his first two seasons, but Roland-Wallace’s versatility has been instrumental as the Chiefs have managed injuries throughout the secondary early on. He played mainly safety to start the year as Chamarri Conner worked his way back from a training camp knee injury. As a safety, Pro Football Focus has given him a grade of 72.2 , ranking 20th out of 100 grades for the position. His 77.6 coverage grade on their metric ranks sixth of the 100 safeties. Pro Football Focus also credits Roland-Wallace with 14 solo tackles in run defense or open-field situations. With much of his work coming in the slot, Roland-Wallace has surrendered a somewhat high 84.6% completion percentage. However, he has been outstanding at limiting the damage in the middle of the field. Over eight games, he has surrendered only 6.4 yards per completion. In two games since veteran L’Jarius Sneed was placed on the Reserve/Injured (IR) list with a chronic knee injury, Roland-Wallace has seen his defensive snap count rise above 70% each of the last two weeks. The results on the field suggest he probably shouldn’t give up the workload, even if Sneed eventually returns. Roland-Wallace may never be a star, but he plays multiple roles and should stretch out a decent career as at least a high-end backup. Kansas City could have an interesting decision on him after the season. Roland-Wallace is in the final year of the three-year rookie free agent contract he signed in 2024. He will qualify for restricted free agency (RFA) following the season. Over the Cap projects the minimum RFA tender to be $3.8 million for the 2027 offseason. Because Roland-Wallace went undrafted, he would not net the Chiefs any draft-pick compensation if he signed with a new team (although Kansas City would have the right to match any offer). It is not hard to imagine another team signing him to a contract that may be difficult for the Chiefs—always tight against the salary cap—to swallow. Don’t be surprised if one of the team’s first offseason moves is a modest extension for Roland-Wallace to get ahead of this scenario.

summary: In Week 9 of the 2026 NFL regular season, the Kansas City Chiefs beat up on the New York Jets to advance to 6-2. Let’s see how the national media reacted to it in this week’s sampling of power rankings: ESPN: 6 (No change) Most important game of the second half: Week 12 at the […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images In Week 9 of the 2026 NFL regular season, the Kansas City Chiefs beat up on the New York Jets to advance to 6-2. Let’s see how the national media reacted to it in this week’s sampling of power rankings: ESPN : 6 (No change) Most important game of the second half: Week 12 at the Bills If the Chiefs want any shot of earning the AFC’s top seed, which would include a first-round bye and home-field advantage in the postseason, they’ll have to go on the road and beat one of their biggest rivals. A win over the Bills on Thanksgiving night would also boost the Chiefs’ odds of passing the Broncos to win the AFC West crown. The Chiefs have played their best this season when at Arrowhead Stadium, averaging 30.0 points per game. — Nate Taylor The Athletic : 4 (Up from 5) Midseason grade: A Sunday was just another example of Patrick Mahomes leaning on Travis Kelce (four catches for 72 yards). The two have now connected for 9,365 yards, surpassing Phillip Rivers and Antonio Gates for the most of any NFL quarterback-tight end pair. The Chiefs may have injuries at wide receiver, but they still rank fourth in the league in EPA per play. — Chad Graff and Josh Kendall Pro Football Talk : 6 (Up from 7) The kicker position shouldn’t be a pick-your-poison proposition. — Mike Florio CBSSports.com : 6 (Up from 7) The defense came alive in a big way against the Jets, getting five sacks. That’s something they will need going forward. The good news was they escaped a possible major injury for Patrick Mahomes. — Pete Prisco Yahoo! Sports : 6 (Up from 7) The most promising part of the Chiefs’ win on Sunday against the Jets might be that Chris Jones and George Karlaftis each had two sacks. Karlaftis had two sacks for the season before Sunday, Jones had just half of a sack, and that’s a big reason the Chiefs’ pass rush ranked near the bottom of the league. Even with five sacks as a team Sunday, Kansas City still has just 14 sacks. That’s the fourth-lowest mark in the NFL. The Chiefs have been doing fine on defense without much of a pass rush, ranking top 10 in yards and points allowed. But it’s hard to be a top-10 defense while ranking in the bottom five in sacks. Perhaps the performance against the Jets will get the pass rush going, and in turn boost a defense that has already played well. — Frank Schwab USA Today : 9 (Up from 10) It’s easy to miss, but coordinator Steve Spagnuolo’s defense is starting to find a groove − allowing more than 300 yards just once since the Week 5 bye and surrendering more than 20 points just once over the same period. — Nate Davis Sports Illustrated : 9 (Up from 12) I wonder if there was a more wild series of events in a professional football game this year than, right before the half, Patrick Mahomes appearing to have sustained a horrific injury, the Jets squandering the subsequent possession with a missed field goal, Mahomes returning after mere minutes on the sideline and Harrison Butker missing both the initial field goal attempt and the post-penalty field goal attempt. The beautiful game, my friend. — Conor Orr Sporting News : 5 (Up from 6) Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce are up to connecting for 9,360 passing/receiving yards, a new record for a quarterback and tight end combination. Kenneth Walker III is on pace for 24 total TDs and can challenge the single-season franchise record of 27. — Vinnie Iyer FOX Sports : 4 (Up from 5) Patrick Mahomes ’ elbow injury gave everybody quite a scare, but the guy is just superhuman, I guess. He got right back in the game and led the Chiefs on a few more touchdown drives in their rout of the Jets, and Andy Reid made it sound like he’s going to be OK in his Monday morning press conference. Obviously, they’re not the same team without him, so his injury needs to be monitored. When healthy, the duo of Mahomes and RB Kenneth Walker is as dangerous as any combo the Chiefs have had during their dynasty. And don’t forget, they’ve got a great chance coming up to prove it in the game they circled on their calendar all along: Thanksgiving night in Buffalo against the Bills. Stat To Know : Patrick Mahomes improved to 18-0 against teams entering at least four games below .500, extending the best record by a quarterback since 1970 (minimum 15 such starts). — Ralph Vacchiano

title: Chiefs Film Review: Analyzing the run game against the Jets
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs’ run game has powered their offense all season, and Sunday against the New York Jets was no different. The Chiefs’ running backs finished with 27 carries for 155 yards (5.7 yards per carry) with two touchdowns. What made the performance impressive was that Kansas City’s longest run of the day only […]
full_text: (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs ’ run game has powered their offense all season, and Sunday against the New York Jets was no different. The Chiefs’ running backs finished with 27 carries for 155 yards (5.7 yards per carry) with two touchdowns. What made the performance impressive was that Kansas City’s longest run of the day only went for 13 yards. It was a surgical performance on the ground, as the Chiefs finished with a 55% success rate. What powered the Chiefs’ impressive run game against the Jets? Let’s dive into some film: This is an impressive play from multiple offensive linemen on this play. Center Creed Humphrey creates displacement on the 1-technique, getting push and keeping him from falling back inside. Left tackle Kahlil Benson and left guard Kingsley Suamataia do a fantastic job on the backside of this run. Suamataia gives enough of a punch, and Benson is able to drive his hips into the defender’s outside shoulder and into the linebacker, opening up the cutback for Kenneth Walker to hit. This is impressive from a run-blocking and scheme standpoint. The pre-snap motion bumps the weakside linebacker out of the box, bringing a smaller safety straight into the run fit. The backside defensive end worries about the bootleg and stays home. This gives the Chiefs six blockers to block five, which creates a ton of space. The Chiefs run weakside zone here. Humphrey creates horizontal movement on the nose by driving on his inside shoulder. Benson cuts off the backside by getting around the three-technique again, which is not an easy block. Benson was dominant on the backside of these blocks, and that’s critical in the zone run scheme. This play is a good example of the value of having a player as dynamic as Walker in the backfield. The Chiefs run a shortside toss to Walker here, but Jets outside linebacker David Bailey is all over it. This should be a 1-2 yard run at most, but Walker’s ability to get all the way backside and make multiple defenders miss is rare. He puts an incredible amount of pressure on a defense horizontally. You’re not always going to get the right run call into the defense, so having a back that can mitigate those moments has transformed the offense. The Chiefs’ under-center run game has been rediscovered this year, and this was a great play using it. The Chiefs are running outside zone from 13 personnel. Benson gets stonewalled by the frontside defensive end to start this play. Benson actually does a good job sustaining his block, but there’s still no frontside gap. Fortunately, a massive gap opens on the backside as right tackle Jaylon Moore and right guard Trey Smith annihilate the three-technique and move him vertically, creating an easy cutback for Walker to hit. Being able to run both directions is an underrated part of a good run game. Kansas City’s offensive line can do that because both Moore and Benson can block frontside or backside in zone blocking, and the Chiefs’ interior offensive line does a great job clearing space to create cutback lanes. Walker’s footwork and vision set this up here. Walker gets the linebacker going the wrong way by getting backside, faking a cut left, then immediately bouncing it back to the right, which lets Humphrey cut him off. Smith and Moore help create the hole, but Walker’s ability to cut at full speed is rare and lets him set up defenders in the hole. Benson is excellent on the backside of these zone runs, and the Jets had no answer for it. Benson creates horizontal displacement and gives Walker the easiest cutback to get north on. Emmett Johnson didn’t get much run into late in the game, but in the limited run he got, he also flashed. The Chiefs run that weakside zone concept again, which Benson isn’t quite as good at. The defensive end is able to disengage his block and, in theory, has the angle to get to Johnson, but Johnson hits the jets to beat him to the spot and gets around the edge. Being able to hit that frontside edge is very important in any zone concept, as teams will overplay the cutback lane if you can’t hit that. Seeing Johnson do that on film is important. The Chiefs mainly run zone blocking with Walker, which makes sense with his skillset. However, this offensive line can block gap runs, and frankly, they should do it more. Johnson feels like a natural fit in that role, and the Chiefs give him a chance to do that here on his touchdown. The Chiefs are running power with Smith pulling. Suamataia and Benson set up this block again, annihilating the head-up defensive tackle. Johnson presses to the left, sees the space created by that block, and scores. The Bottom Line The Chiefs’ run game has been so much better this year for numerous reasons, including Andy Reid’s playcalling. But ultimately, personnel matters, and Kansas City’s personnel is better this year. Having Walker in the backfield has changed everything for the Chiefs. It’s brought life back to the Chiefs’ dormant zone run game, as they now have a back that can explode through the run lanes created by the offensive line. He can make people miss in space and is a threat to take anything to the house. Walker’s vision and agility have been special this year and power the offense. But the offensive line deserves credit too. Benson has been so much better than expected. Moore is shaky in pass protection, but he does give the team something as a run blocker. With Benson and Moore out there, it’s almost like the Chiefs have five guards on the field. Both Benson and Moore have guard traits as run blockers. They’re best when they can move defenders horizontally with their strength and first step. Having what is essentially five guards creates so much extra space for Walker to exploit, and that’s been huge this year.

title: Kingdom Keys revisited: Chiefs check most boxes in win over Jets
summary: Every week, “Kingdom Keys” identifies three things the Kansas City Chiefs must accomplish to win their upcoming game. Now, it is time to revisit those keys and determine whether Kansas City actually turned them. Against the New York Jets, the Chiefs accomplished two keys and partially accomplished another. Let’s revisit this week’s Kingdom Keys. Key […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Every week, “ Kingdom Keys ” identifies three things the Kansas City Chiefs must accomplish to win their upcoming game. Now, it is time to revisit those keys and determine whether Kansas City actually turned them. Against the New York Jets , the Chiefs accomplished two keys and partially accomplished another. Let’s revisit this week’s Kingdom Keys. Key No. 1: Stretch the field Verdict: Partially accomplished The offensive key was for the Chiefs to rediscover their ability to stretch the field. The Chiefs created explosive plays against the Jets, but they did not fully restore their vertical passing game. Patrick Mahomes connected with Travis Kelce for a 38-yard gain, while Rashee Rice produced a 21-yard reception and Walker scored on a 25-yard catch. However, those plays didn’t come from Mahomes consistently beating New York deep. Much of the production came after the catch. Rice’s 21-yard reception came mostly from his ability to gain yards after securing the football, while Walker’s touchdown came on a short pass that he turned into a 25-yard score. Even Kelce’s 38-yard reception was more of an intermediate completion that developed into an explosive gain than a true downfield strike. Mahomes finished 23 of 31 for 242 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions, but Kansas City still did not show that it could consistently threaten a defense over the top without Thornton. The Chiefs did, however, accomplish the larger goal behind the key. Their ability to create chunk plays underneath forced the Jets to defend more than just the running game and helped create opportunities for Walker. Walker finished with 102 rushing yards, 41 receiving yards and three total touchdowns on 22 touches. After being held below 70 rushing yards in consecutive games, he again looked like the centerpiece of Kansas City’s offense. The Chiefs got the result they wanted, but they reached it differently than expected. Kansas City generated explosive plays and reopened the running game, but the offense still needs to prove it possesses a has an impactful vertical threat. Key No. 2: Bring back Sack Nation Verdict: Accomplished The defensive goal was clear: the Chiefs needed at least three sacks. They finished with five. Even more encouraging was how Kansas City generated that pressure. Steve Spagnuolo’s defense recorded all five sacks without blitzing. Chris Jones finally delivered the performance Kansas City had been waiting for, recording two sacks after entering the game with only half a sack this season. George Karlaftis added two more, while rookie Ashton Gillotte contributed the fifth. The pressure became especially important after halftime. New York moved the ball well enough to reach scoring range several times in the first half, but the Chiefs kept the Jets out of the end zone and forced them to settle for four field goals. Once Kansas City took control of the score, Jones and the defensive line attacked Geno Smith in obvious passing situations. The Jets never scored again after halftime. This was the return of Sack Nation the Chiefs needed. Jones played like his CEO again, Karlaftis provided pressure from the edge, and the defensive line closed the game without Spagnuolo having to expose his secondary by sending additional rushers. The challenge now is turning one dominant performance into consistent production. Key No. 3: Win on third down Verdict: Accomplished The X-factor was third-down efficiency on both sides of the football. Kansas City needed its offense to extend possessions while its defense found ways to get off the field. The Chiefs succeeded in both areas. Kansas City converted six of its 11 third-down opportunities, while New York finished just one of 11. That difference let the Chiefs sustain touchdown drives while forcing the Jets to settle for field goals or give the ball back. The Chiefs’ defense was particularly effective when it mattered most. New York reached Kansas City territory several times in the first half, but the defense kept tightening in critical situations. That kept the game within reach even when the Chiefs’ offense and special teams struggled early. Kansas City then controlled the second half. The Chiefs scored touchdowns on their first two possessions after halftime, while the Jets’ offense repeatedly stalled. By the fourth quarter, a two-point halftime margin had become a comfortable three-score lead. Third down told the story of the game: Kansas City finished drives, while New York did not. The bottom line The Chiefs did not completely turn all three Kingdom Keys against the Jets, but they accomplished enough to earn a convincing victory. The performance was not flawless. Mahomes took too many hits, the offensive line suffered another injury, and Harrison Butker missed a 51-yard field goal. Kansas City must also continue searching for a dependable way to threaten defenses downfield without Thornton. But after two consecutive losses, the Chiefs needed a convincing response. Scoring 35 points, shutting out the opponent in the second half, and accomplishing most of their Kingdom Keys provided exactly that.

Butker going to go on a generational run. He won’t miss another kick the entire season.” Ninety minutes later, that generational run ended before it began as Butker missed a 51-yard attempt — after missing from 56 before a penalty gave him another shot. That led fans to believe his tenure with the Chiefs was nearly over, although coach Andy Reid said after the game he wasn’t ready to announce a change. Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker reacts to getting booed off field: ‘It is what it is’ | Entertainment Weekly “It’s part of it, you know,” he told reporters after the game. “I’m booing myself sometimes. People are passionate. Fans are passionate. They want to win games. They want me to make kicks. I want to make kicks. It’s part of it. That’s what you sign up for. I’ve got to do better.” The 10-year veteran is ranked the sixth-most-accurate kicker in NFL history, with an average of 87.1 percent of field goals made. But he’s been struggling significantly this season and currently leads the league with seven missed field goals (over eight games). title: NFL Trade Deadline 2026: Kansas City Chiefs latest news and rumors
summary: At 3:00 p.m. Arrowhead time, the NFL Trade Deadline will pass, and the league’s 32 teams will no longer be able to make deals with opposing front offices to acquire players. It’s the last chance for the Kansas City Chiefs to make a more significant addition than a free-agent signing, although the Cheetah — former […]
full_text: (Photo by Alika Jenner/Getty Images) | Getty Images At 3:00 p.m. Arrowhead time, the NFL Trade Deadline will pass, and the league’s 32 teams will no longer be able to make deals with opposing front offices to acquire players. It’s the last chance for the Kansas City Chiefs to make a more significant addition than a free-agent signing, although the Cheetah — former Chiefs wide receiver Tyreek Hill — is still available and reportedly will be ready to return to play in November. Trade rumors have been swirling around Chiefs Kingdom for a while, but it’s now or never for general manager Brett Veach if the team believes it needs an addition to have a shot at returning to the Super Bowl. The players mentioned in trade rumors Colts wide receiver Josh Downs Jaguars wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. Titans wide receiver Calvin Ridley Eagles wide receiver Dontayvion Wicks Eagles tight end Dallas Goedert Chargers edge rusher Khalil Mack Cardinals edge rusher Josh Sweat Jets edge rusher Will McDonald IV Colts defensive tackle Grover Stewart Arrowhead Pride’s Brandon Kiley broke down a few more options in a trade-deadline article focused on pass catchers: Eagles wide receiver Dontayvion Wicks Texans wide receiver Kayshon Boutte Chargers wide receiver Quentin Johnston Commanders wide receiver Treylon Burks Colts wide receiver Laquon Treadwell Commanders wide receiver Dyami Brown Completed trades across the NFL Guard Quenton Nelson: Traded from Colts to Seahawks Defensive tackle DeForest Buckner: Traded from Colts to 49ers Defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons: Traded from Titans to Bears Quarterback Jacoby Brissett: Traded from Cardinals to Ravens Safety Jessie Bates: Traded from Falcons to Jaguars Defensive tackle Davon Godchaux: Traded from Saints to Jaguars Safety Andre Cisco: Traded from Jets to Lions Defensive tackle Jordan Davis: Traded from Eagles to Jaguars Edge rusher Arnold Ebiketie: Traded to the Bengals According to NFL Insider Jordan Schultz , this trade has fallen through; it “is not physical or performance related.” It appears that Cincinnati wants to keep the compensatory third-round selection it would lose in trading for Ebiketie. Chiefs news and rumors NFL Insider Jeremy Fowler is reporting that the Jaguars plan to keep Brian Thomas Jr. through the trade deadline and have relayed that to interested teams. NFL Insider Ian Rapoport, on “The Aftermath” on NFL Network Monday afternoon , shared that the Chiefs have been interested in Brian Thomas Jr. “going back to last year.” He went on to say “it feels like a matter of when, not if; we just don’t know if something is going to happen this season or maybe in the offseason… one of the issues for the Jaguars is: how much do they want to help a team that could potentially be someone they could see down the road?” Fowler, on “The Aftermath” on NFL Network Monday afternoon, said the Chiefs “are lurking” and have been “looking hard” for a receiver. He floated the question if Kansas City would make a move for one of Thomas or Josh Downs. Rapoport also mentioned a fourth-round pick being the potential price for Downs. On Monday, NFL Insider Adam Schefter on “The Pat McAfee Show” shared that “the Colts have an offer of at least a [fourth-round pick] for [Josh Downs] right now; I don’t know why they wouldn’t move him at this point in time.“ During the second quarter of Sunday’s game, CBS sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson shared that she spoke with Chiefs general manager Brett Veach before the game. Wolfson reported the Chiefs’ focus “continues to be at the wide receiver position. There has been increased dialogue this week, and he found that some of the major franchise players he looked at are off the market, but they will continue to have conversations over the next 24 hours to see if they will get something done before the trade deadline.”

title: Andy Reid on trade deadline: Brett Veach ‘always keeps his eyes open’
summary: The NFL trade deadline is tomorrow, Tuesday, November 10th, at 3:00 p.m. Arrowhead time. Plenty of smoke has surrounded the Kansas City Chiefs’ potential activity before the cut-off, especially at wide receiver. On Monday, during a video press conference, head coach Andy Reid was asked about a potential move at the position. He began with […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The NFL trade deadline is tomorrow, Tuesday, November 10th, at 3:00 p.m. Arrowhead time. Plenty of smoke has surrounded the Kansas City Chiefs ’ potential activity before the cut-off, especially at wide receiver. On Monday, during a video press conference, head coach Andy Reid was asked about a potential move at the position. He began with two thoughts on the young receivers already in the Chiefs’ rotation. “[Jalen] Royals did a nice job,” Reid reflected on the Week 9 win over the New York Jets . “[Cyrus Allen], we’re kind of working in; we feel pretty good about him on some things there and his improvement, although he didn’t have much production yesterday. “But, as you know, Brett always keeps his eyes open,” Reid continued. “He’s always looking and trying to improve the roster. That part hasn’t changed; he’s out there searching and doing his due diligence with his guys.” Reid’s words reflect reports from sources like CBS sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson, who has covered a Chiefs game each of the last two weeks. She has heavily implied that Veach is searching far and wide on the receiver market, especially with how the win over the Jets ended: wide receiver Xavier Worthy (hamstring) came up limp while reaching for his hamstring. The thought of adding more firepower to Kansas City’s offense comes after a game in which the team scored 35 points despite fumbling away two possessions. The Chiefs rank second in total yards per game (384) so far this season. Reid pointed to what the offense looks like when it avoids shooting itself in the foot. “I think when you eliminate some of the penalties that we’ve had that have set us back, you’re playing pretty good football,” Reid said. “You can see, when you get rid of those negative plays, good things can happen. It’s hard to stop a run game, it’s hard to stop a pass game and a blend of that with the screens, it can be tough to stop at times, you just can’t go backwards.” Injury update Reid shared that Worthy is considered “day-to-day.” He shared the same update on quarterback Patrick Mahomes (elbow) and right tackle Jaylon Moore (ankle). “All three of those guys are kind of day-to-day,” Reid shared. “It was more positive news than negative news on Patrick; it looks like just a matter of some rehab in there and getting rid of some of the soreness. We’ll just see where it goes from there, but he’s in good spirits today.” When pressed on whether Mahomes would miss time in practice this week, Reid wasn’t ready to answer. “Give me a couple of days, just until we have to get out there and do it, and we’ll see where he’s at,” Reid answered. “He’s feeling pretty good today, but we’ll see where it goes. He’s sore; I’m glad we’re not practicing today.” No kicking change (yet) During his opening statement in the call, Reid shared that he has not made a decision about kicker Harrison Butker and potentially replacing him with practice-squad member Justin Tucker. It was the same answer he gave at the podium on Sunday. “With Butker, I haven’t made any decisions yet,” Reid said. “I’m just sitting and going to evaluate everything and go forward from there. I haven’t decided on reps during practice; I haven’t done any of that right now, so just going through and evaluating, and we’ll go from there.” Creed Humphrey snaps When asked about center Creed Humphrey and the bad snaps that have popped up often times this season, Reid acknowledged there needs to be improvement. He was asked if the problem was technique, mental or physical. “Yes. All of the above,” Reid responded. “He’s working on that, and that’s not like him, so he’s cleaning all that up; we’ll get that straight.” This season, Mahomes leads the NFL in fumbles recovered (8) primarily because of Humphrey’s low snaps that seem to pop up once a week.

title: Chiefs Week 9 snap count analysis: Kristian Fulton steps up again
summary: Welcome to Arrowhead Pride’s weekly snap-count analysis! Let’s take a closer look at the Kansas City Chiefs’ snap counts in the 35-12 win over the New York Jets in Week 9. The starting lineups are courtesy of NFL Game Stats and Information, and the snap-count data comes from Pro Football Focus’ premium stats. Starters (offensive): LT Kahlil […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to Arrowhead Pride’s weekly snap-count analysis! Let’s take a closer look at the Kansas City Chiefs ’ snap counts in the 35-12 win over the New York Jets in Week 9. The starting lineups are courtesy of NFL Game Stats and Information, and the snap-count data comes from Pro Football Focus’ premium stats. Starters (offensive): LT Kahlil Benson, LG Kingsley Suamataia, C Creed Humphrey, RG Trey Smith, RT Jaylon Moore, QB Patrick Mahomes, WR Rashee Rice, WR Xavier Worthy, WR Cyrus Allen, RB Kenneth Walker and TE Travis Kelce Starters (defensive): DE George Karlaftis, DT Chris Jones, NT Khyiris Tonga, DE Felix Anudike-Uzomah, LB Nick Bolton, LB Drue Tranquill, CB Kristian Fulton, CB Nohl Williams, S Chris Roland-Wallace, S Alohi Gilman and S Chamarri Conner Did not play: N/A Inactive: QB Garrett Nussmeier (Emergency third QB), CB Mansoor Delane (shoulder), FB Ben VanSumeren, DE Jack Pyburn, DT Peter Woods (neck) and OT Diego Pounds The big takeaway: Kristian Fulton continues playing well in relief With Delane out again, veteran cornerback Kristian Fulton stepped into a starting role for the second consecutive week. His role as a reliable outside cornerback was further solidified over 62 snaps and 39 snaps in coverage. He was targeted three times and allowed just one catch for five yards. He had a clean sheet on the penalty front after drawing a flag for over-aggressive coverage against the Denver Broncos . It’s the fourth game this season that Fulton has had to fill in for an injured Delane, and he has stepped up in a big way seemingly every time. When you look at his entire season, Fulton has been faulted for just 50 receiving yards on 8 catches (15 targets) against him in coverage; quarterbacks are registering a 32.6 passer rating when targeting the veteran cornerback. Kansas City has a strong trio of outside cornerbacks as it tries to figure out how best to cover the slot. The Offensive takeaway: Chiefs have a WR3 by committee The Chiefs’ wide receiver position continues to be led by Xavier Worthy (74% offensive-snap rate) and Rashee Rice (58%). After that, there hasn’t been a clear WR3 like there was when the group was completely healthy. Here’s how the rest of the group’s snaps broke down: Andrew Armstrong (22 snaps) — 0 targets Jalen Royals (21 snaps ) — 2 catches for 18 yards (1 first down) Cyrus Allen (19 snaps) — 1 target Allen took a step back in playing time after 30 snaps in Denver; he did fumble a kick return this week. Royals made a strong catch on a pass thrown over the middle in traffic, slightly behind him, to move the chains in the red zone. Armstrong seems to have a defined role as the strongest blocker of the trio, so the coaching staff is trying to use each player to their strengths while general manager Brett Veach potentially adds a proven player to the mix before tomorrow’s trade deadline. The Defensive takeaway: Chris Roland-Wallace has become one of defense’s key players Since veteran slot cornerback L’Jarius Sneed was placed on the Reserve/Injured list before Week 8, the Chiefs have trusted safety Chris Roland-Wallace as the Nickel and primary slot defender. With 45 snaps against New York, he out-snapped teammates in the secondary like safety Alohi Gilman (44 snaps) and safety Jaden Hicks (19 snaps). He has mainly been a staple in defending teams’ quick passes, but he was also used on blitzes a season-high five times in Week 9; he registered two hurries. While I believe rookie Jadon Canady could eventually prove he has the coverage chops to be trusted more in the slot, Roland-Wallace is proving defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo right in trusting him to this extent, even after an undisciplined post-snap play that got him ejected in Week 6. title: Chargers Week 9 PFF Grades: Backups come out better than starters in lopsided loss
summary: Even though the Chargers scored 22 points against the Texans, it somehow seemed like one of their worst outings of the year. Well, it sort’ve was before Quentin Johnston broke a short slant for a big 58-yard touchdown in the fourth quarter and the backups somehow found the end zone on their first drive of […]
full_text: Inglewood, CA - November 08: Los Angeles Chargers wide receiver Derius Davis (12) catches a touchdown pass against Houston Texans safety Calen Bullock (2) during the second half of an NFL football game at Sofi Stadium on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026 in Inglewood, CA. (Eric Thayer / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images) Even though the Chargers scored 22 points against the Texans, it somehow seemed like one of their worst outings of the year. Well, it sort’ve was before Quentin Johnston broke a short slant for a big 58-yard touchdown in the fourth quarter and the backups somehow found the end zone on their first drive of the game once they replaced the starting group. Defensively, this was not a good game for Chris O’Leary’s unit but how can you blame a group looking a bit deflated after balling out for seven weeks just to see their offense make zero improvements two months into the year. I don’t blame them for flopping finally. It was bound to happen. The Texans receivers were also making crazy play after crazy play. Sometimes that happens! But alas, 0-8 is still 0-8. Let’s go ahead and check out the grades from Sunday. Offense Best WR Derius Davis – 90.1 TE Charlie Kolar – 67.0 QB D.J. Uiagalelei – 65.2 OT Joe Alt – 63.8 RB Keaton Mitchell – 63.5 Davis posted his first elite game grade of his career on offense. He caught the second touchdown of the game from D.J. Uiagalelei, which was also the latter’s first career touchdown scored in the NFL. After the starting offense, including Justin Herbert, went 37 drives between touchdown drives, it took DJU and the backups just one! That’s pretty ugly! Alt continues to be the team’s best offensive lineman. He allowed no sacks and two pressures. Mitchell was an efficient player in his stats with some good chunk runs and a trio of passes caught which tied for the team lead on Sunday with Kolar. Worst FB Scott Matlock – 31.1 QB Justin Herbert – 46.3 RB Kimani Vidal – 48.0 C Jake Slaughter – 49.9 OT/G Alex Harkey – 51.6 Herbert threw his 11th interception of the season which also made it eight consecutive games with a pick thrown to begin this season. He did throw his sixth touchdown of the year, but even that was quite the lucky break when Johnston breaks one tackle on a five-yard slant and takes it 58 yards to the house. Slaughter looked rough in this one in all phases. Specifically, there was a screen play to wideout Tre’ Harris who caught the pass in stride to then run behind Slaughter and Cole Strange out in front of him. Both linemen missed the first defender in pursuit and Harris was tackled before he could even get started. Harkey was dealt a bad hand as he was forced to play right guard in place of the benched Strange who was initially replaced by Branson Taylor. Taylor was rolled up on after just nine plays and Harkey had to transition inside after spending most of this year at right tackle. Defense Best LB Marlowe Wax – 91.3 DT Jamaree Caldwell – 79.3 EDGE Akkheem Mesidor – 77.7 DT Justin Eboigbe – 77.7 LB Daiyan Henley – 69.7 Wax made one of the best plays of the game for the defense when he made a diving pass deflection that ended up in the arms of Daiyan Henley. Caldwell recorded the team’s best pass rush grade at 77.5. Mesidor had a top five grade in both run defense and pass rush. With the aforementioned pick, Henley had one of his best games this year with every single one of his individual grades finishing at 60.0 or above. Worst CD Donte Jackson – 28.6 S Genesis Smith – 33.9 CB Tarheeb Still – 34.9 CB Rodney Shelley – 37.4 LB Troy Dye – 40.6 Jackson returned to the lineup for the first time since Week Four and he wound up being the worst-graded player on the Chargers against the Texans. His 29.0 coverage grade was his worst mark this year as he allowed four-of-six targets his way to be completed for 58 yards. He was also called for the penalty. Smith posted a 19.0 tackling grade, by far his worst of the season. He had five previous tackling game grades above 75.0. Still also posted his worst game of the season vs. the Texans. His 29.5 was by far his worst this year as he allowed seven completions on eight targets for 79 yards (also a season high) and a touchdown. The cornerback room continued to look like chopped liver with Shelley also among the bottom five. That’s three cornerbacks in the red in a single week. However, Shelley did post great marks in tackling (79.3) and run defense (72.8).

full_text: Will the offense for the Los Angeles Rams run through Blake Corum and Kyren Williams? The running game for L.A. has been a massive part of their 3-game win streak, and with Puka Nacua missing time, they’ll likely need the run game even more. Will they keep using both backs or will one start to get more run than the other? Sean McVay may be tested to see if he can stay with the run as he and many coaches sometimes abandon the run or don’t use it enough to keep the defense in check. Even if the run game isn’t producing, it can still help take pressure off the quarterback and tire out an opposing defense. The Rams will need to continue to lean on both backs who can both run, block, catch, and seemingly do whatever the Rams are ask. How well can the run game be without Puka Nacua assisting? Week 10 will be a big test for the Rams and their offense. They’ll hope their running backs can help steer their team to their fourth win in a row. Rams PFF grades: Best and worst performers in win vs. Commanders (ramswire) “Jackson allowed two pressures, but both of them were just hurries and he didn’t give up a QB hit or sack. Corum forced two missed tackles on his way to rushing for 58 yards and a touchdown on 11 carries. Williams didn’t force any missed tackles but he did have a 71.1 pass-blocking grade.“ Rams trade deadline tracker: Latest rumors, news and buzz (ramswire) “The Los Angeles Rams went all-in this offseason by trading for Trent McDuffie and Myles Garrett, while also adding Jaylen Watson and Aaron Donald on defense. At 5-4, they’re not where they expected to be at the midway point, but the trade deadline offers them a chance to improve before the second half of the season begins. Sean McVay has indicated the Rams will more or less stand pat, knowing Davante Adams, Kobie Turner and Terrance Ferguson will all be back at some point this season, but plans always change .“ Myles Garrett: ‘I am that closer.
