title: NFL trade deadline grades: Deals for Jordan Davis, Jessie Bates III, Andre Cisco
summary: The Jaguars made a splash, but did they massively overpay for Jordan Davis? What about Jessie Bates III? Let's evaluate 12 trades.
full_text:
NFL analysts Ben Solak and Seth Walder are grading deals ahead of the 2026 trade deadline , which is Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET.

 When grading trades, we evaluate them for each team based on on-field impact, cap implications, draft compensation and effects within the context of a team's overall short- and long-term outlooks. How confident are we in knowing if this is a good or bad decision? And how big is the impact of this decision? Both questions play a role in our grades, though a low-impact decision can still receive a strong or poor grade. Even with lower stakes, clear-cut wins or losses still matter.

 Here are our evaluations for 12 deals so far, including three Jaguars trades from Monday, two quarterback moves for teams in need and multiple deals involving at least one first-round pick. Check back through Tuesday's deadline for grades on the biggest moves.

 

 
 Jump to a trade: 
 Davis |  Godchaux  |  Cisco |  Bates 
 Brissett  |  Simmons  |  Buckner |  Nelson 
 Harrison  |  Jurgens  |  Porter | McCarthy 

 
 

 

 Eagles trade DT Davis to Jaguars 
 Jaguars get: DT Jordan Davis 
 Eagles get: 2027 first-round pick, 2029 second-round pick

 Jaguars grade: F 
 Eagles grade: A

 There's no other way to start this: This trade is a disaster for Jacksonville.

 The Jaguars are absolutely right to go for it. Entering Monday, they had a 12.8% chance to win the Super Bowl, per ESPN's Football Power Index , second highest of any team and best in the AFC. And that's why I was OK with them rolling the dice on Jessie Bates III earlier in the day. A late-round pick for Davon Godchaux , too? Fine. But first- and second-round picks for Davis? Reckless would be putting it mildly.

 The numbers do not paint a picture of Davis being someone who is worth anywhere near that type of trade compensation. He has played 52% of snaps for the Eagles. That number is not particularly unusual for a run-stuffing nose tackle, but that's exactly the point: The Jaguars just dealt first- and second-round picks for a part-time player who helps only against the run! There is no world where that is worth it.

 Davis has a run stop win rate in the 71st percentile among interior defenders this season. He was in the 93rd percentile in 2025 and the 52nd percentile in 2024. This season, he has a 13.5% run stop rate -- the rate at which a player records a tackle on a run that resulted in a successful play for the defense by EPA -- per NFL Next Gen Stats, 14th best among defensive tackles with at least 100 run defense snaps and just behind former Eagles teammate Moro Ojomo . In other words, he has been a good  run defender, not elite.

 

 Though Davis recorded 4.5 sacks last season, the Jaguars can't count on that. Davis has been in the 12th percentile or worse in pass rush win rate among defensive tackles in each of 2024, 2025 and 2026.

 I thought that the Bears' trade for Jeffery Simmons (two first-round picks) was an overpay and that  last year's Cowboys deal for Quinnen Williams (first and second-round picks) was ill-advised. But in each of those cases the acquiring team was getting a much better player -- and someone who is dangerous rushing the passer.

 Davis is under contract through the 2029 season. The Jaguars will be on the hook for $18.4 million (mostly fully guaranteed) in 2027, $26 million in 2028 (most of which will become fully guaranteed in 2027) and $26 million in 2029. So relative to other nose tackles, he's not even cheap for Jacksonville going forward.

 The Jaguars did recently lose nose tackle DaVon Hamilton to a season-ending injury but had seemingly addressed that with the Godchaux trade earlier Monday. Even without that move, overpaying on such a massive scale for Davis does not make sense.

 This is one of those trades that ought to induce marvel at Howie Roseman and the Eagles. How were they able to swindle the Jaguars into this?

 

 With Philadelphia's season effectively over, it's easy for the Eagles to unload their players. But at this kind of price, I'm inclined to think the Eagles would have dealt Davis no matter their contention status or depth chart. Philadelphia should be thrilled at this return. -- Walder 

 
 

 Saints trade DT Godchaux to Jaguars 
 Jaguars get: DT Davon Godchaux 
 Saints get: 2028 sixth-round pick

 Jaguars grade: B- 
 Saints grade: B

 With DaVon Hamilton out for the season with a torn quadriceps , the Jaguars made their second deal of the day to bring in a replacement nose tackle, with Godchaux set to take over Hamilton's spot.

 

 In his 10th season in the league, Godchaux was playing just under 20 snaps per game for the Saints. His run stop win rate ranked in the 65th percentile among interior defenders this season, though he had struggled in the category the prior two years. Hamilton was just slightly better, with a 69th percentile run stop win rate at the position.

 The Jaguars' defense ranks third in EPA allowed per designed run, though they naturally felt there was risk that could drop off without replacing Hamilton externally.

 

 Godchaux has a $1.3 million salary and is in the last year of his contract. Given the Saints' situation -- 3-5 and still in the race for the NFC South but without real hopes of being an actual contender -- it makes sense for them to deal him for a draft pick while they can. -- Walder 

 
 

 Jets trade S Cisco to Lions 
 Lions get: S Andre Cisco 
 Jets get: 2028 sixth-round pick

 Lions grade: C 
 Jets grade: B+

 The Lions have acquired safety depth in Cisco while the team awaits  Kerby Joseph 's return. Brian Branch returned to game action in Week 7 after recovering from an Achilles injury suffered last December and has played alongside Chuck Clark . Joseph hasn't played since Week 6 last year due to a knee injury but recently returned to practice .

 In Cisco, the Lions get a veteran deep safety who could work with Clark to complement Branch until Joseph returns. But Cisco had been mostly relegated to the bench in New York, having not had double-digit defensive snaps since Week 3. That number dropped to zero on Sunday, with Malachi Moore playing ahead of him.

 Cisco is only 26 years old and costs $2 million this year between base salary and per game roster bonuses, with the Lions presumably taking over the remainder of the money owed. To me, this is pricey for a player who hasn't really been playing for the Jets and who, ideally, won't play all that much for the Lions if Joseph is able to return to his previous level of play.

 

 It makes sense for the Jets to trade him -- they are well out of contention and Cisco is on an expiring contract -- and I'm guessing they were pleased to get this kind of return. -- Walder 

 
 

 Falcons trade S Bates to Jaguars 
 Jaguars get: S Jessie Bates III 
 Falcons get: 2027 second-round pick, 2028 fifth-round pick

 Jaguars grade: B 
 Falcons grade: B+

 The Jaguars delivered the opening deal of trade deadline week, acquiring Bates to augment a defense that they hope can be part of a Super Bowl run. Bates is an impact player who delivers splash plays. Over his 3½ years in Atlanta, Bates recorded 14 interceptions and 11 forced fumbles. Yards per coverage snap is a pretty noisy stat for safeties, but over each of his seasons with the Falcons, Bates allowed 0.5 yards per coverage snap or better -- lower than the 0.6 average for the position -- per NFL Next Gen Stats.

 He'll take over the spot vacated by Eric Murray , who is out for the season with an elbow injury, and play next to Antonio Johnson . Johnson aligns as a safety only 57% of the time, as he sometimes plays from the box or on occasion even up on the line, while Bates has had more typical alignments. He is 9.5 yards from the line of scrimmage on average, spending 75% of the time at safety and 17% in the box. Despite that he has delivered big plays in the run game, too. He has 13 run stops this season -- plays where the defender makes the tackle on a successful EPA play for the defense -- tied…

title: NFL Power Rankings: Stacking all 32 teams for Week 10, plus important games left
summary: How does every NFL team stack up as we hit midseason? We made our 1-32 list and picked key games in the second half of the season.
full_text:
As the old sports cliché goes, "the next game is the most important one." But that's not true for all 32 teams at the midpoint of the 2026 NFL season .

 The NFC North is the first division in NFL history to have every team at least three games over .500 through Week 9. And on the other end, the NFC South made history as the first division with every team two games below .500 through Week 9. So, the intradivisional matchups down the stretch will be crucial in those divisions. And don't forget about the race for the No. 1 pick, which could come down to a Chargers-Dolphins matchup in Week 16.

 In addition to the 1-32 rankings, we asked our NFL Nation reporters to pick the most important game remaining for each team. Their selections ranged from matchups with postseason implications  to ones that might affect a team's draft standing .

 To form the 1-32 list, our power panel of more than a dozen NFL analysts evaluates how all 32 teams stack up against one another. Here are a couple of highlights from this week's rankings:

 
 The Packers have won five of their past six games, including a 45-27 win over the Patriots on Sunday. Green Bay is among four NFC North teams in the top 11 of these rankings, and it should stay there given the potency of its passing attack.  Christian Watson and Matthew Golden now rank third and fourth in the NFL, respectively, in receiving yards. They're the first duo to each rank top four in the league in receiving through Week 9 or later since Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle for the 2022 Dolphins. 
 Speaking of dominant passing attacks, the Texans climbed five spots in our rankings after 100-plus-yard performances from  Kayshon Boutte and Tank Dell  in Week 9. Granted, they faced  the winless Chargers . But Houston quarterback C.J. Stroud  has eclipsed 300 passing yards in three of his past five games. He ranks seventh in Total QBR this season. 
 
 Let's get into the full list, starting with the same No. 1 team from last week .

 

 
 Jump to a team: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN 
 CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND 
 JAX | KC | LAC | LAR | LV | MIA | MIN 
 NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF 
 SEA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 
 

 

 1. Buffalo Bills (7-1) 
 Week 9 result: Beat the Vikings 23-6 
 Week 9 ranking: 1 

 Most important game of the second half: Week 16 at the Broncos 

 

 Any game from the Bills' gauntlet between Thanksgiving and Christmas could be the choice, especially the road trip to New England in Week 13 . But the one matchup that could determine the Bills' chances of home-field advantage throughout the playoffs, and potentially force the road to the Super Bowl to pass through the Buffalo winter, is the Christmas Day rematch of last season's playoff loss . That game marked the fifth time in NFL history that the losing team in a postseason game did not punt once, per ESPN Research. -- Nick Suss 

 
 

 

 2. San Francisco 49ers (7-1) 
 Week 9 result: Beat the Raiders 38-17 
 Week 9 ranking: 2 

 Most important game of the second half: Week 12 vs. the Seahawks 

 

 The 49ers have a real chance to earn the NFC's No. 1 seed, so every week matters the rest of the way. But this game represents a great opportunity to stake an early claim to the NFC West. San Francisco is 3-0 in division games so far, and a win here would make it difficult for the Seahawks to catch up. And while the Rams also lurk (and meet the 49ers again in  Week 14 ), San Francisco needs to put the defending champions away before it can worry about anyone else. -- Nick Wagoner 

 
 

 3. Jacksonville Jaguars (6-2) 
 Week 9 result: Beat the Ravens 33-10 
 Week 9 ranking: 3 

 Most important game of the second half: Week 14 vs. the Steelers 

 

 The Jaguars play at Chicago in Week 13  in a matchup of two of the NFL's best offensive playcallers, but the Steelers game is more significant because of AFC playoff seeding implications. The Jaguars have better than a 98% chance of making the playoffs, per ESPN's Football Power Index , so a victory over the Steelers could earn them a higher seed in a tiebreaking scenario. It also would give the Jaguars a season sweep of the AFC North for the second time in franchise history (2017). -- Michael DiRocco 

 
 

 4. Chicago Bears (7-2) 
 Week 9 result: Beat the Buccaneers 27-24 
 Week 9 ranking: 5 

 Most important game of the second half: Week 16 vs. the Packers 

 

 The Bears need to gain ground in their division after early losses to the Vikings and Packers . Chicago's home rematch with Green Bay on Christmas Day carries significant tiebreaker implications and is the first of three straight NFC North games to end the regular season. The Bears will be in good position to defend their division title if they can pick up two NFC North wins over their next six games, beginning with the Lions on Thanksgiving  before the Dec. 25 matchup with the Packers. -- Courtney Cronin 

 
 

 5. Denver Broncos (7-2) 
 Week 9 result: Beat the Panthers 26-21 
 Week 9 ranking: 4 

 Most important game of the second half: Week 16 vs. the Bills 

 

 A road game against the Steelers (6-2) on Black Friday is close, but as things shape up right now, this Bills matchup could have a lot to say about home-field advantage in the AFC if both teams do their part between now and then. The Broncos already have a win over the Jaguars and have split the season series with the Chiefs. The Broncos have faced the Bills in each of the past two postseasons -- a Denver win at home last season and a wild-card loss in Buffalo in the 2024 playoffs. -- Jeff Legwold 

 
 

 6. Kansas City Chiefs (6-2) 
 Week 9 result: Beat the Jets 35-12 
 Week 9 ranking: 6 

 Most important game of the second half:   Week 12 at the Bills 

 

 If the Chiefs want any shot of earning the AFC's top seed, which would include a first-round bye and home-field advantage in the postseason, they'll have to go on the road and beat one of their biggest rivals. A win over the Bills on Thanksgiving night would also boost the Chiefs' odds of passing the Broncos to win the AFC West crown. The Chiefs have played their best this season when at Arrowhead Stadium, averaging 30.0 points per game.  -- Nate Taylor 

 
 

 7. Cincinnati Bengals (6-2) 
 Week 9 result: Beat the Falcons 34-17 
 Week 9 ranking: 10 

 Most important game of the second half: Week 14 vs. the Chiefs 

 

 The Bengals are favored in every remaining regular-season game, according to the FPI. The only game that is close to 50-50? A home game against Kansas City. After last week's results, Cincinnati has a plus-1.2-point differential in a game that carries the highest matchup quality (92.6 rating). The Bengals believe their Super Bowl aspirations aren't a pipe dream. A late-season win against a familiar rival could be what they need to bolster their belief into reality. -- Ben Baby 

 

 
 

 8. Minnesota Vikings (6-2) 
 Week 9 result: Lost to the Bills 23-6 
 Week 9 ranking: 7 

 Most important game of the second half: Week 10 at the Packers 

 

 If the season ended after Week 9, all four NFC North teams would make the playoffs. For the Vikings, that makes every divisional game critical. They put themselves in great position by defeating the Packers and Bears in consecutive weeks to open the season before losing to the Lions in Week 8. So the most important game is always going to be their next NFC North matchup. That happens to be next week. The Packers are playing much better than they did in Week 1, when they coughed up 22 fourth-quarter points to Minnesota. -- Kevin Seifert 

 
 

 9. Seattle Seahawks (5-4) 
 Week 9 result: Beat the Cardinals 17-3 
 Week 9 ranking: 8 

 Most important game of the second half: Week 12 at the 49ers 

 

 The Seahawks already lost to the 49ers in October. That means a season sweep by their division rivals would give the head-to-head tiebreaker to San Francisco, which already has a 2½-game lead in the NFC West standings. The Seahawks will be coming off their bye when they…

title: 2027 NFL draft order projections for Round 1, chances for top pick, more
summary: ESPN's Football Power Index projects the 2027 NFL draft order for Round 1, complete with each team's chances to pick in the top five, in the top 10 and at No. 1.
full_text:
The 2027 NFL draft is still months away, but with the 2026 season underway, we're starting to track pick order in Round 1. Which teams are in position to add elite prospects in the top 10 next April? What about the top five ... or even at No. 1?

 What follows is not the current draft order based on records. It is a projection of what ESPN's Football Power Index thinks the order ultimately will be by the end of the season. Each week during the season, the FPI projects the draft order by simulating the remainder of the season 10,000 times. Game probabilities are based primarily on the model's team ratings and game locations. The draft order is determined by the records the model projects for each team after 17 games, as well as each team's average draft position across the simulations.

 So where do things stand? Here are the full sortable projections, complete with each team's chances to pick in the top five, in the top 10 and at No. 1.

 
 See more on the NFL draft 

 
 

 First-round picks that have been traded: 

 
 The Jacksonville Jaguars ' selection was dealt to the Philadelphia Eagles in the Jordan Davis trade . 
 The Chicago Bears ' selection was dealt to the Tennessee Titans in the Jeffery Simmons trade . 
 The Green Bay Packers ' selection was dealt to the Dallas Cowboys in the Micah Parsons trade . 
 The Indianapolis Colts ' selection was dealt to the New York Jets in the Sauce Gardner trade . 
 The Los Angeles Rams ' selection was dealt to the Cleveland Browns in the Myles Garrett trade . 
 The better of Dallas' two selections (either its own pick or the Packers' original pick) was dealt to the Jets in the Quinnen Williams trade .

title: NFL Week 9 arrivals: Justin Jefferson rocks black leather trench coat before 'MNF'
summary: NFL stars continue to turn gameday arrivals into their own weekly fashion showcase.
full_text:
November football doesn't come with one dress code.

 

 The South could see two takes on fall fashion on Sunday. With sunshine and temperatures in the mid-60s in Charlotte, a varsity jacket or a knit polo would fit right in. In Miami Gardens, temperatures in the 80s leave room for breezy button-downs, relaxed trousers and shades.

 Out West, sunshine in Southern California and the Bay Area sets the stage for short sleeves and lighter fabrics. Seattle could call for a different approach, with possible showers in the forecast.

 The Northeast and Midwest offer more chances to break out fall staples. Temperatures in the 50s in Philadelphia and Foxborough are good territory for knitwear, and a cool Sunday night in Chicago gives players a reason to pull out a statement coat for the walk into Soldier Field.

 Here are the NFL's most fashionable arrivals from Week 9.

 

 Monday night fashion 
 
 
Fashion is what Justin Jefferson does. Ahead of the Minnesota Vikings ' "Monday Night Football" matchup against the Buffalo Bills , the star wide receiver pulled up a long black glossy leather trench coat with his signature sunglasses look. 
 
 
 
 

 Sunday night fits 
 Ahead of "Sunday Night Football," Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams wore a Supreme zip-up covered in varsity-style logo patches. Of course, Williams had an iced matcha in hand to complete his look plus a white cap. On the other side, Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield rocked a plaid bomber jacket.

 

 Sunday's best 
 
 Efton Chism III served up a welcome-back nod to fellow New England Patriots receiver Mack Hollins as he returned from injured reserve. Chism's black "Mack and Chiz" graphic tee featured the duo above a bowl of macaroni and cheese with the message "Don't change the recipe."

 

 Detroit Lions players arrived with tributes to All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell as he recovers from a neck injury. Aidan Hutchinson added a personal touch to his signature gallon water jug, labeling it "Jack," while Derrick Barnes , Malcolm Rodriguez , Joe Bachie , Amen Ogbongbemiga , K.J. Britt and Trevor Nowaske wore Campbell's jersey.

 Campbell, who has been placed on injured reserve, said in a statement Wednesday that he has full movement in his lower body and is making progress with movement in his upper body.

 

 
 Thursday night's fits 
 
Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence doubled up on dark denim for "Thursday Night Football," pairing a zip-front jacket with matching jeans and cream sneakers. Ravens rookie linebacker Ethan Burke , who was born in Annapolis, Maryland, and grew up in nearby Pasadena, showed some love to the Washington Capitals by layering a throwback Alex Ovechkin jersey featuring the Screaming Eagle logo over a black hoodie.

title: Fantasy buzz: James Cook III helps Bills overcome tough Vikings defense
summary: Buffalo's offense struggled on Monday night, but James Cook III was able to do enough to defeat Vikings.
full_text:
Everything that happens in the NFL has additional context when viewed from a fantasy football perspective. From position battles to injuries and so much more, the news cycle will constantly affect player values.

 Our fantasy football buzz file, with contributions from our ESPN fantasy writers and our NFL Nation reporters, aims to provide fantasy managers with the intel they need as news breaks around the league.

 
 Nov. 10: Cook helps Bills overcome tough Vikings defense 
 By Michael F. Florio 

 Despite a valiant effort by the  Minnesota Vikings ' defense, the Buffalo Bills ' offense won out on Monday night.  James Cook III  was the lone standout performance, rushing 31 times for 107 yards and a touchdown. Only Jahmyr Gibbs has run for more yards against the Vikings this season. Cook finished with 16.7 fantasy points, enough to be the RB8 for the week. His 31 carries are the second most in any game in Cook's career.

 Josh Allen had his worst fantasy night of the season, finishing with only 12.86 fantasy points. He threw for just 234 yards, with one touchdown and one interception. He also ran the ball six times for 15 yards. That was actually the most fantasy points any QB has scored against the Vikings since Jordan Love in Week 1 (19.48). Allen has a bounceback opportunity next week against the  New York Jets .

 Other notes from Monday's game 

 
 Buffalo's pass catchers were largely held in check. DJ Moore saw only five targets, catching three for 25 yards. In his four full games this season he has a 26% target share and a 41% air-yard share, averaging 14.3 fantasy PPG. 
 Dalton Kincaid caught all three of his targets for 28 yards. He has a rebound opportunity next week against the Jets, who have allowed the fourth-most TE yards. 
 Khalil Shakir led the Bills with four catches for 58 yards. He's a "safe floor" option who can be used in deeper leagues or as an injury/bye week replacement. 
 Minnesota's offense was a slog all night.  Carson Wentz   struggled to make competitive throws all night long, finishing just 8-of-25 for 81 yards, no touchdowns and two interceptions. He also lost a fumble. Wentz was replaced by  Max Brosmer  for the Vikings' final drive, with the team down by three scores. 
 Justin Jefferson  did see 11 targets, but was able to reel in only three of them for 58 yards. He has now finished with single-digit fantasy points in four of his last six games. He's averaging a career-low 56.1 receiving yards per game. It's not his fault, but the team's QB play has dragged him into "boom or bust" WR3 territory! Fantasy managers have to be hoping the Vikings trade for a quarterback. 
 Given the current state of the Vikings' passing attack, fantasy managers cannot trust either  T.J. Hockenson or Jordan Addison . Hockenson finished with 33 yards, while Addison had 28. 
 Jordan Mason led the Vikings with 48% of the team's snaps, Aaron Jones saw 35%. Mason turned eight opportunities into 42 yards, while Jones had six touches for 21 yards. Neither has reached seven fantasy points in the three games since Mason's return. Both can be benched until we see them produce. 
 
 
 Nov. 9: Nacua likely headed to IR 
 

 By Michael F. Florio 

 Puka Nacua is likely to be placed on the IR due to MCL and PCL sprains .

 There is no replacing Nacua on the Rams roster or on fantasy waiver wire. Konata Mumpfield , Jordan Whittington and Tutu Atwell will be the Rams' top receivers. With Davante Adams also on the IR, it wouldn't be a surprise to see the Rams trade for a wide receiver before tomorrow's NFL trade deadline.

 If they do not, expect the tight ends and running backs to be more involved. Tyler Higbee should be added off waiver wires. Also, Terrance Ferguson was set to return last week before suffering a hamstring injury. He should see a lot of volume if and when he is able to return.

 This likely means running back  Kyren Williams will see even more targets. Both he and Blake Corum should be started next week against the Cardinals.

 For those in need of waiver wire targets, check out Eric Karabell's Week 9 waiver wire article .

 
 Nov. 9: Cardinals lose Wilson for the season, await word on Minshew 
 

 By Michael F. Florio 

 Michael Wilson is out for the season due to a neck injury , the team announced Monday. Wilson had established himself as the Cardinals' WR1 and as someone fantasy managers could trust on a weekly basis, but he can now be dropped when waivers run this week. Arizona is extremely thin at receiver after losing both Wilson and Kendrick Bourne to the IR and having traded away Marvin Harrison Jr .

 Devin Duvernay , Simi Fehoko and Reggie Virgil  are the receivers still on the active roster. Zay Jones , James Proche II and Shedrick Jackson are on their practice squad. This likely means more targets and even more defensive attention for Trey McBride . He is the lone Cardinal that is a must-start fantasy option. In fact, with Jeremiyah Love on IR and Jacoby Brissett traded, he is the only Cardinals skill position starter from Week 1 that is currently playing for Arizona. He's worth stashing in deeper leagues as insurance behind Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins , if either misses time.

 Chase Brown is still Cincinnati's lead back, but fantasy managers have little to show for it. He had 12 touches for 75 yards and 10.5 fantasy points against Atlanta, despite leading the backfield in snaps, routes and targets. Samaje Perine had more carries (11-9) though much of his work came late with the Bengals ahead. Brown is averaging 17.8 touches per game to Perine's 6.8 this season. He also hasn't scored since Week 1, despite Cincinnati ranking in the top 10 in both yards and points per game.

Flournoy remains a flex option in deeper leagues if Pickens misses more time, though he'd have a better chance at consistent targets if Pickens were traded.

 Ashton Dulin led all Colts WRs with 12.8 fantasy points, but nearly all of it came on a 55-yard TD catch. He ranked fifth among Colts wide receivers in both snaps and routes run, remaining limited despite the touchdown. title: Seven things Solak thinks for NFL Week 10: Jaguars trades, All-Pro picks, more
summary: Get ready for Week 10 with takes on the Jaguars winning the AFC, Shedeur Sanders not earning a starting role, Fred Warner being the best player in football and more.
full_text:
Are you excited for NFL Week 10 ? With nine weeks in the history books and nine more weeks to go, I can't remember a season with as dense a top tier of NFL contenders. Nobody feels immortal, but many teams feel mighty. We're gonna learn a lot in Week 10 -- the Patriots against the Lions in Munich, the Vikings in Green Bay for a critical divisional rematch, and the Steelers at the Bengals on Sunday night -- and a lot more in the weeks to come. November should be fun.

 Every Tuesday of the NFL season , I'll turn the page from the previous week to the upcoming one with seven things I think. These aren't full-scale predictions. They aren't concrete takeaways from the past week of NFL action, either; those are fired off Sunday or Monday. Instead, these are the uncertain topics. They are things that might be true, but it'll probably take the next few games to find out. And at the bottom, you'll find a few extra half-thoughts ... just those little inklings I'm unable to shake.

 
 Subscribe: 'ESPN's Leaguewide' 

 
 This week, I'll start by lauding the Jaguars for going all-in on the trade deadline Monday, play some deadline bingo and then cast my votes for a midseason All-Pro team.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Jaguars are AFC favorites?   
 Quiet trade deadline on the horizon? 
 Who makes the midseason All-Pro team? 
 Sanders isn't good enough to unseat Watson? 
 Could Lock be a bridge QB in 2027? 
 Warner is the best football player? 
 Vikings need to trade for a QB? 
 Some extra inklings 

 
 

 

 I think ... the Jaguars are going to win the AFC (and maybe more) 
 They certainly think so, too!

 Monday was Jaguars day in the NFL, as second-year general manager James Gladstone made three trades during the day. He sent a 2027 second-rounder and 2028 fifth-rounder to Atlanta for safety Jessie Bates III . Then, he sent a 2028 sixth-rounder to the Saints for nose tackle Davon Godchaux . These two trades addressed Jacksonville's two biggest sudden needs after the season-ending injuries to safety Eric Murray and nose tackle DaVon Hamilton .

 

 But then, the stunner: The Jaguars sent their 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick to the Eagles for defensive tackle Jordan Davis , a premier run stuffer whom the Eagles had given a three-year, $78 million extension in March.

 It doesn't take a degree in trade deadline analysis to figure out that the 6-2 Jaguars, who traded away five picks, three of which were top-64 selections, are going for broke with a team they believe is on the inside track for the Super Bowl. These three players all serve critical roles in that effort. Let's talk about all three, starting with the most important.

 Godchaux is a -- nah. Just messing.

 Davis is a tricky player to figure out. He broke out in 2025 -- Year 4 of his NFL career -- with a career-best 16.5% run stop rate, good for fourth best among all defensive tackles. His run stop EPA (total value he generated on all of his run stops) was also fourth in the league. He ranked alongside Cameron Heyward , Quinnen Williams , Leonard Williams and Jeffery Simmons . 

 Year 3 or Year 4 breakouts for defensive tackles -- especially heavier tackles who really need to manage their weight and conditioning -- are more common than you'd think. Vita Vea made his first Pro Bowl in Year 4 and had his best run stop rate and run stop EPA of his career in that season. Dexter Lawrence II was a good run stuffer early but popped as a pass rusher in Year 4, as his pressure rate in that season remains his career-best mark.

 Davis entered 2025 with a lighter frame and tremendous conditioning. This season, Davis has seemed slower and more prone to sitting on blocks. His effort has waned at times. He could be in worse shape. He could also be disengaged from a bad team and bad defense overall.

 The Jaguars are betting that he'll play better on their competitive roster -- perhaps something closer to his 2025 form. They need him to, as he has huge shoes to fill. Through the first seven weeks of the season, the Jaguars' defense was the league's best against running back carries, ranking first in yards allowed per carry, first in yards allowed per game, first in success rate, second in EPA per carry allowed and first in opponent first-down rate. Hamilton was not the only contributor to that effort (edges Travon Walker and Josh Hines-Allen help, too), but he was key. The Jaguars want to be a light box defense -- six or fewer defenders in the box -- (35.6% light boxes through Week 7, 10th-highest rate) and need defensive linemen who can take more than one opposing player in the run fit. Hamilton was that player for them on the interior ... a space eater.

 

 Hamilton went down with a season-ending injury early in Week 8, and the potential decline in the Jaguars' run defense became a weakness worth monitoring. And the trade for Davis makes it clear that the Jaguars believe their defensive structure doesn't work without that scale-tipping player at nose tackle. When Hamilton was healthy, the Jaguars were allowing 3.8 yards per play with him on the field and 6.9 yards per play with him off the field, per NFL Next Gen Stats. That role cannot be platooned.

 Hamilton wasn't much of a pass rusher for the Jaguars, and Davis doesn't need to be, either. The Jags are one of the most aggressive teams in the league for mug fronts (defenders filling gaps near the line of scrimmage), stunts and twists, and fire zone blitzes. Remember, defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile was Brian Flores' linebackers coach for three seasons in Miami before he spent one year under Vic Fangio, who coached Davis in Philadelphia. (That shared year of language should help ease Davis' on-ramp into the new defense.)

 Though Campanile's blitz rate (30.9%) doesn't look particularly Floresian, he spins many of the same dials. The Jaguars are seventh in team pressure rate and first in time to pressure (Vikings are first and fifth, respectively) thanks to how many free rushers they manufacture in their blitzes and simulated pressures. Minnesota is first in quick pressure rate; Jacksonville is third. The Jaguars are second in total unblocked pressures; the Vikings are fourth.

 Flores uses these wild blitz looks on all three downs, and Campanile deploys them on long-and-late downs. Davis' value will be in creating run stuffs and manufacturing more second-and-longs and third-and-longs. He'll come off the field for these heavy-blitz looks and never have a high pass rush win rate accordingly, but his wins on early downs create these opportunities. The same can be said for Godchaux as Davis' backup.

 Bates, meanwhile, will be on the field for all of those wacky third downs, and he will feast on them. He is one of the smartest players on the field at any given time, quarterbacks included. The 29-year-old is not as fast as he once was, but his play recognition and ball skills still allow him to make high-impact plays on the football (three forced fumbles, four passes defensed). The Jaguars manufacture plays on the ball already; they're second in the league in defensive turnover EPA since the start of this season and first since the start of last season. Bates is another player who is excellent at addressing the football.

 So why make the move? Well, the Jaguars still needed better coverage presence in the last level of the defense. All of their defensive metrics are healthy -- third in EPA per drive, second in success rate, second in points allowed per drive -- save for one: explosive pass rate. They allowed an explosive pass on 14.4% of dropbacks, the sixth-highest rate. If Bates' center-field presence knocks that number down to league average, the Jaguars' defense will be difficult to expose.

 

 Bates is also a great tackler, which is critical in this system. Thanks to all the coverage rotations, mugged looks and sudden droppers, the ball comes out fast against Jacksonville. Opposing quarterbacks have a 2.73-second time to throw (fourth…

title: As the 'Peanut Punch' takes over NFL, how do teams counter it?
summary: After Charles Tillman popularized the punch 14 years ago, it has really taken off this season.
full_text:
ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. -- On Oct. 11, New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo fumbled away a win. The Giants lined up in field goal range coming out of the two-minute warning in overtime. Any points would have won the game.

 Washington Commanders defensive lineman Daron Payne had other thoughts. After Skattebo was hit in the backfield and had to use his forearms to shed a tackle, he couldn't get the ball back up to his chest. Payne threw his blocker out of the way and threw his fist at the daylight between Skattebo and the football. Ball out. The Giants' chance at a win was erased, and the game ended in a tie.

 Payne executed an increasingly popular -- and violent -- maneuver called the "Peanut Punch," wherein a would-be tackler throws a haymaker at the football in an attempt to pop it loose rather than wrapping up the ball carrier -- a technique popularized around 2012 and named after former Chicago Bears defender Charles "Peanut" Tillman.

 One day later, Buffalo Bills running back  James Cook III  fell victim to the same fate.

 

 Carrying from the Los Angeles Rams' 22-yard line early in overtime, Cook squeezed the ball low, around the left side of his abdomen. Had Cook had the ball higher, the incoming punch from linebacker Nate Landman might have left a bruise, but the ball wouldn't have had anywhere to go.

 With the ball at Cook's side, Landman found a crease between Cook's armpit and wrist and wedged the ball through. Ball out. Rams possession. Had it not been for a blocked field goal minutes later, Cook's fumble would've meant Bills defeat.

 But with fumbles come consequences.

 Though the Giants didn't explicitly call it a benching, Skattebo didn't receive any carries the week following his fumble. And despite Cook being the NFL's reigning rushing leader, Bills coach Joe Brady threatened punishments -- including decreased playing time if Cook didn't clean up his ball security.

 The NFL does not track punch attempts or their success as official statistics, and punches are almost impossible to track given the way defenders wield their arms while going for tackles, but it's clear that some of the NFL's best and most reliable ball carriers struggle with it.

 Since the start of the 2025 season, including the playoffs, Cook has fumbled 11 times to lead all running backs, a rate of once for every 44 carries. Skattebo, while not as prolific in total rushes, fumbles once every 40 carries.

 Defenders are punching at the ball nearly every drive, and being labeled a ball security risk makes you a target. The more you fumble, the more opponents try to make you fumble. As Brady puts it, every team the Bills play will have on the scouting report to punch at Cook.

 So as Cook and the fumble-prone Bills (6-1) prepare for their matchup against the Minnesota Vikings (6-1), who led the NFL in forced fumbles in 2025, let's examine the Peanut Punch's popularity, why it works, what offenses can do to counteract its effectiveness and what the state of ball security is in this ever-changing league.

 

 

 Countering the Peanut Punch 
 Offenses know how to prevent the punch. The technique exists.

 
 Carry the ball "high and tight," squeezing it across your chest diagonally at an incline. 
 One point of the ball should be in the crook of your elbow. 
 The other point needs to be somewhere between your chin and your opposite shoulder. 
 Apply pressure with your fingertips, bicep, forearm and rib cage. 
 Lower your pads. 
 Make sure your wrist is always above your elbow. 
 Make sure there's no air between the ball and your body. 
 Make sure the ball isn't visible from behind. 
 And when you sense contact coming, think "double in trouble" and brace by crossing your off-ball hand over your on-ball wrist. 
 

 

 The technique works, but ball security is a lot like darts. Darts isn't difficult because no one's cracked the mystery of how to throw a bulls-eye. It's tricky because there's a huge gap between knowing what to do and being able to do it with precise consistency every time.

 The punch has been more successful because carrying a football properly defies basic human instinct. We don't pick up speed by tucking our arms into our ribs. We don't change direction with our wrists above our elbows. And we don't fall to the ground without using our hands.

 As long as ball carriers are human, there's always going to be a sliver of daylight for defenders to punch at.

 "You've got to realize you've got the baby in your hands," former All-Pro running back Jamal Lewis told ESPN. "You've got the game in your hands. You've got the play in your hands when you're carrying the football. It's really just understanding that this is not a natural running style."

 

 'High and tight' 

 Lewis fumbled 22 times in his first three full seasons. He wasn't alone. Over the same four-year span (Lewis missed the 2001 season with a knee injury), Giants stalwart Tiki Barber fumbled 35 times.

 Reflecting on that period, Barber told ESPN he didn't think he had a ball security problem. A newspaper reporter actually tipped Barber off to just how frequently he'd been putting the ball on the ground, and it wasn't until 2004 when coach Tom Coughlin arrived in New York when Barber started to foresee consequences.

 "Coughlin comes in and he says 'Tiki, you're a great player, but if you keep fumbling you're not going to play,'" Barber said.

 So Barber and running backs coach Jerald Ingram went into the lab. "High and tight" became Barber's entire life. Anywhere he went, he had a football high and tight. On the treadmill. In the meeting room. Walking to the cafeteria.

 He instructed teammates to try to rake the ball away from him any time, anywhere.

 

 "It ultimately became second nature, so when I got in the games I wasn't even thinking about it anymore," Barber said. "You know what's interesting is I've been retired for 20 seasons now, but whenever somebody throws me a football, the first thing I do is put high and tight. It's so ingrained in my mind, I can't not do it."

 After fumbling once every 27 carries from 2000 to 2003, Barber fumbled just once every 112 carries from 2004 to 2006, making the Pro Bowl all three years and twice leading the league in scrimmage yards.

 Lewis noticed. Sometime after his 2,000-yard season in 2003 with the Baltimore Ravens , Lewis says he saw a TV special about Barber's adherence to the high-and-tight lifestyle and adopted it as his own. After fumbling once every 46 carries from 2000 to 2003, Lewis only fumbled once per 90 carries for the rest of his career.

 All these years later, Lewis is still such a believer in the importance of high and tight that he scours the internet for proof of its efficacy. Lewis says he was watching footage of current Ravens running back Derrick Henry's workouts before the 2025 season and felt Henry was pumping the ball too much when he ran. Henry fumbled in each of that season's first three games.

 This year, Lewis says he saw more of a high-and-tight ball security emphasis in Henry's offseason workout footage. Through nine weeks, Henry fumbled once only in 175 carries.

 

 Punch specialists 

 The Bears drafted Tillman in 2003, but his patented punch didn't become well-known until 14 years ago this week when Tillman forced four fumbles in the same game. What's standard practice today barely existed during Barber's and Lewis' heydays.

 Today's ball carriers have to contend with punch specialists on just about every defense. In Baltimore, there's Marlon Humphrey . In Atlanta, there's safety Jessie Bates III , who seems to jar a ball loose every weekend. In San Francisco, there's All-Pro linebacker Fred Warner , who led the league with four forced fumbles through the season's first seven games and is even more renowned for forcing fumbles in practice.

 

 "I think obviously they all understand what it requires to protect the ball anytime they're practicing against me," Warner said, "which in turn is obviously going…

title: Jeff Hafley calls out Dolphins' discipline after 11 penalties
summary: Jeff Hafley said penalties helped negate what was arguably Miami's best defensive performance of the season.
full_text:
MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. -- The Detroit Lions deserve credit for their win Sunday. They have a good defensive front and can play as well as anybody, Jeff Hafley said.

 The Miami Dolphins coach also thinks his team deserves its share of the blame, too.

 The Dolphins committed a season-high 11 penalties in Sunday's 19-9 loss, including one that wiped out a 51-yard completion in the second quarter. Hafley said the penalties put Miami into negative game scripts and essentially negated arguably the best performance of the season from the team's defense.

 "We had some missed assignments yesterday. We had some technique errors," he said. "We had a chance to hit some (plays) where we just missed that we had been hitting. And then most importantly, the penalties put us in a lot of hard positions where we were in a lot of get-back-on-track situations where it's hard to stay balanced."

 Eight of the team's 11 accepted penalties were against its offense, including five holding calls. Miami was also flagged for three false starts and an offensive pass interference.

 The infractions penalized the Dolphins' offense 65 yards and nullified another 70. As a result, their average conversion distance Sunday was 10.9 yards, the highest single-game mark in the NFL this season.

 Excluding first-and-10 plays, 32 of Miami's 50 offensive plays faced a distance of at least 10 yards to gain a first down -- 24 of which were behind the sticks.

 "It's hard to call anything (when you're behind the sticks) and that's where we have to be better," Hafley said. "We have to stay on track. It's OK to have it be second-and-eight or it's OK to have it be second-and-seven or -six. It's not OK to have it second-and-20 or first-and-20. It's just we can't play the game like that.

 "So again, give (the Lions) credit, but a lot of it was self-inflicted yesterday and we have to be better."

 Hafley said when holding calls, in particular, are that frequent in a game, players have to be mindful of their hand placement, eyes and footwork -- although the quality of the players they're attempting to block is also a factor.

 All-Pro center Aaron Brewer , who was flagged twice for holding Sunday, said players are typically aware of certain officiating crews' tendencies to call games tightly and have to make necessary adjustments in those situations.

 "Once it's started, you know what type of game it is," he said. "So you're just trying to give each other a heads up and try to do as much as you can to limit the calls."

 Quarterback Malik Willis was critical of the team's self-inflicted wounds, which he said have been a recurring issue.

 A taunting call on cornerback  JuJu Brents  extended an eventual touchdown drive for the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 1, while an illegal shift penalty on rookie wide receiver Chris Bell wiped out a game-tying touchdown against the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 3. Bell also was flagged for illegal touching against the Minnesota Vikings in Week 4 -- a play in which he stepped out of bounds and was the first player to touch the ball on what would've been a 68-yard touchdown catch for him.

 In Sunday's game, Willis found rookie wide receiver Kevin Coleman Jr . for a 51-yard completion to the Lions' 19-yard line, but the play was called back for holding on rookie tight end Will Kacmarek . Miami could've taken the lead with points on that drive but instead gained just 2 yards after the penalty and was forced to punt.

 Detroit took the lead for good on the ensuing drive.

 "It was one of those situations where the last few weeks I've been telling you we need to have all 11 out of 11 doing the job instead of 9 out of 11 or 8 out of 11," Willis said. "And it just showed up more today in the penalty factor. It's unfortunate. We can't keep saying the same things like, 'Oh, we got to get better, we got to get better.'

 "We've got to continue to fight to actually do it and make sure that shows up on game day."

 Despite their performance Sunday, the Dolphins' 61 accepted penalties this season rank 17th-most in the NFL; they committed only 11 combined penalties in Weeks 7 and 8.

 Hafley said the hope is that Sunday's game was "a one-off" but insisted his team can't make excuses and must work to strengthen areas it can control.

 "We can't have that many penalties. I mean, we're not going to be efficient to play the game that way and we're not going to win if we continue to have penalties like that," he said. "Since the bye week, it had been better, but it wasn't good enough yesterday. So again, let's look at what we did lately and let's correct it.

 "And when you look at those penalties, it wasn't like it was the same penalty, the same guy holding, the same reason he was holding. It just accumulated over time and it kind of snowballed on us. But we need to get that corrected. I'm not going to make excuses and pretend that's OK. We need to be better than that."

title: Gibbs, Allen, JSN and more Knockout league pickups for Week 10
summary: As the number of teams shrink, the number of stars available in Knockout leagues grows. Here are the ones to get.
full_text:
The super-teams are coming.

 

 Ten weeks in -- and with nine teams remaining in full-season Knockout leagues -- the strategy shifts. Weekly upside is becoming increasingly important, as rosters become ever-richer in talent. Aiming only for statistical floor is no longer getting it done quite as effectively. You need those big scores in order to stay afloat now.

 Additionally, FAB (Free Agent Budget) funds are shrinking, perhaps dramatically in your league. Take our two in-house Knockout leagues, for example. In one league, 36% of collective FAB funds remain. In the other, it's 41%. Among those 18 managers, eight have less than 30% remaining.

 If you're in a good position in terms of FAB, we've reached the stage where you're now in command of the free-agent market. Bully your competition for top free agents, examining likely competitors for newly available superstars and strategizing your bids dependent upon their resources. Pinpoint ideal times to acquire the superstars you need, rather than tossing FAB at each and every superstar who comes available.

 That's why the FAB recommendations in this space in each coming week will be exactly that: Recommendations. If you need to open your FAB wallet wider to get the player you need, do it. If your competition won't be as aggressive in pursuit of a specific player or position, hold back.

 To the point about optimal pickup times, here are a few thoughts to consider with some of this season's most fantasy-relevant teams:

 Green Bay Packers : They roster the league's No. 3 scoring quarterback (No. 4 if going by fantasy points per game)in Jordan Love , and Nos. 3 and 5 (Nos. 7 and 8 by points per game) wide receivers in Christian Watson and Matthew Golden , but the toughest part of their entire 2026 schedule is upcoming. They've got the Minnesota Vikings -- the league's No. 2 defense (in yards allowed; they lead the league in points allowed) -- up next, then a Week 11 bye, then the Los Angeles Rams on the road. Those matchup downside points present opportunities to get Packers via their managers being knocked out, but that might also prove the trend over each of the next three weeks rather than merely exiting Week 10 alone.

 Consider that among the Packers' five opponents throughout Weeks 13-17 in Knockout leagues, all but the Buffalo Bills are below league-average in passer rating allowed, setting them up for strong finishes. Target Packers as free agents accordingly, but amplifying your FAB amounts across each of the next three weeks -- remembering that any might still only make it to free agency in your league once in that time -- is a sound strategy.

 Atlanta Falcons : Mentioned last week, they're especially relevant because of their superstar running back, Bijan Robinson . Remember, the Falcons are among the teams off during Week 11 "bye-mageddon," then they return to a miserable road matchup against the Vikings. There's an excellent chance that Knockout managers will get a crack at a Robinson bid coming off Weeks 11 or 12.

 San Francisco 49ers : The 49ers have their bye in the rearview, but they've got a pair of tough-as-nails matchups in Weeks 11-12 in the Vikings and Seattle Seahawks , the league's Nos. 2 and 1 defenses. There's also a Week 14 game against the No. 3 defense in the Rams. The 49ers' schedule after (@LAC, @KC, PHI) isn't as high-level as the aforementioned Packers', but the 49ers also have three potentially elite Knockout pieces in Christian McCaffrey , George Kittle and Brock Purdy , all of whom rank among their positions' top four in fantasy points per game. Budgeting FAB for prospective 49ers exiting Weeks 11-12 is a wise move.

 The 20 most-knocked-out players exiting Week 9 
 Note that FAB recommendations are in three tiers: "% OF FAB TO BID (ENFORCE)" is a low-end recommendation, if you don't necessarily need the player but don't want him gifted to the competition. "% OF FAB TO BID (MEDIAN)" is the recommended bid for a team with average needs at that position. "% OF FAB TO BID (AGGRESSIVE)" is advised for teams thin at that specific spot. 

 
 My favorite pickup of the week 
 Jahmyr Gibbs , RB, Detroit Lions (10.1% Knocked out, 21st overall, RB9): Just beneath the chart cut-off above, you'll find Gibbs, in one of those rare weeks where he was bumped in more than 10% of Knockout leagues. His Lions' seemingly inexplicable season lows of 19 points and 270 total yards against the Miami Dolphins resulted in a season-worst 13.4 fantasy points for the running back. This gives many the chance to pick up a superstar that we might not see again in 2026. To be clear, I am not remotely concerned about his Week 9, as Gibbs remains No. 1 among running backs in fantasy points per game (26.2) and rushing share (77%), third in snap rate (77%), fourth in target share (17%) and sixth in goal-line carries (7). Feel free to be even louder with your FAB bid than you might've been exiting his Week 6 bye. Recommended FAB bid: 28-68% of your full-season FAB budget.

 Go get 'em 
 

 Josh Allen , QB, Buffalo Bills (13.1% Knocked out, 6th overall, QB2): I'm not generally one to pay up for quarterbacks at this stage of the Knockout season, but Allen is a rare bird. Even with his four sub-20-point fantasy games in his past six, he's still the position's leader in points per game (25.1) and he has more 20- (23), 25- (13) and 30-point (10) fantasy games than any other quarterback since the beginning of 2024. Allen's remaining schedule isn't top-shelf, but it also doesn't have a singular scary matchup (with the possible exception of the Packers in Week 14, which nevertheless has the chance to be a throw-throw-throw game). Recommended FAB bid: 21-40%.

 Jonathan Taylor , RB, Indianapolis Colts (11.7% Knocked out, 12th overall, RB4): I'm still a believer because of his trade possibility, and more so than I was last week considering the dearth of clear-cut free agent adds in this week's market. Taylor's prospects of landing in fantasy-friendly backfields of the New England Patriots , Vikings or (gasp) Packers are strong enough to make him worth a slightly beefed-up bid entering this particular week. If you're in decent enough position with your running backs but could stand to put a final bow on your backfield and you've got excess funds to take a big dice roll, Taylor is a good acquisition. Recommended FAB bid: 18-58%.

 George Pickens , WR, Dallas Cowboys (14.6% Knocked out, 3rd overall, WR2), and Jameson Williams , WR, Detroit Lions (13.8% Knocked out, 5th overall, WR3): They're No. 2 wideouts in their respective top-eight (going by passing yards per game) offenses, meaning the stats should be there at times but perhaps on more of a risk/reward scale. If wide receiver depth, rather than a stable collection of high-floor candidates, is what you need, either is worth your while. Recommended FAB bids: 12-28% for Pickens, 11-26% for Williams.

 Worthy, with worries 
 

 Zay Flowers , WR, Baltimore Ravens (12.9% Knocked out, 7th overall, WR4), and Justin Jefferson , WR, Minnesota Vikings (11.1% Knocked out, 16th overall, WR6): Flowers and Jefferson are No. 1s for their teams, but their quarterback situations have cast doubts about their ability to meet their weekly statistical ceilings moving forward. Flowers has totaled 5.6 fantasy points the past two weeks while Joe Fagnano has largely handled the quarterbacking duties, while Jefferson has averaged only 10.5 fantasy points despite nine targets (again, on average) the past three weeks. In Flowers' case, at least, the acquisition of Jacoby Brissett improves his fantasy prospects from where we were a week ago at this time, while Jefferson having his bye week in the rearview is a help. Recommended bids: 9-19% for Flowers, 11-30% for Jefferson.

title: Commanders running low on time to 'put it all together'
summary: Dan Quinn knows it's repetitive to say the Commanders are close, but now they're painted into a corner.
full_text:
LANDOVER, Md. -- Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels didn't hesitate. After yet another loss, and after falling three games under .500, Daniels -- and his teammates -- know that their season is slipping away.

 So, when asked Sunday night if he worried they had enough time to turn it around, he quickly replied, "Yeah. Next week is a must-win."

 Earlier, teammate K'Lavon Chaisson said, "Yeah, damn right" when asked a similar question.

 Unfortunately for the Commanders, it's a familiar place. But it's also indicative of their season. At 2-5-1, they're three games behind the New York Giants (5-2-1) in the NFC East.

 Mathematically the Commanders remain alive, but with nine games remaining, any realistic hope the team has for a strong finish likely begins and ends vs. the Giants on Thursday (8:15 p.m. ET, Prime Video). A win and they would be two games back with eight to play and own the tiebreaker -- if that eventually mattered.

 "We all know how badly we need this," Washington coach Dan Quinn said. "Everyone in this building understands that."

 Another loss would drop them to 7-18-1 since the start of last season and likely intensify the speculation by analysts over Quinn's future. Owner Josh Harris has not publicly commented on Quinn's job. Quinn said he regularly meets with Harris before and after games and also on Mondays.

 But in training camp, one team source said what has been repeated by others at various points: "It's a results business."

 And the results need to improve. Washington has now played five one-score games; the Commanders are 1-3-1 in those games -- and 3-7-1 since the start of 2025. In 2024, when they went 12-5, Washington was 8-4 in one-score games -- but that included a four-game winning streak at season's end.

 The Commanders were in another one Sunday before losing 20-13 to the Rams. They had the ball last, drove to the Rams' 32-yard line with eight seconds left, but two failed plays ended the threat.

 They lost 23-17 in Week 6 at San Francisco, failing in the red zone -- a touchdown was nullified by a face mask penalty -- and again on the last series when they reached the 28 with 22 seconds to play.

 "We get in those moments and we have to finish," Daniels said. "We have to make plays; that's for myself, that's for the O-line, for the running backs, receivers, the playcalls, and everything like that. We have to make plays. Regardless of what they call, we have to make plays."

 They have a first-time playcaller in David Blough, but they also commit penalties or fail to execute plays properly. Perhaps no play summed it up like the final play in overtime in the last meeting against New York. Washington drove to the Giants' 24-yard line in overtime with 50 seconds remaining.

 But the Commanders ran one play, snapping the ball at 12 seconds -- the play took too long to be relayed, from the coach to the players and then they sent subs, taking more time. Daniels failed to throw the ball away, resulting in a sack and, with no timeouts left, the end of the game.

 It has added up to Quinn repeating the same lines each week, about seeking consistency and being able to play a complete game.

 He said it again Monday.

 "What I do know is that, man, do we have to put it all together," Quinn said. "There have been halves and quarters and good plays. That's what I'm looking for most: consistent football."

 And then this: "Yes, I am tired of [saying] it and I'm not going to back off it."

 The run game, which they had hoped would become a staple, has been inconsistent. In three of the past five games, the running backs haven't surpassed 50 yards. Washington's backs rank 24th in total yards and 23rd in yards per carry. When quarterback runs are included the Commanders rank ninth in yards per carry and 11th in yards per game.

 They have shown progress: In the past 10 quarters, the defense has allowed just 33 points combined, forced five turnovers and held opponents to 34.2% conversion on third downs compared to 40% for the season.

 But that has resulted in only a 1-2 record in that stretch.

 "You see the progress," Chaisson said. "The results are obviously the main thing, but we're getting closer and closer. We're making great strides, but we just have to find a way to come out with a win."

 But that's the problem: They haven't done so and now their season teeters once again. This is nothing new for the franchise: In the last eight seasons -- only four of which have occurred with Harris as owner -- Washington has been two or more games under .500 through eight games on six occasions.

 "They know I'm agitated about it, to make sure it's the whole game," Quinn said. "Playing and being competitive is not what we stand for."

 And it has left them in a bad spot.

 "I've been in the league a long time and seen a lot of crazy scenarios," Quinn said, "so you never know how the season plays out. I'll refrain from one-game statements, but I will say we need this game."
